For Bykhovchenko and his teammates, including veterans with multiple amputations, finishing the event marked a milestone in their recovery. It also carried a broader message about a country still fighting after more than 4 1/2 years of war.
“It means a lot to be here and show the world what a veteran of the Russia-Ukraine war is,” endurance athlete and team member Oleh Tserkovnyy said. “We want our actions to inspire the world.”

After leaving active duty, Tserkovnyy dedicated his time to helping veterans recover from serious injuries. In Valencia, he stood over Bykhovchenko, shouting words of encouragement as his teammate worked through the circuits.
Some team members were relatively new to sports and relied on trainers who volunteered hours to help them get into shape.
Yasia Shandrii, a fitness trainer in Kyiv, worked with Bykhovchenko ahead of the competition.
“The guys have quite a variety of amputations – double lower-limb amputations, single-leg amputations, high arm amputations, and below-the-knee amputations,” Shandrii said.
Bykhovchenko's training partner, Oleksandr Dashko, who had his left leg amputated due to a combat injury, said sports provided a welcome distraction from the war in Ukraine.

“Every meeting with your friends is about the war. The news on Instagram is about the war. The war is everywhere,” he said. “When I’m doing sports, when you work hard, not just during training but for several hours afterward, you forget about the war.”
AP writer Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Ukraine contributed to this report
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Iranian leader threatens immediate response to potential attack, and other Mideast news
summary: Iran's supreme leader has threatened an immediate response to any potential attack from the U.S. or Israel
story: Iran's supreme leader has threatened an immediate response to any potential attack from the U.S. or Israel
Iran's supreme leader threatened an immediate response to a potential attack as diplomatic efforts continue in an effort to reduce the threat of a return to all-out war.
Meanwhile, Iran's foreign minister said a proposal has been reached that would fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz in just two days as talks with mediators remain on track.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here.

Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said that “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel should face an immediate response without geographic limits, the official IRNA news agency said.

State media said that Khamenei, who still hasn't been seen publicly since the war began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, made the comments while meeting with the military. He also called for an updated list of potential U.S. and Israeli targets.

Khamenei became supreme leader after the first wave of strikes killed his father and other high-ranking officials. He has been meeting with a series of senior officials in recent weeks, according to state media.
Iran’s top diplomat says that a new proposal has been reached with mediators that would shorten the time to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to two days.

Last month, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi floated a proposal to reopen the critical waterway within a week if the U.S. agreed to lift its blockade of Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian assets and waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, among other conditions. That was rejected.

In an interview with Qatar-based broadcaster Al Jazeera, Araghchi also said that Iran isn't planning to meet with U.S. officials, but said that recent American efforts toward “broader dialogue” are considered a positive step.

He said that Iran has carefully reviewed a letter that was sent days earlier by U.S. Vice President JD Vance. And he said a decision on whether negotiations will be direct or indirect would be made “once Washington agrees to Iran’s conditions."
Saudi Arabia's vice minister of foreign affairs, Waleed ElKhereiji, said that the message from the region is that it wants a return to peace.
Efforts were being made to prevent a military escalation and reach an agreement that ends the Iran crisis, ElKhereiji said at a security forum in Bahrain.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said at the same event that an escalation in the region would be extremely destructive.
“We are very confident that … the second round will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere,” he said.
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani said that border security with Jordan is a shared responsibility and a high-level meeting is expected next month to discuss arrangements.
Speaking at the security forum in Bahrain, al-Shibani said there are no “skirmishes” between the countries. The comments came after Jordanian strikes in Syria raised tensions between the neighbors.

Jordan said that the strikes last week killed 20 militants with the Islamic State extremist group, but acknowledged that civilians also had been killed. Syrian authorities reported seven people killed, most of them women and children.
Separately, al-Shibani said that Syria is in discussions to evaluate joining the Mecca Pact, the Saudi-led defense alliance that includes Turkey and Pakistan.
“Whether Syria joins or not, Syria thinks the region is in dire need of a structure that protects its security,” he said.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a US election
summary: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. general election
story: Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope in history to vote in a U.S. general election
VATICAN CITY -- Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election.
The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.
Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen” and has done so “whenever he was eligible to do so,” the Holy See press office said.
The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.
“The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” it added.

This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they’re also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin’s retirement.

Leo’s vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk’s office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude’s, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.
The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.
The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.
Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants.
Earlier this year, Trump called Leo “weak” and captive to the “radical left.”

Responding to Trump’s public rebuke, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria: “I’m not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for.”
“I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems,” he said.
The public dispute has subsided in recent months.
AP editor Holly Meyer contributed from Nashville, Tenn.

title: Netherlands coast guard rescues 38 people adrift in a rubber boat
summary: Dozens of people adrift at sea in a rubber boat have been rescued off the coast of the southern Netherlands
story: Dozens of people adrift at sea in a rubber boat have been rescued off the coast of the southern Netherlands
THE HAGUE, Netherlands -- Dozens of people adrift at sea in a rubber boat were rescued early Saturday off the coast of the southern Netherlands, in one of the first such interceptions in the country.

The Marechaussee military police and Netherlands coast guard rescued the boat early in the morning and towed it to shore. It had no motor and was drifting off the coast of Zeeland province near the town of Breskens, some 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Amsterdam, Marechaussee spokesperson Doron Wallin said.

There were 38 people on the boat, including two who were detained on suspicion of people smuggling, Wallin told The Associated Press in a telephone interview. No one was wearing a life vest. It was not immediately clear where they came from or where they were heading.
Those on board were taken to dry land, checked for signs of hypothermia and then taken to another location while their nationalities and migration status are investigated.
“We don’t know where they came from — France, the Netherlands or Belgium — and we don’t know where the boat was heading,” Wallin said.
In recent years, tens of thousands of migrants have sought to cross the narrow sea dividing France from the United Kingdom, but it is very unusual for a boatload to be discovered off the Dutch coast.

Earlier this year, the U.K. and French governments signed a new multimillion-euro deal aimed at reducing the number of migrants crossing the English Channel, with increased police patrols and enhanced surveillance in northern France.
“These are things you usually see in France and Belgium. We rarely see it here in the Netherlands before today,” Wallin said.

title: Protests erupt around a top court in Poland after its president is suspended
summary: Anti-government protesters denounce the tribunal president's suspension.
story: Anti-government protesters denounce the tribunal president's suspension.

WARSAW, Poland -- Hundreds of anti-government protesters rallied overnight outside Poland's Constitutional Tribunal to denounce the suspension of its president, a move they blame on the country's pro-European government.
Police said they detained three protesters after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Saturday, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal despite the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building.
Nawrocki said that a “breach of Poland’s constitutional order” had taken place and invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution.

“Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to the Polish president, told The Associated Press.
The government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it acted to restore the independence of the judiciary.

The government is a broad coalition made up of Tusk's centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Third Way and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Third Way and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday, while Tusk did not attend.
The president’s camp is hoping the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority.

The protests over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal are likely to sharpen the battle between Poland's pro-European government and its opponents, chiefly the main opposition party, national-conservative Law and Justice, or PiS.

Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Reforms introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland.

Tusk's pro-European government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki.

On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal's website announced the suspension of court president Bogdan Święczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński and far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building.

The government says Święczkowski repeatedly broke the law and jeopardized the tribunal's work. Święczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal.

“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking.
Politicians from PiS have criticized Święczkowski’s suspension.

“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X late Friday. “That is why I call for resistance that will be loud, firm, solidary and fearless.”

title: Who pays for a $1B riot? Europe looks past rioters to their parents
summary: France's Senate has approved a controversial measure that could deduct riot-related damages from a family’s housing aid
story: France's Senate has approved a controversial measure that could deduct riot-related damages from a family’s housing aid
PARIS -- In France, the bill for a riot could soon be paid from a family’s housing aid. Some people in a violent crowd could be made to pay for windows they never broke.

France’s Senate approved the measure 229-105 this week, less than two weeks after cost-of-living protests spiraled into the country’s worst unrest in years, leading to estimated damage of over 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion). In one weekend, police arrested nearly 2,400 people; authorities say thousands of shops were looted or damaged. Fire gutted Limoges’ 19th-century city hall.
France is not alone: Across Western Europe, governments are reaching past the rioters — to their parents, and to the apps that carry the call to the streets.
And it may not be over. Spanish fact-checker Maldita.es has found calls for Halloween protests in 46 cities in at least nine European countries. Some urge looting.
Officials say the aim is to prevent the next riot and pay for the last. Critics warn that widening responsibility could punish people who committed no violence and make others afraid to protest.

In France, anyone who knowingly joins a group preparing violence could be made to pay up to 10,000 euros ($11,200) for what others destroy. So could anyone who knowingly stays after police order a violent crowd to disperse, for damage done afterward.
Collecting is the hard part, a Senate report says: Offenders often have little money, or income the law protects from seizure.
The bill would open another source: money the state pays to help families live.

French law already generally holds parents liable for damage caused by their children under 18. Under the bill, once a court ruling is final, the money could be deducted from family allowances and housing aid. Senators added the RSA, France’s minimum-income benefit, worth up to about 650 euros ($730) a month for a single person, and even the back-to-school allowance families get for supplies. A minimum amount would remain protected for living expenses.
Communist Sen. Fabien Gay cited monthly deductions of 57 euros ($63) from a household receiving RSA. At that rate, repaying 10,000 euros would take nearly 15 years.

Supporters say victims deserve compensation and taxpayers shouldn’t carry the cost. One large shop window can cost tens of thousands of euros to replace. After riots in 2023, insurers paid 793 million euros ($888 million) on 16,400 claims, according to France Assureurs, the insurers’ federation.
Human rights groups urged lawmakers to reject the bill, warning it could discourage peaceful protest and hurt families who depend on benefits.
Seizing those payments “could have disastrous consequences for the poorest,” Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said in a statement.
The far right backed the bill in the conservative-led Senate. Next comes the National Assembly, where no bloc has a majority.

Seizing rioters’ benefits was long an idea of Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally party. Now the government has made it its own, and she leads the polls for next spring’s presidential election.
French students call a protest that shuts their school a “blocus,” or blockade. In Barcelona, it became a hashtag.

TikTok posts under the tag called people to Catalonia Square on Saturday, Oct. 24, and QR codes sent them to WhatsApp or Telegram channels, Catalonia’s interior chief, Núria Parlon, told Cadena SER radio.

On paper, it was a protest over education. There was no route, Parlon said. No banners. No manifesto. Just groups of 10 to 15 young men looting stores, burning trash containers and smashing bus stops.
When police arrived, the looters scattered, said an AP journalist who was at the scene.
Police reported 130 arrests, including 76 minors, according to Spanish news agency EFE.

Some TikTok accounts promoting the gatherings disappeared, while others advertised new Halloween protests, Maldita.es reported. In one Telegram group, messages urged people to wear masks and gloves and wait to be told of a shop “without police.”

In Italy, the argument starts with another family. “Behind that shop window there is a family that has invested a lifetime of sacrifices,” Premier Giorgia Meloni said Oct. 20, announcing a security decree after looting in Milan.
Her principle fits in three Italian words: “Chi rompe paga” — you break it, you pay. “And if the one who breaks it is a minor,” she said, “their parents pay.”
Parents now face fines of up to 1,000 euros ($1,120), doubled for a repeat offense, unless they prove they couldn’t have stopped their child. They can be made to pay for damage.

Holding parents accountable may help, said Claudio Bertolotti, director of START InSight, a security research firm, but “fines alone are unlikely to deter teenagers driven by peer pressure or a desire for group recognition.”
Organizing protest violence, even online, now carries four to 12 years in prison.
Telegram and WhatsApp “must shut down such channels when they incite violence,” Parlon said.

Telegram spokesperson Remi Vaughn told The Associated Press the company supports peaceful speech and protest, but “calls for violence, vandalism and theft are explicitly forbidden and are removed whenever discovered.”
He said Telegram had removed such calls linked to protests in Madrid.
TikTok and Meta, which owns WhatsApp, did not respond to requests for comment.
Telegram closed a Barcelona group promoting Halloween looting, but a replacement drew more than 2,000 members, Spanish media reported.

The French bill would let authorities demand removal of certain illegal calls to violence or looting without prior court approval. If they stay up 24 hours, they could order the web addresses blocked. Those decisions could be challenged in court.
The United States is going the other way. Its law generally shields platforms from civil liability for users’ posts, and the Trump administration calls Europe’s rules censorship.

Britain shows the limits of takedowns. After three girls were killed in Southport in 2024, false claims spread online and riots followed. A parliamentary committee found that algorithms amplified harmful material, much of it legal.
Under France’s bill, money meant to house and raise children could help pay for a looted shop.
Associated Press journalists Sylvie Corbet, Joseph Wilson, Hernan Muñoz, Giada Zampano, Kaitlyn Huamani and Jill Lawless contributed to this report.

title: Flávio Bolsonaro’s departure to the US sparks a flurry of viral Brazilian memes
summary: Political memes have exploded in Brazil since Sunday’s election that saw underdog President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, who responded to his loss by fleeing the country
story: Political memes have exploded in Brazil since Sunday’s election that saw underdog President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, who responded to his loss by fleeing the country

RIO DE JANEIRO -- Political memes have exploded in Brazil since Sunday’s election that saw President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat his opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, who responded to his loss by fleeing the country.

Social media played an outsized role in Lula's win, with the unprecedented mobilization of the country's left on digital networks a critical factor in how Sunday's vote played out. Bolsonaro, who is under investigation for money laundering and corruption, said on Monday that he had no intentions of leaving Brazil, then departed the country shortly thereafter.

The extraordinary sequence of events kicked Brazil’s famed meme-making machine into overdrive, turbo-charged by artificial intelligence. The posts got hundreds of thousands of likes and shares on multiple social media platforms.

“Brazilians treat serious questions with lightness, irony and humor,” said Carolina Terra, a professor at the University of Sao Paulo’s communications and arts school. “Everything that is extremely relevant and important, whether political or not, tends to turn into memes that become viral.”
“Where is Flávio?” many on the internet asked, depicting former President Jair Bolsonaro’s eldest son as Waldo, the famous character of a children’s puzzle book series.
One meme titled “Which costume would you use to flee?” presented Bolsonaro in a range of outfits to resemble a Rastafarian, Mario, former soccer player Ronaldo and John Lennon, among others.
Another showed “Flyvio Bolsonaro” as the captain of a “Fly 22 Airlines” – a reference to the number of Brazilians who voted for him punched into the country’s electronic voting machines.

The 45-year-old Trump ally landed in Miami on Wednesday and posted a letter in which he declared himself the “true president-elect of Brazil” — a term he later softened to “leader” — and said the vote was fraudulent, without offering evidence. He compared himself — among other figures — to Charles de Gaulle, who led the French resistance to the Nazi occupation of France from London during World War II.

The letter, posted on X, also used a coat of arms referring to Brazil as “United States of Brazil” instead of the “Federative Republic of Brazil” as the country has been known since 1967. It also misspelled Brazil in Portuguese, using the English spelling with a “z” rather than the Portuguese “Brasil.”

Some Brazilians received an “invitation” to a mock inauguration of Bolsonaro as the president of the “United States of Brazil,” signed by cartoon character Goofy and with Disneyland in the background.
Other internet users declared themselves all sorts of things — from the King of Soccer, a reference to Pelé, to Brazil’s president.
Some social media users parodied the slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.

Other memes drew inspiration from famous movies. An AI-modified version of the poster for “Catch me if you can” replaced Leonardo DiCaprio with Bolsonaro and Tom Hanks with Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who issued the order canceling Bolsonaro’s passports on Sunday night.

Another tampered with the poster for “Home Alone” and pictured Flávio and his brother Eduardo — who also lives in the U.S. — as the thieves in the background, and a shocked-looking Jair Bolsonaro in a red jumper at the forefront.
One referenced the movie “Dark Horse” — a biopic and propaganda film about Jair Bolsonaro.

Flávio Bolsonaro is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion for receiving millions of dollars from a disgraced banker to finance the movie. The meme depicted the poster for an imagined “Dark Horse 2” — showing Bolsonaro on a horse bearing a presidential sash galloping on a highway toward an airport. “The fugitive is different” read the poster, referencing the elder Bolsonaro’s similar departure to Florida after he lost the 2022 election and also refused to concede. He was later sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.

Fewer memes circulated in Brazil during this year's election campaign due to a lack of opportunities ahead of the first round because there were no debates involving the two main candidates, said Viktor Chagas, a professor at Fluminense Federal University and coordinator of the Colab research group that analyzes political memes.
In the lead up to the runoff vote, the two debates did generate more memes but the three-week period was principally characterized by high political tension, Chagas said.
“The memes regarding Bolsonaro’s departure to the U.S. have a cathartic element” for Lula's supporters, said Chagas. “The idea is: Now that we’re back on track, so to speak, we can laugh together.”
Follow AP’s coverage of Latin America and the Caribbean at https://apnews.com/hub/latin-america

title: Mexico comes alive during annual Day of the Dead celebrations
summary: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations
story: Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles, and painted faces fill Mexico's streets during the Day of the Dead celebrations

MEXICO CITY -- Bright orange marigolds, glowing candles and faces painted like the elegant skeletons known as catrinas fill the streets of Mexico every year during the country's Day of the Dead celebrations.
Festivities begin in October and lead up to Nov. 1 and 2, when the souls of deceased loved ones are believed to temporarily return to earth to reunite with their families.

No one knows when the first observance took place, but it is rooted in agriculture-related beliefs from Mexico’s pre-Hispanic era. Catholic traditions were incorporated into the celebration after the Spanish conquest in 1521.

Today, celebrations are marked by massive parades running along Mexico City's main avenue. Streets, businesses and markets are cloaked in orange Mexican marigold flowers, or cempasuchil, believed to light the path of the dead back to earth with their bright colors. Traditional pan de muerto, or bread of the dead, lines the display cases of bakeries.
Families decorate altars to their loved ones in their homes, placing treats, food and mezcal as offerings next to photos of their loved ones.
On the night of Nov. 1, families gather at cemeteries across the country to reconnect with their dead just as their ancestors have done for centuries.

But as the tradition and the Mexican capital have increasingly gained an international spotlight, and states like Oaxaca and Michoacan have seen an influx of tourists, some regions have experienced tensions around overtourism.

In Mexico City, many locals are skeptical of an annual parade featuring floats decorated with catrinas. The procession was created for the 2015 James Bond film “Spectre” and later incorporated into the city’s celebrations, though it was not previously part of the tradition.

In Janitzio, a small island on a lake in the central state of Michoacan, where celebrations were recognized by UNESCO as Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008, authorities closed the pantheon to tourists for the first time this year. The closure came after the island's community council reported the collapse of damaged tombs, crosses and parts of the cemetery's perimeter wall because of the flood of people.
Only local families and friends of those buried there would be allowed in.

title: This mayor crusaded against cartels in Mexico. Now his assassination haunts his city
summary: Mayor Grecia Quiroz navigates the streets of Uruapan with heavy security, nearly a year after her partner, Carlos Manzo, was assassinated
story: Mayor Grecia Quiroz navigates the streets of Uruapan with heavy security, nearly a year after her partner, Carlos Manzo, was assassinated

URUAPAN, Mexico -- Three armored cars and two military trucks packed with armed bodyguards carry Mayor Grecia Quiroz through the streets of Uruapan, the Mexican city where her partner was gunned down during Day of the Dead celebrations nearly a year ago.

Carlos Alberto Manzo gained a reputation as a mayor crusading against cartels, a thorn in the side of criminals and political powerbrokers. But a year later — even as Quiroz has succeeded him and vowed to continue his fight — the targeted assassination casts a pall over a region long haunted by violence.

“No one can fill his void,” said Quiroz, who is escorted around the clock by 60 federally appointed bodyguards. “I’m extremely worried that if tomorrow, something happens to me, what will (my children) do without a father and a mother?”

Manzo was among at least 13 mayors killed across Mexico in the two years since Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took office, according to an Associated Press tally based on official reports. That compares with 23 sitting mayors killed during the previous administration's six years in office, according to civil society groups.
The killings present a challenge for Sheinbaum as the Trump administration presses her government to crack down on cartels and root out corruption in local governments.

Political violence has long been part of Mexico’s cartel conflict, but it rarely touches the highest ranks of government. Cartels instead target local leaders, either corrupting them or killing those who stand in their way. Such killings often silence voices that threaten or interfere with cartel profits, said Miguel Meza, a researcher at the investigative organization Narcopoliticos.

In Uruapan, 250 miles (400 km) west of Mexico City, Manzo's killing has sowed fear and uncertainty within his grassroots opposition Sombrero Movement, where he's gone from leader to martyr. The aftermath has fueled a bitter political fight dividing Mexico's central Michoacan state over who was behind his death. At the same time, the city has been marked with a recent burst of violence as some criticize Quiroz for failing to carry on her partner's fight against crime.
“They didn’t just kill the mayor, they killed the person who was leading this fight against cartels, a symbolic leader,” Meza said.
Those close to Manzo long feared that his campaign against criminal groups would inevitably end exactly as it did: with a bullet in his chest.

In Michoacan, where cartels often wield more influence than the government, Manzo gained political notoriety for taking the fight against cartels into his own hands and also openly challenged Mexico’s ruling party, Morena, up until the week of his death.

He was often criticized for heavy-handed tactics that became as central to his image as mayor as the white sombrero always perched on his head. That included publicly instructing police to use lethal force on criminals resisting arrest or attacking civilians. He personally directed patrols, searches and arrests, urged parents to report their children's criminal activity and publicized confrontations with criminals on his social media.
“We’re fighting to clean up this filth that’s killing us all,” Manzo said in one video.

The public assassination of Manzo in the city’s crowded main plaza, cloaked in marigold flowers, shocked the country on a day when many criminal groups quietly set down their weapons as families honor their dead.
It also triggered a political feud marked by rival factions slinging accusations at one another of exploiting Manzo’s death to profit politically ahead of local elections.

Federal and state authorities have blamed the killing on one of Mexico’s most powerful cartels, the Jalisco New Generation Cartel, or CJNG, one of the more than 20 criminal groups designated foreign terrorist organizations by the Trump administration. Quiroz accused state officials in Sheinbaum’s party who were long at odds with Manzo and Quiroz's political movement and criminal groups of being behind the death.
As Quiroz prepared the city for Day of the Dead this week, she said she was haunted by the memory of Manzo meticulously preparing the previous year's celebration.
“It's all come back to me like a countdown of what happened that last week he was alive," she said. "He poured his body and soul into this.”
Authorities have detained 34 people in connection with Manzo's killing as state prosecutors have described a complex conspiracy that they say extended to Manzo’s inner circle.

Among those detained are seven of the mayor’s bodyguards who were with him when he was attacked, members of his government accused of leaking his movements, and Manzo’s own godson, who is accused of helping plan his assassination, according to prosecutors.

On Thursday, prosecutors announced the detention of the city's current secretary of welfare on accusations of obstruction of justice. They said she was related to two alleged CJNG members arrested for Manzo's killing.

Quiroz herself has also come under scrutiny as she has declined to turn over Manzo’s cellphone to prosecutors. Manzo’s brother, a member of Morena in the state government now at odds with Quiroz, has accused her of defending some of those detained after the killing.

“I can’t directly accuse her,” Juan Manzo said. “But the reality is that she has covered for many of those responsible for the murder of her children’s father. She has not been transparent during the investigation.”
Quiroz has denied the accusations, and said her family was “betrayed” by those closest to them.
“Slandering us, resorting to dirty tactics and low blows has never stopped us and never will,” she told members of her political movement.
As the political rift has deepened, Uruapan has experienced a surge of violence in recent weeks.

Just over the weekend, a masked man on a motorcycle shot two women working at a taco stand, killing one. The same day, local media reported that police found two men, one who had died, in an avocado field with severe burns and signs of torture. State authorities said they have documented 17 killings, eight gunshot injuries, four attacks on businesses and homes and a series of robberies in October.
The violence prompted Quiroz to request help from Sheinbaum’s government.
“We cannot allow violence to become our new normal," she wrote Sunday on X. “Uruapan deserves to live in peace.”
On Tuesday, state authorities sent 200 law enforcement officers to boost security in the city.
Some residents, including store owner David Vázquez, said extortions by local mafias have mounted since Manzo was killed, forcing his family to temporarily close down their business.

He expressed resentment watching the fleet of state bodyguards escorting Quiroz, saying “they only protect her and her family.” Others said that they had not been affected by the violence and believed Quiroz was doing her best in the face of trauma.

Meanwhile, Manzo's presence still looms over Uruapan. Posters and busts paying tribute to him paint the plaza where he was killed. His grave, open to the public, is covered with flowers, food offerings and white sombreros.
“Not a single step backward,” the headstone reads.
Janetsky reported from Mexico City. Associated Press photojournalist Eduardo Verdugo Tucto contributed to this report from Uruapan, Mexico.

title: Greenland opens new international airport to lure tourists
summary: Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark
story: Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark

ILULISSAT, Greenland -- ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — Greenland has opened a new international airport, seeking to lure visitors from around the world as the Arctic island looks toward eventual independence from Denmark.

Thursday's inaugural international flight between Copenhagen, Denmark, and Ilulissat, Greenland, was part of the island government's efforts to grow its tourism industry to boost and diversify an economy still reliant on fishing.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen described the new airport as “one of the biggest investments” in the island’s history. Nielsen was one of 169 passengers on Thursday's 4.5-hour flight on an Airbus A330neo. An Associated Press journalist also took the flight, operated by government-owned Air Greenland, as part of a trip organized by tourism agency Visit Greenland, for this story.
“If Greenland wants to be independent, we need to have a strong foundation, both economically and in terms of industry and business,” Nielsen told the AP before the plane departed.

The strategic island, home to roughly 56,000 people, has been a focus of U.S. President Donald Trump since his first term, when he initially expressed his desire to acquire Greenland. His repeated threats to seize the territory from Denmark, a NATO ally, during his second term prompted months of tensions with other NATO allies. In September, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.

“There’s no doubt that it has been a shadow over the entire Kingdom of Denmark, but especially Greenland,” said Danish Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, who also took the inaugural flight. “The opening of this new international airport marks, I think, hope and optimism.”

Ilulissat, known as the "City of Icebergs," sits along the island's western coast and is home to some 5,000 people. Greenland's third-largest city is also one of the island's most-visited destinations. More than 550 kilometers (342 miles) north of the capital, Nuuk, its tourism offerings range from sled dog tours to icefjord cruises in picturesque Disko Bay, known for its towering icebergs.

Previously, travelers reaching Ilulissat had to arrive by cruise ship, take a small plane from Iceland or fly to one of Greenland’s international hubs and connect to smaller aircraft. There are no road connections from other big towns.

For decades, Greenland’s main international aviation gateways were former U.S. military air bases, distant echoes of World War II, in Kangerlussuaq and Narsarsuaq. Locals and international visitors had to land there before catching smaller aircraft to the island's major towns, including Ilulissat and Nuuk. That changed in late 2024, when an international airport opened in Nuuk.
United Airlines last year began a new seasonal route between Nuuk and Newark, New Jersey. The inaugural flight was the first direct from the U.S. to Greenland by an American airline.

The Ilulissat airport, meanwhile, has a 5,000-square-meter (53,820 square feet) terminal and a new 2,200-meter (1.37-mile) runway, long enough to accommodate larger passenger aircraft. Air Greenland has committed to as many as six weekly flights between Copenhagen and Ilulissat during next year’s peak summer months, and Icelandair will also fly large jets from its Keflavik hub. Jens R. Lauridsen, CEO of Greenland Airports, said the company is also hoping to lure airlines in the U.S. and mainland Europe to serve Ilulissat.

“It’s quite wonderful that you can go directly right now,” said Kirsten Berthelsen, a 35-year-old Ilulissat resident and student who booked a ticket for Thursday's flight without realizing it was the inaugural service. “Sometimes it’s quite difficult to travel from Nuuk and to other countries.”

While the number of international visitors to Greenland has grown by at least 65% since 2018, reaching almost 150,000 in 2024, the expected travel boom has yet to materialize. In 2024, tourism accounted for less than 5% of the territory's GDP. Infrastructure, including hotel capacity, remains limited.

Aalborg University associate professor Carina Ren, who specializes in Arctic tourism, said some U.S. tourists were even deterred from visiting the island because of the recent Trump standoff, with a few canceling their flights.

“I’ve heard of people canceling their bookings, but also others canceling because they were afraid that perhaps they would not be welcomed,” she said, adding that many Americans still visit, particularly on cruise ships.
Even so, there are some local concerns about mass tourism and potential damage to Greenland’s fragile nature.
Palle Jerimiassen, a former regional mayor, said he fears the city's environment, population and infrastructure may be overwhelmed by too many visitors.
“How many can we invite?” he said. “We are welcoming all the tourists, it’s a possibility to earn some new money."
He added: "But we have to be careful.”

title: Carney expects to conclude talks in June on making Canada EU's first associate member
summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he expects to conclude negotiations with the European Union in June on an unprecedented partnership that would make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member.”
story: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says he expects to conclude negotiations with the European Union in June on an unprecedented partnership that would make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member.”

MONTREAL -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Friday he expects to conclude negotiations with the European Union in June on an unprecedented partnership that would make Canada the bloc’s first “associate member,” even though the designation was left out of a joint declaration launching a new economic and security alliance.
Carney said he would attend a meeting of European leaders in June to conclude negotiations on the proposed relationship, which would stop short of full EU membership.
“In parallel, we are working towards the deepest possible partnership, short of accession — with Canada becoming the European Union’s first Associate Member,” Carney said.

The joint declaration issued at the end of a two-day summit in Montreal made no mention of associate membership. Instead, the leaders agreed to define an “ever-closer association” by their next summit in 2027.
Carney said Canadian Cabinet ministers and European commissioners would meet in March to advance negotiations before he attends European Council meetings in June.

Carney, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa launched the “Alliance for the Future,” announcing progress on digital trade, European investment in Canadian critical minerals and artificial intelligence as Canada and Europe seek greater economic independence.
The two sides concluded substantive negotiations on a digital trade agreement intended to make it easier for businesses to operate across the Atlantic and move data between Canada and Europe.

Canada and the European Investment Bank also concluded negotiations on an agreement to encourage European investment in Canadian critical minerals, which are essential for industries ranging from electric vehicles to defense.

Canada will also participate in a European supercomputing initiative that Carney said could dramatically accelerate research. He said Europe’s JUPITER supercomputer could complete in one day calculations that would take Canada’s most powerful research computer six months.

Costa said the alliance would be the closest relationship the EU has ever established with a country outside the bloc, expanding cooperation on trade, research and security as U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war strains relations with traditional allies.
“Canada is by far the most European of non-European countries,” Costa said.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said shared values mattered more than geography in determining which countries should work together.
“It is not so important where the countries are on the map,” von der Leyen said. “What is important are the values that a country defends and where countries stand in international relations.”
Carney said the alliance would strengthen the sovereignty of Canada and Europe and help them withstand economic shocks.
“Above all, this is about sovereignty. Our ability to live our lives as we wish,” Carney said.
Von der Leyen has been pushing for Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member,” despite resistance from some European governments to the designation.

“We want Canada as close a partner as possible to the European Union,” von der Leyen said. “We know that Canada cannot be a full-fledged member of the European Union, but to have a relationship as close as possible, this is our goal.”

Carney said the digital trade agreement would make it easier for Canadian businesses to sell goods online in Europe. The two sides also concluded negotiations on a competition agreement intended to curb anti-competitive practices and lower prices for consumers.
Canada and the EU will explore linking their instant-payment systems to make cross-border money transfers faster and cheaper.
The broader Alliance for the Future could eventually include other like-minded countries, with Canada and the EU at its core.
The leaders also agreed to study the feasibility of exporting Canadian liquefied natural gas to Europe and explore new undersea cables connecting Canada, Europe and Asia.

Canada and the EU will begin negotiations on expanding Canadian participation in Erasmus+, the European student exchange program, and explore ways to make it easier for young people to study and work across the Atlantic.
The two sides also agreed on a new border security arrangement and pledged closer cooperation on defense, cybersecurity, Arctic security and countering foreign interference.

Trump has suggested Canada’s proposed EU arrangement could be a “hostile act” and threatened tariffs on Europe if he considered it unfriendly. The United States accounted for 71.7% of Canada’s merchandise exports in 2025, underscoring the challenge Carney faces as he seeks to double exports to other countries over the next decade.

title: Pope Leo tells Villanova and Notre Dame basketball teams he is neutral. Prevost has other ideas
summary: Pope Leo XIV has told the basketball teams from his alma mater, Villanova, and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral
story: Pope Leo XIV has told the basketball teams from his alma mater, Villanova, and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral

VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Saturday told the basketball teams from his alma mater Villanova and fellow Catholic university Notre Dame — in Rome for their season opener — that in matters of sport, the pontiff is neutral.
Then the pope, who was born Robert Prevost, said his former self might disagree.

“Prevost has another opinion, but we won’t do that now,” he said to laughs during a whooping, cheering audience of 7,000 people from both schools — players, coaches, fans and their families — in the Vatican audience hall.

The teams were in town for the U.S. college basketball season opener in Rome. The Villanova and Notre Dame men’s and women’s teams will play a doubleheader on Sunday at the 11,000-seat Palazzo dello Sport, about a half-hour drive from the Vatican.
The event has been dubbed the Eternal City Tip-Off and was created to honor the first American pope.

Jay Wright, the former Villanova coach who led the men’s team to two NCAA championships and was inducted this month into the National Collegiate Hall of Fame, said “this pilgrimage to Rome and meeting the pope is bigger than the game.”
The audience had been up in the air after the 71-year-old pope underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13 and is still recovering. But Leo kept the appointment ahead of Sunday’s opener.

Leo graduated in 1977 with a Bachelor of Science in mathematics from Villanova, the Augustinian school near Philadelphia. He was born in Chicago — not all that far from Notre Dame, which is located in South Bend, Indiana.

Leo, an avid sports fan and tennis player, dribbled a golden basketball presented to him by the Villanova women’s team. And when the towering players from Notre Dame presented him with a jersey and another golden ball, Leo stepped up to the podium where his chair sits to try to gain a few inches (centimeters) on them.

He gamely posed for a photo with the Fighting Irish, holding the banner they gave him “Pope Leo, Play like a champion today” — a riff on the famous Notre Dame sign at the university's football stadium.
But he gave Villanova equal time, making the "V'" gesture with his hand as chants of “Let’s Go 'Nova” erupted in the audience hall.
“He is a true Villanovan,” said the Villanova women’s coach, Denise Dillon. “I said, ‘OK everyone: V’s up.’ And he immediately was in with it.”
After mistakenly starting out in Italian, Leo switched to his mother-tongue English and spoke off the cuff, recalling that in his native Chicago, he grew up hearing “Go Irish,” the Notre Dame chant.
“But as you all know, Prevost graduated from Villanova,” Leo said, referring to his past self in the third person.
“So the pope doesn’t take sides,” he said to laughs, before revealing that “Prevost has another opinion."
In his prepared remarks to the crowd, Leo urged the teams and their families to embrace sports as a way to grow in saintliness.
“No one is born a champion, just as no one is born a saint,” Leo said.
He warned against letting sporting rivalries get out of hand and he said he hoped the fans in Rome this weekend would actually get to know one another as they cheer, “even passionately.”

“In any competition, the members of two teams, even when they have a competitive rivalry, are certainly not enemies,” he said. “I hope, therefore, that despite the competitive nature of college basketball, there will be opportunities for the players and the fans of both teams to get to know each other in your days here in Rome.”
He noted that the game will take place on All Saints’ Day, and that the church teaches Christians to pursue saintliness in every aspect of their lives, including in sports.
“Our true goal, beyond emerging victorious in any one event, is to win the prize of everlasting life,” he said.

Like popes before him, Leo has praised the value of sport for both physical and spiritual development, calling sport a “school of fraternity” that nurtures friendship, respect and teamwork. But he also warned about how the win-at-all-cost mentality of sport has contributed to episodes of doping, match-fixing and other forms of corruption.

The Rev. Robert Dowd, president of Notre Dame, acknowledged Villanova had something of an edge in Sunday’s game, considering it counts the pope as an alumnus. But in an interview Saturday, he said, "The pope is a pope for all of us.
“The pope talks about the importance of bridge building," Dowd said, "and I’m sure he’ll be a bridge builder when we play each other.”
Villanova’s president, the Rev. Peter M. Donohue, said there was “a little extra pride” being with Leo, given his allegiance. But he said what happens on Sunday was not the point.

“No matter what happens on the court, this is the true highlight of the trip,” Donohue said in his introductory remarks to the audience. “Tomorrow we will cheer, we will compete, but today we are simply grateful.”

Philadelphia Archbishop Nelson Perez celebrated a private Mass for traveling fans in St. Peter’s Basilica on Saturday morning, and asked the thousands of people in the pews to give a round of applause to the players. The English-language liturgy was unusual in that it had all the trappings of a papal Mass celebrated at the main altar and televised live by Vatican Media.
Leo is an avid Chicago White Sox fan, and has been known to follow basketball, too.

Asked about the upcoming games on the papal plane during a recent trip to France, Leo said, “They tell me that the people coming to the match, 90% are Villanova and 10% Notre Dame, so the voice of the people of God will be very strong on the Villanova side.”

title: North Korea fires missile barrage toward the sea as tensions with South rise
summary: South Korea says North Korea has launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the sea
story: South Korea says North Korea has launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward the sea

SEOUL, South Korea -- North Korea launched a barrage of ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters Thursday, South Korea’s military said, days after the North threatened to resume front-line propaganda loudspeaker broadcasts and deploy new weapons along the rivals’ tense border.
The launches also followed leader Kim Jong Un’s surprise weekend visit to China, the North's main ally and economic pipeline, to push for greater cooperation.

South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected about 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the North's eastern costal town of Wonsan and that they each flew about 250 kilometers (155 miles). It said South Korea's military maintained its readiness to repel any provocations by North Korea under a solid alliance with the United States.
Japan's Defense Ministry said it detected a suspected ballistic missile launch by North Korea.

Animosity between the Koreas have deepened since last month’s land mine blasts at the border that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of planting mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded it apologize. But Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of retaliation if provoked.

Last week, North Korea said it would restart propaganda broadcasts and place new weapons systems on alert along the border in protest of what it called repeated warning shots by South Korean troops at border areas. South Korea later proposed talks on clarifying the border to prevent accidental clashes, but North Korea hasn't responded.
During a visit to a South Korean border town earlier this week, Associated Press journalists saw North Korean artillery guns located on the other side of the border, which weren't previously visible.

In recent years, North Korea has been placing more mines, barbed-wire fences and other defense structures along the border in line with Kim's policy of severing ties with South Korea. Seoul has said North Korean troops have repeatedly violated the border during the work and that South Korea's military has responded with firing warning shots. North Korea has denied the alleged border breaches.

Thursday's launches were the latest in a series of weapons tests by North Korea in recent weeks, which included submarine-launched cruise missiles and hypersonic missiles. Experts say North Korea likely aimed to pressure the U.S. into making bigger concessions as President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim.

On Saturday, Kim visited the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly inaugurated bridge to pay respect at a memorial marking China’s support of North Korea during the 1950-53 Korean War. It was his sixth visit to China since succeeding his father as North Korean leader in late 2011.

At the memorial, Kim said North Korea will firmly carry forward “the invincible" friendship with China. Later he met top Chinese Communist Party official Wang Huning and reaffirmed his resolve to develop bilateral cooperation.
Kim has recently taken steps to bolster ties with China after years of prioritizing ties with Russia by sending troops and ammunitions to support its war against Ukraine.
Associated Press writer Mari Yamaguchi in Tokyo contributed to this report.

title: Europe's economy brushes off energy shock from Iran war, shows moderate growth in Q3
summary: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before
story: Europe’s economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the US-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before

FRANKFURT, Germany -- Europe's economy persevered with moderate growth in the third quarter despite higher oil prices from the U.S.-Iran war, as gross domestic product increased by 0.4% over the quarter before.

The figure released Friday for the 21 European Union member countries that use the euro currency was better than the 0.2% expected by market analysts. Compared to the same quarter a year ago, the economy of the 21 countries using the euro grew by 1.3% in the July-September period, according to EU statistics agency Eurostat.
The continued growth shows that “households and businesses have not pared back their spending due to the Iran war,” said Jack Allen-Reynolds, deputy chief eurozone economist at Capital Economics.
“All in all, the eurozone economy remains resilient amid geopolitical turmoil and a worsening inflationary environment,” wrote Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics.

That is despite “worrying signs” that higher oil prices are spreading to other sectors. Those so-called second-round effects — where high oil prices start to influence wages and prices throughout the economy — would support higher interest rates from the European Central Bank.

Inflation of 3.8% remains above the 2% target set out by the ECB, which left rates unchanged at its policy meeting Thursday. That means the ECB may raise rates at its next meeting in December to cool inflation, imposing higher borrowing costs on the economy even as growth remains modest and unevenly distributed among member countries.

Germany, the largest of the euro economies, saw growth of 0.2% despite headwinds from high energy prices and low river levels that disrupted commerce. France, however, shrank by 0.1% as a political deadlock over how to address an outsized budget deficit continues to weigh on business confidence. Stronger performers were Spain, the Netherlands and Estonia with 0.6%

The eurozone growth figure was distorted by an increase of 5.5% in Ireland, where figures are volatile because it is host to multinational tech and pharmaceutical companies whose global activities can influence the figures. Excluding Ireland, growth was 0.2%.

title: The sell-off for tech stocks drags Wall Street toward its worst day since June
summary: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
story: A sell-off for tech stocks is worsening on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around AI sent prices too high
NEW YORK -- A sell-off for tech stocks is getting worse Friday on worries that Wall Street's frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high.

The S&P 500 dropped 2.3% and was heading toward its worst day since June and a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 3.5%, as of 3:05 p.m. Eastern time, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 723 points, or 1.4%.

The U.S. stock market remains only 3.4% below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers' 401(k) accounts, but it's become increasingly shaky just days before Tuesday's midterm elections in the United States. Worries about AI in general have already become a bipartisan concern for voters, and President Donald Trump has historically used the stock market's performance as a measure of his own success.

Intel's stock led the way lower and is flirting with the worst day in its history, which goes back to 1972, after tumbling 30.7%. The chipmaker gave a forecast for profit in the final three months of this year that fell short of analysts’ expectations, as CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the personal-computer industry continues to feel pressure. The drop came even though Intel reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.

Amazon  sank 1.9% after reporting a weaker profit for the summer than analysts expected. Potentially more concerning for investors was Amazon’s reporting that it burned through $42.4 billion of cash over the prior 12 months, according to a measure called free cash flow. It spent $94.8 billion on property and equipment, primarily through investments in artificial-intelligence technology.

A day earlier, Alphabet’s stock dropped more than 12% to its worst day on record and dragged the S&P 500 lower after telling investors it burned through more cash during the summer than the spring. The company behind Google and YouTube cited similar, mammoth investments in AI.

Worries are rising about whether all those hundreds of billions of dollars will produce enough profit and productivity to make the investment worth it. At the same time, stocks of computer chip companies and other winners from the frenzy to build AI data centers have come under pressure on concerns that high interest rates may slow the further build out of data centers.
“We’re moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the ‘show me’ phase,” said Joe Tigay, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, in a note to investors.
A drop of 4.9% for the stock price of Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward, even more than Intel.

In the cryptocurrency industry, meanwhile, stocks tumbled following a hack on the world’s biggest crypto exchange. The price of bitcoin fell below $77,000 from more than $86,000 earlier this month, and a U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean unit was likely behind the attack that impacted more than $6 billion worth of crypto at Binance.

Coinbase Global fell 13.6% even though it reported stronger results for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Strategy, which says it owns about 4% of the total supply of bitcoin, fell 8.3%. It also reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected, while saying its chief financial officer will resign next week for personal reasons.
Outside of tech, stocks were more resilient as many rallied after reporting stronger profits for the summer than analysts expected. Nearly as many stocks rose in the S&P 500 index as fell.
ExxonMobil climbed 1.8%, and Chevron added 1.7% after the oil giants both reported stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected.
Mondelez International rose 4% after the company behind Oreo cookies and Ritz crackers reported stronger-than-expected growth.
Colgate-Palmolive climbed 2.9% after higher prices for its products around much of the world helped it deliver better revenue and profit than analysts expected.

Expectations are high for U.S. companies’ ability to make bigger profits, even though people around the world are feeling discouraged about high inflation and high fuel prices. Such expectations are what drove the S&P 500 to its record earlier this month.

In the bond market, Treasury yields eased in a signal that investors were buying U.S. government bonds in search of something safer to own. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 4.98% late Thursday and from more than 5.30% earlier this month.

Treasury yields fell even though oil prices bounced higher, something that usually drives yields higher because it worsens inflation. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 2.4% to $113.43. It’s near the high end of its range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation higher.
In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following sharper swings in Asia.
South Korea’s Kospi dropped 3.5% as worries about AI hit its tech-heavy market, while the Hang Seng in Hong Kong climbed 1.5%.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 2.1% after the Bank of Japan decided to keep interest rates steady, echoing moves made earlier in the week by the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank.
AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

title: Spain’s latest deadly train crash puts human error and systemic failure under scrutiny
summary: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
story: Spain's second major train collision this year has sparked debate over whether human error or rail network failures are to blame
BARCELONA, Spain -- Was Spain's second major train collision this year caused by human error or failures in its once touted high-speed rail network?
It depends on whom you ask.
Spain’s transport minister was quick to lay most of the blame a traffic controller’s poor judgment for Wednesday's collision in Toledo province, which killed 69 people.

But railway unions are pushing back. They point instead to what they describe as deteriorated working conditions — fewer traffic controllers with more work than ever — that have made it increasingly difficult to ensure the safety of 45 million passengers annually.
A judge and a special government commission are conducting separate investigations into the deadly crash, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has pledged to get to the bottom of it.

“This investigation must determine how and why this catastrophe happened,” Spain’s King Felipe VI said on Thursday after visiting injured passengers in a Toledo hospital. “We will have to take measures so this never happens again.”

The chain of events that ended in disaster started at 8:30 a.m. on Wednesday, when the communication system key to the functioning of the line’s security system went down. The system, called LZB, monitors the position of trains and can even trigger the automatic braking of a train to prevent a collision.

That malfunction meant that human controllers based at a control post in Madrid took over full responsibility for monitoring the positions and safety of the trains on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) between Madrid and Seville. At that time authorities believe there were six trains on the affected stretch of track.

At 8:36, a controller told one train, belonging to the state-owned RENFE company, that it could start running again at normal speed. The other train, operated by privately owned IRYO, located 15.5 miles (25 kilometers) down the line, also tried to restart, but the engineer was unable to override the automatic stop and informed the controller.
At 8:53 the collision occurred, derailing carriages and shredding parts of the trains to bits.

It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, over two hours further south, one train jumped the track and hit another train going the other direction, killing 46 people.

Transport Minister Óscar Puente, who is under pressure to resign, called the controller's decision to let one train restart at full speed while the other remained still “inexplicable” and “erroneous.”
Puente said that the RENFE train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a stop signal active on that line.

“An order is given for the train to restart, an erroneous decision,” Puente told reporters. The decision “was taken in inexplicable circumstances given that a train was stopped and with a red light," he said.
Unions, however, argue that the context matters.

Raquel Ayllón, spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told The Associated Press that the workload is regularly too much for the current staff to safely handle. She said that traffic controllers have been asking for more personnel for years, while the safety systems keep failing.

“We believe (the minister) is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” she said. “Human error isn't incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”

Spain's union for train engineers, SEMAF, said that this was not the first time the three-decade-old LZB security system, which is still in use on the Madrid-Seville line while being phased out, has gone offline and left human operators to fend for themselves.

“The LZB system should have been replaced some time ago,” said Diego Martín, spokesperson of the SEMAF union of Spain’s train engineers. “It failed us yesterday (Wednesday) and it has gone offline on repeated occasions in the past.”
Train workers went on strike Thursday in a previously planned action to demand the government fulfill its commitments to improve safety conditions after the January crash.
Representatives from several unions also criticized what they called the “irresponsible” leak of audio clips of conversations between the control room and the train engineers to Spanish media.
Spain’s railways only serviced state-owned trains until it opened its high-speed rail to private operators in 2021.
Both of this year’s collisions involved a train operated by RENFE and one operated by IRYO.

Rail traffic increased after the market was opened to competition. Between Madrid and Barcelona, for instance, the average number of daily trips increased from 56 to 89 between 2019 and 2024, according to the SCF union.
A spokesperson for Spain’s train workers’ union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on railways.

“We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines,” Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. “I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind.”

title: DEA approvals could bring big tax benefits for medical marijuana businesses
summary: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses
story: The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana businesses

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration has for the first time issued registrations to medical marijuana dispensaries, a bureaucratic maneuver under President Donald Trump's historic rescheduling of the drug that could pave the way for the businesses to receive tax benefits long denied the industry.

The agency issued the registrations Friday to more than 900 state-licensed dispensaries in Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, South Dakota, Texas, Virginia and West Virginia, the Justice Department said in a news release. The department did not immediately identify the approved businesses.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said in the statement that the regulated distribution of cannabis for medical use from those shops “will help ensure broader access to chronic pain treatment and the safety of the American people.”

In April, Blanche signed an order shifting the classification of state-licensed medical marijuana from Schedule I — reserved for drugs without medical use and with high potential for abuse, like heroin — to the less strictly regulated Schedule III.

The decision largely legitimized medical marijuana programs in the 40 states that have adopted them, and it set up an expedited system for state-licensed medical marijuana producers, manufacturers and distributors to register with the DEA. Businesses must undergo a pre-registration investigation and have security, recordkeeping, inventory controls and other safeguards governing the handling of controlled substances.

Registering with the agency is also expected to ensure immense tax benefits. Historically, state-licensed cannabis businesses haven't been able to deduct normal business expenses — like advertising, rent or labor costs associated with sales — on their federal taxes because they were dealing with a federally illegal, Schedule I drug. Many in the industry have found that financially crippling.
Nearly 7,000 other cannabis dispensaries, manufacturers and distributors across the country have similarly applied for registration, according to a list published by the DEA on Friday.

Steph Sherer, the founder of the medical cannabis organization Americans for Safe Access, noted that the registrations were issued just days before the 30th anniversary of California becoming the first state to legalize the medical use of marijuana.

“For the first time, the federal government is recognizing and registering the medical cannabis dispensaries that patients fought to establish," Sherer said in a written statement. "This is a tremendous victory for patient access and an opportunity to build on 30 years of progress.”

But questions abound. The way state-licensed medical marijuana businesses are regulated is vastly different from how most companies dealing with Schedule III drugs are overseen, and it remains unclear exactly what requirements the DEA may seek to impose on medical cannabis.

For example, some cannabis industry attorneys have noted, state regulators have often sought to mitigate the effects of the drug war by allowing people with some criminal history to run licensed marijuana businesses. It isn't certain whether the DEA will adopt that approach with the businesses it registers.

Furthermore, many states have merged their recreational and medical marijuana industries. While the Trump administration has sought to reschedule marijuana more broadly, it remains unclear how the DEA will treat businesses that handle both adult-use and medical cannabis.

Two dozen states plus Washington, D.C., have authorized adult recreational use of marijuana, 40 have medical marijuana systems, and eight others allow low-THC cannabis or CBD oil for medical use. Only Idaho and Kansas ban marijuana outright.

“It's obviously a positive step to see the program taking shape,” said Chris Lindsey, vice president of policy and state advocacy at the American Trade Association for Cannabis and Hemp. “What everybody's watching for is, what can we expect to see now that we have companies that are going to be operating in this class? What are they going to have to start to do?”
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz in New York contributed.

title: ExxonMobil and Chevron top Q3 estimates on higher prices and strong output
summary: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
story: ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production
ExxonMobil and Chevron both reported better than expected quarterly results Friday as the oil majors benefited from higher prices and record production.

Besides the disruption caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine that have driven up the cost of fuel, Exxon is also seeing strong production in its fields in Guyana and the Permian Basin in the Southwest. Chevron said its results include one month of production in Venezuela where it’s making a big investment.
Utilization at Exxon's U.S. Gulf Coast refineries was at 100%, and U.S. Gulf Coast diesel production was at the second-highest on record.
The price of diesel, currently about $6.32 per gallon, is up 71% since last year, according to AAA. Regular gasoline is up about 38% in the past year as well.

Darren Woods, ExxonMobil chairman and CEO, noted that investments such as the expansion of its Beaumont refinery in Texas have contributed to an increase in its distillate production by approximately 40% since 2019.
For the third quarter, net income more than doubled to $3.72 per share. On an adjusted basis, profit totaled $4.23 per share, easily topping the average analyst estimate of $4.12 per share.
Revenue during the three months ended in September rose 33% to $113.16 billion, also beating estimates.
The Spring, Texas-based company also raised its quarterly dividend to $1.07 and set a $20 billion stock buyback plan.
Houston-based Chevron said Friday it earned $9.9 billion, or $5.06 per share, during the third quarter, as revenue surged 36% to $67.8 billion. Its results handily topped estimates.
Crude utilization at Chevron's U.S. refineries totaled 98%. The company said it set production records at its Eastern Mediterranean and Australian assets.

Chevron, the second-largest U.S. oil company, has had a presence in Venezuela since 1923. Last month it announced it will invest $7 billion over the next five years in Venezuela. It said Friday that following an accounting-related change during the quarter, it’s now including those results.
Overall capital expenditures during the quarter were lower compared with a year ago because it spent less in the Permian Basin.

Mike Wirth, Chevron’s chairman and CEO, said that the company signed agreements to reduce Bakken midstream costs by about 50%, strengthening the asset’s competitiveness. Chevron increased its holdings in the Bakken fields in North Dakota and Montana following its $53 billion acquisition of Hess Corp. last year.
In premarket trading, Exxon shares rose 1.9%. The stock is up 64% in the past 12 months. Chevron shares rose 1.1%.

title: Hundreds of thousands of young protesters take to the streets across France
summary: Thousands of young protesters take to the streets of France for a third weekend.
story: Thousands of young protesters take to the streets of France for a third weekend.
PARIS -- Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.
About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are much higher.
Authorities in France reported about 300 arrests nationwide so far — down from 800 at the same point in last week’s protests.
