title: Internal documents show failed scramble to save "forever cruise"
summary: The MV Odyssey was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It ended abruptly in Cambodia.
story: When the journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship came to a sudden end earlier this week in Cambodia, giving residents on the ship just hours to disembark, it marked the culmination of several attempts over a period of about three months to save the unique voyage.

According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, those included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.

The voyage of the Odyssey, which is operated by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, was billed as a continuous around-the-world cruise when it launched in October 2024. It allowed passengers to become residents of the ship by purchasing cabins for several hundred thousand dollars.
However, more than 200 passengers and dozens of crew members became stranded in Cambodia on Tuesday when Villa Vie suddenly suspended operations because of major financial issues.
In early August, the Odyssey was docked in Singapore when Villa Vie warned that the ship was at risk of being detained and the operator said it urgently needed to raise money.
"There's no question that we ran out of money in Singapore," said Darrell Carp, a Villa Vie resident who told CBS News he is out $250,000.
Residents believed finances were being mismanaged by cruise operator
Multiple residents told CBS News they were concerned about giving money directly to the company because they believed the finances were being mismanaged by Villa Vie.
"We never fully understood the level of their debt," Carp said. "They were already behind on their payments on crew, and provisions, and fuel, and things like that."
A source close to the company said that when fuel prices spiked this year after the U.S. attacked Iran, it was a disaster for the company's business model.

After some passengers raised money while the ship was stuck in Singapore, $400,000 was paid to a fuel supplier directly out of one resident's personal checking account so the Odyssey could continue its journey, sources said.

At that time, Villa Vie was in the hole for several million dollars, according to internal documents reviewed by CBS News. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were owed to a port agent, fueling companies, food vendors and the crew.
Those internal documents showed that in a town hall on Aug. 4, residents were warned there was a real possibility of halting operations, laying off staff and repatriating the crew.

According to documents reviewed by CBS News, the ship was potentially days away from losing its insurance. It said that it would cut internet service to save money and was paying just enough to keep sailing.
Villa Vie introduced VIP program to raise emergency funds

In early August, Villa Vie introduced a so-called VIP "Villa Incentive Program" to help raise emergency funds, according to the documents. The VIP program was only open to current Villa Vie passengers so they could purchase more cabins at a discounted rate.
By Aug. 18, the company posted: "We have the commitment of over 20 cabins on the VIP sales!"

The program was initially an idea by the residents. Instead of just raising funds, it was designed to give passengers an even greater ownership stake in the ship, according to passengers and a source close to the company.
There was urgency to sell the cabins. The last slide of a PowerPoint presentation by Villa Vie on the VIP program read, "Funds are due today."
The VIP program was able to raise enough funds to keep the ship operating, but it continued to struggle, sources said.
A source with knowledge of the VIP program also said cabins aboard the Odyssey were still being sold to Villa Vie residents despite the company operating at a loss at that point.

According to one document, the ship's finances showed that even at full occupancy, it would operate at a $600,000 loss. Average monthly operating costs were $3.1 million, but revenue at 100% occupancy with everyone paying full fees would only have been $2.5 million, the document showed.
A source close to the company disputes the $3.1 million number and claims that the ship's monthly operating costs were under $1 million.
In August, 139 of 490 cabins were unsold, according to the documents.
Ship director had to bribe Vietnam officials to get food aboard, source says

When the ship reached Vietnam, crew members allegedly had to buy food from local grocery stores to feed passengers because the company owed money to a food vendor that would no longer deliver food, according to sources familiar with the situation.
According to one source, the ship's hotel director allegedly had to bribe local customs officials in Vietnam in order to get food onto the ship.
Later, in Hong Kong, court records obtained by CBS News showed the ship was detained until the company paid $167,844.48 to a fuel provider.
Villa Vie founder Mike Petterson has said skyrocketing fuel costs were what ultimately caused the ship's journey to come to an end.

When asked by CBS News Wednesday if creditors might seize the ship, Petterson told CBS News: "We will likely file for Chapter 11 here any day, right, which will put a stay on that while we go through the restructure process."
A source close to the company said Villa Vie stopped conducting cabin sales externally after Aug. 4, once the ship knew it was essentially out of money and needed to raise funds.

Yet on July 27, just a week before the ship ran out of money, Villa Vie had announced it was in the process of purchasing a second ship, the Legacy, and offered residents who were buying a cabin on the future ship an opportunity to take up immediate residency on the Odyssey.
A source close to the company said it was necessary to buy more ships to scale up for the business model to work.
This story published first on CBS News at 7:03 a.m. on Oct. 30, 2026.

title: Patrick Stewart, best known for "Star Trek" and "X-Men," dies at 86
summary: Patrick Stewart starred on stage and screen across his decadeslong acting career. He died at his home on Wednesday.
story: Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his work in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises and his prolific award-winning stage career, has died at 86 years old, his spokesperson confirmed.
Stewart died at home on Wednesday, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement. His death followed "a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," Novak said.

"He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," Novak said.
Stewart began his acting career doing stage plays in the United Kingdom, joining the Royal Shakespeare Company in the 1960s.

Stewart's most recognizable role began in 1987, when he started playing Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." The show ran for seven seasons and also spawned four "Star Trek" films featuring Stewart as Picard and the rest of the "Next Generation" cast. Stewart later reprised the role for Paramount+ series "Star Trek: Picard," which ran for three seasons.
In a 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart said "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry initially turned him away.
"He was talked into employing me by the other producers," Stewart said.

Fellow "Star Trek" legend William Shatner posted: "Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work."

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the original "Star Trek" series, said on Threads that "Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before, and he inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain."

Stewart also played "X-Men" leader Charles Xavier in over half a dozen films in the "X-Men" franchise. He reprised the role for the upcoming "Avengers: Doomsday," which will be released in December 2026. Marvel Studios said on social media that it was "deeply saddened" by Stewart's passing, calling him a "singular talent" who defined the character "for generations of fans."

"X-Men" co-star Hugh Jackman said in a social media post "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days."
Stewart appeared in dozens of other film and television roles, including voice work on Seth MacFarlane's animated shows "Family Guy" and "American Dad."

"Patrick was one of those icons who we somehow all took for granted would always be with us," MacFarlane wrote on social media Thursday. "... He was that rare actor who could take any bit of dialogue and elevate it, making a good writer sound great, and a great writer sound masterful. He was also as humble as they come ... We have lost a legendary actor today, and for many of us, a good friend. He will be deeply missed by the entire planet."

The bulk of Stewart's work was on the stage: He was a frequent presence on Broadway and in London's West End, where he played characters from Shakespearean villains to Charles Dickens' Ebenezer Scrooge. He appeared with "X-Men" co-star Ian McKellen in "Waiting for Godot" in London in 2010, then again in New York City in 2013. He also performed his one-man version of "A Christmas Carol" frequently over the decades.

Stewart appeared in over 60 Royal Shakespeare Company productions. The company named him an "Honorary Associate Artist" to celebrate his contributions to their work. He has also been awarded three Olivier Awards for his London stage performances and received one Tony nomination for his work on Broadway.
Stewart was nominated for multiple Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG awards for his on-screen roles. He won a Grammy Award in 1995 for "Best Spoken Word Album for Children."
In 2001, Queen Elizabeth II appointed Stewart an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. In 2010, Stewart received a knighthood, again from Elizabeth II, for his services to drama.
In 2023, Stewart published the memoir "Making It So." The book landed him on the New York Times' best-sellers list. He also recorded a companion audiobook.

Stewart was actively working until 2026. In addition to his role in "Avengers: Doomsday," he recorded an audiobook where he narrated and commented on all 154 of William Shakespeare's sonnets. He also had a voice role in the animated comedy "The Sheep Detectives."

Stewart was married three times. He wed Sheila Falconer in 1966. The pair had two children — Daniel and Sophia — before divorcing in 1990. From 2000 to 2003, he was married to producer Wendy Neuss. In 2008, he began dating singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell. The two married in 2013 and were wed until his death. Novak said Ozell was at Stewart's side when he died.
In that 2023 interview with "CBS Mornings," Stewart reflected on what he believed made a successful relationship.

"I think it's being open and a good listener and to make connection," he said. "You don't have to be exactly the same but it's necessary that you can share – I think very important. So sharing and respecting."

Stewart was also "a fierce advocate for causes he strongly believed in," his spokesperson said. Those causes included social justice, women's rights, domestic abuse advocacy, veterans' rights, the refugee crisis, animal rights and political reform.

"We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace," Novak said. "His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre. … He will be remembered for the dignity, compassion and humanity he brought to every role — in his art and life."

title: No clear winner in Israeli election as negotiations to follow
summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party won more votes than his main challenger, but both sides will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
story: No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections even as the complete voting results were released on Thursday. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to the official results.
Netanyahu's Likud party secured 27 seats in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, while Eisenkot's Yashar party won 21 seats, according to official election data.

Likud and its allies secured 53 seats; Yashar and its allied parties secured 48 seats; and the Arab-led parties, The Joint List and Ra'am, secured 19. With none reaching 61 seats, negotiations will follow to form a majority and then pick a new prime minister.
On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.

"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."
Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."
"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

If the opposition breaks their pre-election vow — a common occurrence in Israeli politics — they could take power and remove Netanyahu. A central tenet of Netanyahu's election campaign was keeping the Arab parties out of power.

Another possibility given the current stalemate, analysts say, is a unity government between the pro-Netanyahu and opposition blocs without the Arab parties or the ultra-Orthodox. The question in this scenario is who would be prime minister or whether Eizenkot or Netanyahu could rotate out of the position.

This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis headed to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multifront war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for renewed strikes.
For many Israelis, after three years of war on multiple fronts, the election is seen as existential, and voter turnout appeared to be high.
Netanyahu vs. the "change bloc"

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.
Netanyahu is telling voters that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.
"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of parties with different ideologies but one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister," Eisenkot said in a rally late Tuesday, according to Reuters. "A worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics."

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.
Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.
What happens next?
With neither bloc winning a clear majority in the Knesset, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than the 50% of the 120 available.
Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.
If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.
Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.

title: Russian strikes kill 14 in Ukraine but local truce brings some hope
summary: A Russian drone hit two trains at a station in central Ukraine, killing at least 14 people, but a local truce credited to Melania Trump is bringing some hope elsewhere.
story: Kherson, Ukraine — A jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.

A Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, meanwhile, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central city of Kremenchuk, Ukrainian authorities said.

In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children, as Russia continued its deadly attacks on civilians even as a localized ceasefire credited by both sides to U.S. first lady Melania Trump held in the stricken city of Oleshky.

Humanitarian aid was poised to roll into Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as the limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.

Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but the neighboring nations remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia's full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.

Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.

Both sides thanked Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.

"The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported," Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.

"Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded," she said. "This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy."
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, per their wishes, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work remained unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents had told her they want to leave the city.

She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine's military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.

"Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn't have under the attacks," she said. "For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop."

The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. "It's a breath of freedom, when you don't look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you're not afraid of dying. It's so great," she said, adding: "It's such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon."
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but President Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelenskyy, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.

Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow's invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.

Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.

"Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius," Putin said late Wednesday. "We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together."

title: Items found in Pompeii home hint at life before volcanic explosion
summary: Coins, jewelry and other artifacts were found in a sealed closet in Pompeii, giving new insight into life in the historic Roman city before it was destroyed in A.D. 79.
story: Ancient items found in a sealed closet in Pompeii hint at what life was like in the historic Roman city before it was destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in A.D. 79.

The closet was located in a home in the central area of the city, the Pompeii Archaeological Park said in a news release. The house had previously been excavated in 1912, but an investigation of the surrounding areas is just now underway.

Inside, archaeologists found cosmetics, an incense burner, a bronze lantern and a balsam jar. Weights, likely used for commercial activity, were also found inside a wooden chest of drawers. The researchers also found vases and pots made of materials such as bronze, glass and ceramic, and a "refined snuff bottle" decorated with pine.

A necklace representing multiple deities and made of several materials was also found. The piece of jewelry might have been considered "magical" during the Roman era, the park said. Now these pieces are known as "crepundia," or rattles. The necklaces have amulets, meant to protect the wearer as a child. Many carried them into adulthood as mementos of childhood, the park said.

There were high levels of "geographical mobility" in the Roman world, the archaeological park said, explaining that many people, from slaves to wealthy merchants, lived far from relatives and the places they were raised.
The necklace found in the closet contains at least 20 miniature objects and materials including bone and crystal.

The wardrobe also held 38 bronze coins, preserved in a container made of plant material. The presence of the coins has led researchers to believe that the owner or owners didn't have time to recover valuable items.

It's impossible to know what happened to the people who owned these items, the archaeological park said. They may have escaped the eruption of Vesuvius and been unable to return to the site and dig for their belongings. They may have died in the disaster, along with about 15% to 20% of Pompeii's population, or afterward, without heirs who could reclaim the objects.

Little is known about the residents of the house. The items in the closet, including the paintings, and the location of the home on one of Pompeii's main streets suggest "a certain standard of living." But mouse skeletons found inside the home cast some doubt on this belief. However, such skeletons have been found in other spots of Pompeii, showing the city contended with "unwelcome guests," the park said.

The home has previously been attributed to a person named Cornelius Maximus, the archaeological park said. That identification was based on the discovery of inscriptions that are no longer visible. The newly found items likely won't bring researchers closer to identifying the home's owner, but they allow archaeologists to study "the various traces of a life," said archaeological park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel in the Facebook post.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily lives," said Zuchtriegel.

Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and popular tourist attraction. Archaeologists are also constantly exploring the ruined city, searching under heaps of volcanic ash and pumice to peer into its preserved remains.

In January, the archaeological park announced that researchers had found a 2,000-year-old love note and illustrated gladiator fight scene inscribed on a city wall. In December 2025, archaeologists found evidence suggesting that some Pompeii residents returned to live in the city after the eruption.

title: King faces calls for apology, slavery reparations in Caribbean
summary: King Charles III faces renewed calls for a slavery apology and reparations on a visit to the Caribbean, as protesters demand: "Pay us what you owe us."
story: Britain's King Charles III continued his nine-day tour of the Caribbean Thursday under mounting pressure to issue a formal apology for the U.K. royal family's historic role in the transatlantic slave trade and to support calls for reparations.

Charles was to visit Guyana on Thursday before traveling to Antigua and Barbuda for a meeting of heads of state of British Commonwealth nations, where leaders are expected to discuss the legacy of slavery.
His tour began Tuesday in the Bahamas, where the king addressed hundreds of young Bahamians and acknowledged Britain's colonial past.

"Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said. "It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."
On Wednesday, the king embraced the country's vibrant culture, joining a colorful Junkanoo street parade in Nassau surrounded by performers in elaborate costumes and feathered headdresses.
But around the celebrations, protesters held placards declaring: "Pay us what you owe us," demanding compensation for Britain's involvement in centuries of transatlantic slave trade.
Charles' remarks appeared to do little to satisfy campaigners who have long called for a formal apology and reparations.

Speaking to The Guardian newspaper on Wednesday, Dr. Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, dismissed the monarch's remarks as "hollow platitudes" and said, "we deserve so much more than what was offered."

Buckingham Palace has said Charles will not offer a formal apology for slavery, saying such decisions are for the British government, not the royal family, but that he will not shy away from broader discussions about the U.K.'s involvement.

Experts say the royals are concerned that issuing a formal apology could open the door to legal claims for reparations, potentially exposing the family, and/or the British government, to substantial financial demands.

"The reason why he doesn't go further is that he's aware [of] what it will mean to actually apologize, in terms of the legal obligation to make reparation," Esther Stanford-Xosei, a lawyer and reparations expert, told CBS News in 2023, as Charles' second son Prince Harry's book "Spare" acknowledged the family had profited from the slave trade.
Stanford-Xosei said the family feared a formal apology could end up costing the monarchy, "not only money, but status … He will be exposing the criminality of this institution."
Calls for reparations

Between the 15th and 19th centuries, approximately 5 million enslaved Africans were transported to the Caribbean, including more than 2 million to British colonies, where they endured brutal conditions working in sugar, coffee and cotton plantations.

Historians have documented the monarchy's direct involvement in the trade, including investments by King Charles II and his brother James in the Royal African Company, which trafficked enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.

When slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire in 1834, the government allocated £20 million ($23 billion in today's money according to one estimate) to compensate slave owners, but not the enslaved. The compensation was part of a political compromise that helped secure abolition's passage by British lawmakers.

Britain subsequently played a significant role in suppressing the international slave trade during the 19th century, deploying the Royal Navy and investing substantial resources in abolition efforts. Its West Africa Squadron seized more than 1,600 slave ships and freed approximately 150,000 Africans between 1808 and 1869. One study estimated that Britain's wider anti-slavery efforts cost the equivalent of 1.8% of its national income annually over that period.

The debate over reparations has intensified in recent years, particularly following the global Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, which prompted renewed scrutiny of Britain's colonial past and the royal family's historical connections to slavery.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has been among the leading voices calling for reparations, including investment in education, healthcare and economic development.

Speaking to The Guardian, the head of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Hilary Beckles, said people in the Caribbean wanted "proprietary justice, beginning with remorse" from British leaders.
She urged Charles to "dig deep within his consciousness" and to offer young people he meets on his visit "the empowerment that he would give to his own children."
Not everyone in the Caribbean supports the idea of direct reparations, however.

Rasheed Griffiths, a Barbadian economist, told CBS News that "Caribbean leaders have consistently refused to implement prudent fiscal policies over the last few decades, which has led to the decay of Caribbean economies. But instead of realizing they have all the power to turn these countries around they prefer to seek scapegoats."

"The calls for reparations from the U.K. are nothing more than Caribbean leaders attempting to externalize their own failures," Griffiths said. "It should not be taken seriously by anyone, least of all the U.K. public."
Charles previously described slavery as an "appalling atrocity" that "forever stains our history" during Barbados' transition to a republic in 2021.

During a Caribbean tour in 2022, heir to the British throne Prince William and his wife Kate also faced protests over slavery and demands for reparations. William expressed his "profound sorrow" and described slavery as "abhorrent," but stopped short of a formal apology.

Many of the Caribbean nations Charles is visiting are former British colonies and several, including the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, remain constitutional monarchies, which, despite them having gained independence decades ago, makes Charles their official head of state.

title: Heidi Klum leads celebs with over-the-top couples' Halloween costumes through the years
summary: Over the years, Heidi Klum's green Medusa prosthetics stole the show, but Selena Gomez, Paris Hilton and Kourtney Kardashian also delivered iconic couples looks.
story: ‘America’s Got Talent’ judge Heidi Klum tells Fox News Digital she doesn’t want to give away too much when it comes to this year’s Halloween costume.
Couples' costumes on Halloween are always fan favorites, and even more so when it's a celebrity couple.

Heidi Klum and her husband look unrecognizable on the red carpet every year in head-to-toe prosthetics, while Sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr. have referenced iconic movies from the '80s in the past.
Here are some of the best couples' Halloween costumes from over the years.
Klum and Kaulitz leave fans waiting every year for their Halloween couples costume reveal. (Getty Images)
Heidi Klum and Tom Kaulitz
Klum and Kaulitz dressed up as Medusa and someone she turned into stone at her Halloween party in 2025. (Taylor Hill/WireImage)
The official Queen of Halloween always goes above and beyond for her annual Halloween party, and her husband, Tom Kaulitz, plays along each year.

At her party in 2025, the couple looked unrecognizable as they posed for photos on the red carpet. Klum dressed as the Greek mythological character, Medusa, while Kaulitz dressed as a warrior she had turned into stone.

Heidi Klum and Tom Kaulitz attend Heidi Klum’s 24th Annual Halloween Party presented by Butterfinger and Huluween on Disney+ at the Hard Rock Hotel New York on Oct. 31, 2025. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for Heidi Klum Halloween)
The costume consisted of a full green prosthetic bodysuit with scales and a tail following behind her, with fake teeth and a crown of snakes on top of her head, which actually moved.

"I love for people to see this and think whatever they want to think for the first time when I go on the red carpet," she told Fox News Digital in 2024. "I never like to share it before, because then people are gonna be like, ‘Oh, it wasn’t as good as I thought it was gonna be.'"
Kaulitz and Klum turned heads as different versions of E.T. in 2024. (Noam Galai/Getty Images for Heidi Klum Halloween)
In 2024, Klum and Kaulitz arrived to the annual Halloween party dressed as different versions of E.T. from the hit '80s movie, "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial."

Kaulitz dressed as the more traditional version of E.T., while Klum dressed as the version of the character from when the kids in the movie try to disguise him, donning a black hat, blonde wig and red shawl.
Klum dressed as the version of E.T. that was in disguise. (Sunset Boulevard/Corbis via Getty Images)

"As a 9-year-old in Germany, E.T. introduced me to the idea that there’s life outside planet earth," she said on Instagram. "I know E.T. wanted to go home, but I hope that if the movie took place in 2024, that my favorite extra terrestrial would come to my party instead."
Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco
Gomez and Blanco embraced their madness when they dressed as Alice in Wonderland and the Mad Hatter in 2024. (Selena Gomez Instagram)
Selena Gomez and Benny Blanco were late for a very important date as they followed the white rabbit down the rabbit hole and into Wonderland for Halloween in 2024.

The couple dressed as Alice in Wonderland and the Mad Hatter, with Gomez wearing a whimsical blue dress with white socks and a blonde wig. Blanco wore black pants with a brown jacket and multicolored undershirt, paired with a big top hat and an orange wig, as he got into character with white face makeup.
"Curiouser and curiouser.." Gomez captioned the Instagram post.
Paris Hilton and Carter Reum
Paris Hilton and Carter Reum dressed up as Britney Spears from the "Toxic" music video and an airline pilot. (Michael Kovac/Getty Images for Casamigos)
Paris Hilton channeled her inner Britney Spears when she dressed as the singer in her music video for "Toxic."

The 45-year-old media personality posed for photos at the Casamigos Halloween Party in 2023 in a futuristic blue flight attendant uniform, which she paired with metallic silver-heeled boots and sunglasses.
Reum was all smiles as he stood next to her donning an airline pilot uniform.
Kourtney Kardashian and Travis Barker
Kardashian and Barker dressed up as Beetlejuice and Lydia on their wedding day for Halloween in 2023. (Kourtney Kardashian Instagram)
"I’m the ghost with the most, babe," Kourtney Kardashian captioned a 2023 Instagram post featuring her and Travis Barker in their ghoulish Halloween costumes.

The celebrity couple dressed up as Beetlejuice and Lydia Deetz at their wedding. Barker wore white makeup on his face with dark circles around his eyes, paired with green hair and a burgundy red suit, perfectly capturing the essence of the spirit.

Kardashian embodied his blushing bride in a red dress with a lace neckline and sleeves, and wore her hair in an intricate updo as she posed for the photo with a serious expression and holding a bouquet of roses.
Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber
Gerber and Crawford dressed as different pop icons from the 80s in 2018. (Michael Kovac/Getty Images for Casamigos)
Cindy Crawford and Rande Gerber embraced their inner rock stars when they dressed as David Bowie and Debbie Harry at their Halloween party in 2018.

Gerber's costume consisted of black pants and a black shirt, which he paired with a Union Jack flag coat, a red and white scarf tied around his neck and a spiky orange mullet wig. He also painted a red lightning bolt over one of his eyes to emulate Bowie's alter ego, Ziggy Stardust.

Crawford, on the other hand, wore a yellow T-shirt dress over ripped-up black tights and knee-high heeled boots with a black belt around her waist and a red handbag. She styled her hair in a big blonde wig and wore heavy eye makeup.
Lisa Rinna and Harry Hamlin
Rinna and Hamlin channeled one of television's favorite couples, Lucy and Ricky Ricardo. (Steve Granitz/WireImage)
One of reality TV's most iconic characters dressed up as one of TV's most legendary icons, when Lisa Rinna and her husband Harry Hamlin cosplayed Lucy and Ricky Ricardo from "I Love Lucy."

Rinna channeled the comedy legend with a red wig, over-the-top makeup, a blue dress with white polka dots and a white apron. She posed for photos by pursing her lips and putting her finger up to her mouth, mimicking Lucy's classic expression.
Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz played Lucy and Ricky Ricardo on "I Love Lucy." (CBS via Getty Images)
Hamlin stood next to her wearing a suit, and raised one eyebrow as he gave the camera a serious look.
Sarah Michelle Gellar and Freddie Prinze Jr.
The celebrity power couple dressed up as Doc Brown and Marty McFly for Halloween in 2019. (Sarah Michelle Gellar Instagram)
After decades together, Freddie Prinze Jr. and Sarah Michelle Gellar have had some pretty iconic couples costumes.
In 2019, the couple dressed up as Doc Brown and Marty McFly from the hit 80s movie, "Back to the Future." They shared the costume on Instagram, captioning the post, "Great Scott!!!"

The "She's All That" star wore a white jumpsuit, yellow hazmat gloves, a messy white wig with lab goggles as he posed next to Gellar, who wore jeans, a button-up shirt with denim sleeves and a red puffer vest. She accessorized with a skateboard to perfect the Marty McFly look.
The longtime couple topped themselves in 2021 when they dressed up as Baby Houseman and Johnny Castle from "Dirty Dancing." (Sarah Michelle Gellar Instagram)
The couple also recreated an iconic scene from the 1987 movie, "Dirty Dancing," choosing to dress up as characters Frances "Baby" Houseman and Johnny Castle.

In the photo, Gellar is wearing a cropped white button-up and capri denim shorts, as well as a curly short wig, as she crawled on her hands and knees towards Prinze, who was dressed as dance teacher Johnny Castle in black pants and a black tank top.
Patrick Swayze and Jennifer Grey in "Dirty Dancing." (Vestron/Getty Images)
"Nobody puts baby in the corner #happyhalloween from Baby Houseman and Johnny Castle #dirtydancing #loverboy," she captioned the post.

Kelsea Ballerini and Chase Stokes
Ballerini and Stokes were Sandy and Danny from "Grease." (TheStewartofNY/WireImage)

Former couple Kelsea Ballerini and Chase Stokes were hopelessly devoted to one another when they posed for photos together at Heidi Klum's Halloween party dressed as Danny Zuko and Sandy Olsson from the movie "Grease."

The country singer's take on the iconic character included tight leather pants, an off-the-shoulder black shirt and a leather jacket, which she paired with red high heels. She styled her hair in curls and a deep side part, and got into character with red lipstick.
John Travolta and Olivia Newton-John as Danny Zuko and Sandy Olsson in "Grease." (Paramount Pictures/Fotos International/Getty Images)

Stokes played the part of a greaser effortlessly in an all-black outfit, including a leather jacket with "T-Birds" written across the back. He styled his hair with a curl in the front, and accessorized with a cigarette in his mouth.

Molly Sims and Scott Stuber
Sims and Stuber dressed as Jeannie and Captain Nelson from the hit show "I Dream of Jeannie." (Michael Kovac/Getty Images for Casamigos)
Molly Sims was ready to grant partygoers three wishes when she arrived to the Casamigos Halloween Party in 2019 dressed as Jeannie from "I Dream of Jeannie."
She channeled the iconic character in flowing sheer pink parachute pants and a pink cropped shirt with red velvet sleeves, a blonde wig tied in a high bun and a headpiece.

title: Tatum O'Neal steps out with family ahead of 63rd birthday years after near-fatal stroke
summary: Tatum O'Neal's outing with family follows years of recovery from a stroke, seizures and cardiac arrest after an overdose during the COVID-19 pandemic.
story: The actress was spotted walking with a cane in Los Angeles in an all-black outfit with her daughter and son-in-law.
Tatum O'Neal was recently spotted enjoying a day out with her family in Los Angeles.

The "Little Darlings" star was photographed at a fan convention with her family, wearing a black dress paired with a coat, glasses and layered necklaces. She styled her hair in an updo and walked outside the convention with the assistance of a cane.
O'Neal was accompanied by her daughter Emily McEnroe and son-in-law Tim Massarelli.
The sighting comes ahead of the actress' 63rd birthday on Nov. 5 and more than six years after she had a near-fatal stroke in May 2020 following an overdose on morphine, opiates and pain medication.
O'Neal was photographed in an all-black outfit during the recent outing.  (Backgrid)
'LITTLE HOUSE ON THE PRAIRIE' STAR SAYS CHILD ACTORS GET 'DROPPED' AFTER HOLLYWOOD FAME FADES

In a July 2023 interview with People, O'Neal and her son, Kevin McEnroe, opened up about the health scare, with her son telling the outlet there were moments when he and his siblings, Sean and Emily "didn't think she was going to survive."
McEnroe shared that in addition to the stroke, O'Neal had multiple seizures and went into cardiac arrest. She spent six weeks in a coma.
O'Neal was spotted out in Los Angeles with her daughter and son-in-law. She is pictured here in 2018. (Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for New York Magazine)

O'Neal has struggled with drug addiction for decades, with McEnroe saying she "had become very isolated" during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, and had begun abusing medications, including some prescribed to her to treat neck and back pain and rheumatoid arthritis.

"She had become very isolated," he told People. "With the addition of morphine and heavier pharmaceuticals, it was getting scary. COVID, chronic pain, all these things led to a place of isolation. In that place, I don't think, for her, there was much hope."

She went on to make history for her role in the film, as the youngest winner of a competitive Academy Award, when she took home the award for best supporting actress at the 46th Academy Awards in 1974, when she was 10 years old.
"All I really want to thank is my director Peter Bogdanovich and my father. Thank you," she said in her acceptance speech.

title: 'Baywatch' star Nicole Eggert exposes financial toll of cancer battle: 'The bills don't stop'
summary: Nicole Eggert reveals the financial toll of her breast cancer battle as a single parent, from lost income to mounting bills during treatment.
story: Actress Nicole Eggert explained the real cost of her cancer diagnosis to Fox News Digital.
Nicole Eggert admitted that finances are a neglected conversation when it comes to fighting cancer.
Eggert, 54, was diagnosed with stage 2 cribriform carcinoma breast cancer in December 2023. Two years later, the actress revealed her cancer status was "NED," or no evidence of disease.

While the "Baywatch" star is a survivor of a club she "never wanted to be a part of," Eggert told Fox News Digital that the financial strains of her battle added an entirely different stressor to her life.
BRANDI GLANVILLE SPEAKS OUT ON COMPLEX DIAGNOSIS AND $6K MONTHLY MEDICAL BATTLE
"Baywatch" actress Nicole Eggert shared the financial realities of battling breast cancer. (Olivia Wong)

"I'm a 100% single parent," Eggert explained. "One of my daughters is an adult, so she is very self-independent, and she does great, but I do have a teenager still at home ... I have that responsibility, and then I have all the household and homemaker, head of household responsibilities and then the cost of what this diagnosis brings, which is a lot ... really you can't even wrap your head around it."
‘BAYWATCH’ STAR NICOLE EGGERT SAYS IT'S ‘VERY HARD TO BE HEALTHY IN AMERICA’ AS SHE BATTLES CANCER
Eggert noted that the costs consistently "add up," so much so that she was afraid of being able to provide for her family.

"In my line of work, I couldn't commit to being on any kind of production because I'm gonna be in treatment and in and out of treatment ... three-to-five at least days a week," she said. "So, it's not like it's work from home kind of work."
Nicole Eggert has one teenaged daughter, Keegan, and an adult daughter named Dilyn. (Amanda Edwards)

She added, "I had to completely come to the realization that I wasn't gonna have income, and yet the bills don't stop, and the teenagers still need their things, and life needs their things and the car still needs the gas, and you know, all of it."
The "Charles in Charge" actress noted that when she took a step back and truly looked at the disease, "money seemed very trivial."
LINDA PERRY SAYS SHE WAS FEELING HEALTHY WHEN DOCTORS DISCOVERED ‘ANGRY’ CANCER BY CHANCE

"It's sort of like, well, 'Ah, I'm alive.' Then, you know, if you have any kind of financial strain, it's like, 'Well, at least you're alive to deal with it,'" she said. "At least you are alive where you can go out and fix it."
"I had to completely come to the realization that I wasn't gonna have income."
She added, "So there's that part too, where suddenly you're like, 'Wow, whatever. It's just it's just money.' And that comes and goes. So, you know, it's ebb and flow of life."
Nicole Eggert was shocked to realize the financial strains of cancer. (Getty Images)
In December 2023, after experiencing unexplained weight gain and pain in her left breast, Eggert was diagnosed with a rare form of breast cancer.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

She underwent her first mastectomy soon after, and later explained that she'd wanted to do a double mastectomy at the time, but her doctor advised that if she just had one breast removed, she'd be able to get into treatment faster, and her immune system wouldn't take as big a hit, so she agreed.
WATCH: 'Baywatch' star Nicole Eggert details financial toll of cancer battle
Over a year later, in August 2025, she had her other breast removed, and surgeons performed a reconstruction.
Eggert admitted that one major component in her cancer journey was being able to rely on community.
Nicole Eggert, best known for her role in "Baywatch," shared that she underwent a hysterectomy after troubling test results. (Getty Images; Nicole Eggert/Instagram)

"You really have to find your community, and you really have to be OK with asking for help or asking other people how they do it, and getting tips and tricks and just all the information you can get," she said. "That's why these conversations are just so, so important and so necessary. Because what else would you do?"
As part of Breast Cancer Awareness Month, Eggert partnered with Novartis and shared a little more insight into her cancer journey on the Voices of MORE podcast with Amy Robach and Dr. Helen Coons.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Eggert explained how helpful it can be for women to get together, share stories and find interwoven commonality in experiences.

"If we keep talking about these things, it becomes so much easier to talk about, and maybe we don't feel like we have to hide things anymore because in the past it's not ... it's kind of been a taboo topic," she said. "And now I think more and more women are becoming more comfortable to discuss what their journey looks like, what it feels like, how it's gone for them."
Nicole Eggert noted that while her oldest daughter was independent, her teenaged daughter still relied on her financially. (Robin L Marshall/Getty Images)
While the past has its place, Eggert is looking forward to the future and spending more time enjoying life to the fullest with her family.

"I also am really looking forward to stepping back into life not having to be in treatment or in the treatment facility with this newfound power and fearlessness that I have, and this new appreciation for life that I have, and It's like this second chance at life," she said.
"I know that that's so cliche, but it's to jump back in with all of these crazy changes that have happened in the past two years, three years. There's been very, very big changes inside myself."

title: Tim McGraw says brutal toll of filming 'Yellowstone' prequel pushed him to edge: 'Wouldn't have survived'
summary: Between 14-hour days and late-night flights for concerts, Tim McGraw says filming Taylor Sheridan's "1883" was the hardest job he and Faith Hill ever had.
story: Eric Nelsen and LaMonica Garrett share was it really like bringing the Western drama to life. The series, created by Taylor Sheridan, originally became available for streaming in December 2021. The show is now airing on Paramount Network.
Tim McGraw was pushed to the brink while filming Taylor Sheridan's Western drama "1883."

The country music superstar revealed that the brutal production schedule left him questioning how much longer he could keep going. Between 14-hour shooting days, six-day workweeks and late-night flights for concert performances, McGraw said the grueling experience was unlike anything he and his wife, Faith Hill, had faced before.
"If it had gone on any longer, I probably wouldn't have survived, put it that way," McGraw told Esquire.
MATTHEW MCCONAUGHEY GIVES UPDATE ON RUMORED 'YELLOWSTONE' SPIN-OFF SERIES, YEARS AFTER REPORTS FIRST SURFACED
Tim McGraw said the grueling filming schedule for Taylor Sheridan's "1883" pushed him to his limits, with 14-hour days and six-day workweeks taking a brutal toll. (Terry Wyatt/WireImage)
The "Live Like You Were Dying" singer described the demands of filming the "Yellowstone" prequel.

"I learned a lot, certainly because it was such a tough shoot," McGraw said. "I think we shot for right around six months. It was a long shoot. Five or six months. It was close to it. And we shot mostly six days a week, and like 14 hours a day."
But filming wasn't McGraw's only commitment.
The country star was also juggling concerts, sometimes going straight from the set to an airplane before returning home in the middle of the night and starting the cycle again just hours later.

Country superstar Tim McGraw recalled juggling exhausting days on the set of "1883" with concert performances, sometimes getting just hours of sleep between commitments. (Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)

"And during that time, I had a handful of shows that I had to do," he explained. "So there were times that I would finish up around six o'clock in the evening, jump on a plane, go do a show and then get home at 1:00 in the morning, then be in the gym at 3:00 and be in the makeup chair at 5:30, 6:00. So, I had a few of those."

Although "1883" followed the Duttons' journey from Texas to Montana, much of the series was filmed in Texas before production moved north. The cast also endured a rigorous cowboy camp, learning to ride, rope, work cattle and shoot guns before filming began.

"We all got to do it together, which was an incredible experience," "1883" co-star Eric Nelsen previously told Fox News Digital. "But it was a time for us to get comfortable on our horses, to learn how to cut cattle, how to rope, how to shoot guns – all the things we're going to have to do on the show."

The real test came on set. McGraw and Hill recalled filming a dangerous river crossing around 3 a.m. on their 25th wedding anniversary, with temperatures hovering around 36 or 37 degrees, according to Entertainment Weekly.
The grueling schedule left little room for sleep or recovery.
"I told Faith it was probably the hardest job we've ever had. I had some hard jobs growing up."
McGraw then revealed how close the demanding schedule had pushed him to his limit.
Tim McGraw and Faith Hill portrayed James and Margaret Dutton in Taylor Sheridan's Western drama "1883," which follows the family's dangerous journey across the Great Plains. (Rich Fury/Getty Images)
Despite the physical demands, McGraw said the experience was worth it, particularly because he got to work alongside Hill and Sheridan.
MICHELLE PFEIFFER FOUGHT 'BATTLE' WITH TAYLOR SHERIDAN BEFORE SURRENDERING TO HIT SHOW 'THE MADISON'
"It was tough, but it was worth it because we were getting to work together, and we were getting to work with Taylor, who was fantastic, and like I said, a brilliant writer."
McGraw also said he gained a greater appreciation for preparation, explaining that the demanding production taught him the importance of arriving on set ready to work.
Although McGraw had previously appeared in films, "1883" marked his first major role in a television series.The demanding shoot also required McGraw to contend with unpredictable conditions on set.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"The elements were always fighting us, and you were working with animals, and you were working with extras, and you were working with horses, which I grew up riding horses, so it was fun for me," McGraw said.

"But I think I learned more than anything is there's so much value in preparing. And the more you prepare and the more you're ready to do what you're going to do, it takes away a lot of the nervousness."

Tim McGraw described filming "1883" as one of the toughest jobs he and Faith Hill had ever faced, but praised Taylor Sheridan's writing and said the demanding experience was worth it. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)
McGraw and Hill starred as James and Margaret Dutton in "1883," which follows the couple's perilous journey across the Great Plains in search of a new life in Montana.

title: Former Miss USA contestant made a life-changing decision at 26 after cancer devastated family
summary: Allyn Rose lost nearly every woman in her family to breast cancer before choosing a preventive double mastectomy that even sparked hate mail.
story: After losing her mother and several relatives to breast cancer, former Miss USA contestant Allyn Rose made a life-changing decision to break her family's cancer legacy.
At age 26, Allyn Rose made a life-changing decision after cancer had devastated her family.

The model, who competed in both the Miss America and Miss USA pageants, underwent a preventive double mastectomy, a decision she said even sparked "hate mail" from critics. Today, the mother of two is the founder of The Previvor, a nonprofit organization that educates women about breast cancer risk and prevention options. Oct. 31 marks the last day of Breast Cancer Awareness Month.

"I know a lot of people think that's a pretty radical choice for someone who hadn't been diagnosed with breast cancer yet," Rose, now 38, told Fox News Digital. "But I lost my mom when I was 16. And by the time I was 16, I had lost my grandmother, my great aunt, almost every woman in my family to this disease. And I said that legacy ends with me."
KAI TRUMP REVEALS HOW FAMILY RALLIED AROUND MOM VANESSA AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE: ‘IT’S A LONG JOURNEY’

Allyn Rose competed in both the Miss America and Miss USA pageants. She won the Miss Maryland USA title in 2011 and later competed at the national Miss USA pageant that year. (Miss Universe Organization/Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

"I don't want that to be my story," she said. "I don't want to have to tell my 16-year-old daughter someday that she's going to have to spend the rest of her life without her mom. This sad family legacy was not going to take my life if I had anything to do with it."

Rose's mother, Judy Rose, was first diagnosed with breast cancer at 27 and had her right breast removed. The cancer later developed in her remaining breast, reaching stage 3, according to People magazine. Judy died at 51.
Allyn Rose’s mother, Judy Rose, died from breast cancer in 2004. (Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the U.S. after skin cancers, accounting for about 1 in 3 new cancer cases diagnosed in women each year, according to the American Cancer Society. About 1 in 8 U.S. women will develop breast cancer during their lives.
WATCH: ALLYN ROSE CHOSE DOUBLE MASTECTOMY AT 26 SO CANCER LEGACY 'ENDS WITH ME'
The organization estimates that 321,910 new cases of invasive breast cancer will be diagnosed among U.S. women in 2026 and that about 42,140 women will die from the disease.
FOX NEWS MEDIA TEAMS UP WITH BREAST CANCER RESEARCH FOUNDATION
Allyn Rose's mother Judy is seen here with her children. (Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

Rose was considered at elevated risk of developing breast cancer because of her extensive family history. In 2012, she was crowned Miss District of Columbia, earning the opportunity to represent the district at the 2013 Miss America pageant. That same year, at 24, Rose announced her decision to undergo a preventive double mastectomy. She had the surgery two years later, at 26.
Allyn Rose had a double mastectomy at age 26. (Miss Universe Organization/Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

For women with a strong family history of breast cancer, a bilateral risk-reducing mastectomy can lower the risk of developing the disease by up to 90%, according to the National Cancer Institute. The procedure does not eliminate the risk entirely because it is impossible to remove all breast tissue that could become cancerous.

"So much of my life and my identity was wrapped up in the way that I looked and how I presented myself to the world," Rose said. "I paid my bills and my rent with the way that I looked. I didn't think [my looks] were 100% of my identity, but I would be lying if I didn't consider the repercussions of having a surgery like this. It would very likely end my modeling career, my career in pageantry, my career really in the entertainment industry. There were so few women talking about having a procedure like this and coming out on the other side."

Randi Sundquist, Miss Nevada, Allyn Rose, Miss District of Columbia and Mallory Hytes Hagan, Miss New York, perform during the opening of the 2013 Miss America Pageant at PH Live at Planet Hollywood Resort & Casino in Las Vegas, on Jan. 12, 2013. (Getty Images)

"I wasn't married," she said. "I didn't have any children. These were all conversations I was going to have with a future partner someday. And so, it was a really tough choice, and it's one that I'm glad that I made, but it's very difficult to make the decision to have a surgery to prevent a cancer that didn't exist yet."
Allyn Rose is seen here following her surgery. (Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

With her father's support, Rose underwent a preventive double mastectomy to reduce her risk of developing breast cancer. She ended up having three surgeries, including reconstruction, and went through what she described as "very graphic periods of looking completely different, having no breasts, wondering who is ever going to be happy looking at me like this."
Allyn Rose lost her mother, grandmother and great aunt to breast cancer. (Miss Universe Organization/Courtesy of Allyn Rose)
Then she remembered her mother, Judy.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Allyn Rose is seen here with her family. (Courtest of Allyn Rose)

"[Losing my mother] drastically impacted my life, not only because it was my mother, but because I didn't know how to be a woman yet," she said. "[When I lost her] I hadn't even gotten my driver's license. I hadn't graduated from high school. I hadn't sent myself off to college yet. I spent a lot of those real pinnacle years of my life without a mentor, without someone to guide me through that. It was a very challenging time really, having to be my own cheerleader, experience all those crowning achievements in my life by myself."
"But I think I've come out stronger on the other side of it," Rose said.
Allyn Rose attends the Breast Cancer Research Foundation's Hot Pink Party at The Glasshouse in New York City on May 13, 2025. (Getty Images)
Rose said she received hate mail over her decision, while her father also faced criticism after people learned he had encouraged his daughter to undergo the double mastectomy.
Miss District of Columbia Allyn Rose is introduced at the 2013 Miss America Pageant "Meet and Greet" Fashion Show at the Fashion Show mall in Las Vegas, on Jan. 5, 2013. (FilmMagic)

"To see a young person who walked on the Miss USA stage, who worked full-time as a model, who was really in this beauty industry — choosing to almost end my career to prolong my life seemed like a foreign concept," Rose said.

"And there were a lot of radical responses to my decision. I got hate mail. My father received hate mail. People just couldn't fathom that I would take this preventative step. But I didn't want cancer to be part of my story. I wanted it to end with me."
Miss District of Columbia Allyn Rose speaks at the Date for the Cure to benefit Susan G. Komen For the Cure on Feb. 16, 2013, in Universal City, California. (WireImage)
Rose made her decision before actress Angelina Jolie publicly revealed that she had undergone a preventive double mastectomy after genetic testing showed she carried a harmful BRCA1 gene variant.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Angelina Jolie poses ahead of a screening of the film "Coutures" at the Pathe Palace cinema, in Paris on Feb. 9, 2026. (Thomas SAMSON / AFP via Getty Images)

In a May 2013 New York Times op-ed, Jolie explained that her mother had battled cancer for nearly a decade before dying at 56. Jolie said her doctors estimated she had an 87% risk of developing breast cancer and a 50% risk of ovarian cancer. She chose to have both breasts removed, which she said reduced her estimated breast cancer risk to less than 5%.
Jolie, who was 37 at the time, said she shared her experience so other women could better understand their own risks and options.

Miss Maryland USA Allyn Rose attends a bike build celebrating the 60th anniversary of the Miss USA Pageant and the 70th anniversary of the USO at Pier 88 on May 26, 2011, in New York City. (Getty Images)

Rose said she thought her modeling career was over. But in 2019, Sports Illustrated Swimsuit featured her, making her the first woman who had undergone a double mastectomy to appear in the publication.

Allyn Rose attends the 1st Annual Celebrity Beach Soccer After Party presented by GACP Sports & Sports Illustrated at W South Beach on Nov. 17, 2018, in Miami Beach, Florida. (Getty Images for GACP Sports & Sports Illustrated)
Today, Rose travels across the country to raise awareness about "the power in prevention."
Allyn Rose later became the first woman who had undergone a double mastectomy to model for Sports Illustrated Swimsuit. (Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

"The thing I wish someone had told me when I was first navigating this was that there is a light at the end of the tunnel," Rose said. "Everything was a question. It was this fear of the unknown. But I said to myself, 'I'm going to still chase all of those dreams. I'm going to go accomplish all the things that I wanted to.'"
When she looks back on her journey, one person comes to mind: her mother, Judy.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Allyn Rose's late mother Judy is seen here. (Courtesy of Allyn Rose)

"I do think about what my mom would think, and I know she would be incredibly proud of me," Rose said, fighting back tears. "One of the last things she said to me was, 'Don't let my life be in vain.' And I made a promise to her that I would make use of every day that she didn't have. And so, that has been my mission from the day that she passed to ensure that I could help as many women as possible not have to walk their lives without their mom. That's my goal."

Allyn Rose attends the Breast Cancer Research Fund Awards Luncheon at New York Hilton Midtown on Oct. 16, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

"I have two children," Rose said. "They don't have the same gene mutation that I have. They no longer have an increased risk of cancer. And that legacy ended with me, and I know my mom would be very proud that I did that."

title: Liam Neeson, 74, says he doesn't need a gym to stay ready for action scenes

title: Miranda Lambert's friend kidnapped by her own father at age 7 recalls daring rescue that brought her home
summary: Lauren Burns was 7 when her father abducted her from Dallas to Jordan. Miranda Lambert's family helped spark the daring rescue mission home.
story: Lauren Burns reveals how her father kidnapped her and took her to Jordan at age 7 and how Miranda Lambert's family helped her mother fight to bring her home. She has written a memoir, ‘Stolen.’

Lauren Burns was dressed in a cheerleader costume for Halloween weekend in 1987 when she climbed into her father's car. But instead of taking her trick-or-treating, he drove the 7-year-old to the airport and flew her thousands of miles from her Dallas home.

Ali Bayan assured the little girl that the trip to his home country of Jordan was a "surprise" and that her mother, Cathy Mahone, knew all about it. But as days turned into weeks and her father refused to let her speak to her mother, Burns began to realize she might never return home.
"I didn't think I would ever see my mother again," Burns recalled to Fox News Digital.
MIRANDA LAMBERT, CARRIE UNDERWOOD 'SHOULD GET A RIBBON' FOR SURVIVING COUNTRY MUSIC IN MALE-DOMINATED ERA
Miranda Lambert's (left) childhood friend, Lauren Burns (right), has written a memoir about her abduction and miraculous rescue. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

Burns recounts the abduction and the international rescue mission it sparked in her memoir, "Stolen." Her childhood friend, country music superstar Miranda Lambert, whose family played a crucial role in bringing Burns home, wrote the foreword.
Fox News Digital reached out to Lambert for comment.
Miranda Lambert performs onstage during the 61st Academy of Country Music Awards at MGM Grand Garden Arena in Las Vegas May 17, 2026. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for ACM)
"By the time I was 6 weeks old, my parents got divorced," Burns said.
WATCH: MIRANDA LAMBERT'S FRIEND RECALLS BEING KIDNAPPED BY FATHER AT AGE 7

"All I ever knew was that kind of upbringing. I went between two homes. My mother had full custody of me when I was 6 weeks old, but she did not want to keep me from my father. He was a good dad. He was loving and kind. I saw him almost every other weekend or maybe extra if she needed help. They had a good relationship despite the reasons that they had gotten divorced."
During the drive to the airport, Burns wondered why her stepmother and siblings weren't coming along.
Cathy Mahone and Ali Bayan during happier times. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

"He'd never done anything to make me feel like I couldn't trust him," Burns said. "He was my dad, my provider. He was the one that loved me dearly. So, if he tells me something, I'm going to trust him. But it didn't quite add up."
Lauren Burns as a baby with her father, Ali Bayan. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

Burns' parents met while Mahone, a Christian, was working as a waitress and Bayan, a Muslim, was studying engineering in Texas. Mahone had full custody, but Bayan, who owned a restaurant in Dallas, saw his daughter regularly. There were "no red flags," Burns said, until that Halloween weekend.

The Monday after Halloween weekend, Mahone went to Burns' elementary school to have lunch with her, as she typically did. She expected to hear about her daughter's weekend of trick-or-treating with her father. Instead, she discovered that Burns had never arrived at school. She soon learned that her ex-husband had abducted their daughter and taken her to Jordan.
Lauren Burns on Halloween with her mother before her abduction. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

A desperate Mahone rushed to a pay phone. She called the one man she believed could help her — Miranda Lambert's father, Rick Lambert. The former Dallas police officer ran a private detective agency with his wife, Beverly.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE
Rick Lambert is a former Dallas police officer. (Rick Diamond/Getty Images for BMI)

"Rick and Beverly were home," Burns said. "They got Miranda, they moved out of their house and they were with my mom day and night trying to figure out a way to help my mom get me back. They were calling everyone they knew. Rick pulled some strings and got an appointment at the Dallas County Courthouse, so my mom could try to get a warrant out for my father's arrest."
The Lamberts had known Mahone for years, long before Burns and Miranda were born. Their friendship began when Mahone worked for Miranda's grandmother, Wanda, at an apartment complex.
Beverly Lambert and Lauren Burns in 1987. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

Until then, Burns had traveled only to Florida to visit her grandmother. Now, the 7-year-old was in the Middle East, unable to speak Arabic and struggling to adjust to unfamiliar customs and a different way of life.
Lauren Burns with her mother in Florida, circa 1985. (Courtesy of Lauren Burns)

"I had to cover my hair," Burns said. "I could not wear shorts. We had to take our shoes off and wash our feet. There were no toilets. It was a hole in the ground with a chain above. I had never seen anything like that. Even the way we ate, it was a communal type of eating. You would sit on the floor with a big rug that was underneath and big plates of food, fresh food. You could smell all the different spices and the fresh hummus. We would all sit together, and you would eat with your hands."
But for Burns, the most painful change was in the father she had always trusted. Once in Jordan, the man she viewed as her protector became "distant."
Fox News may be compensated for or earn a commission if you buy through our referral links.
"Stolen: A True Story ― Kidnapped, Rescued, Redeemed" by Lauren Burns is available now. (Post Hill Press)

"I quickly realized that my father was not going to take care of me in Jordan like he did in Texas," she said. "It was different roles that I didn't quite understand. I quickly got the sense that it was my grandmother and aunt's job to take care of me because it wasn't the man's job to take care of the child. But at a time in my life when there was so much confusion, I really needed my father. I really needed my mother, and I didn't have that either."
