BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR

Hackers are using artificial intelligence to accelerate cyberattacks, raising concerns about personal data security as researchers uncover critical vulnerabilities affecting millions of websites. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
Why cybersecurity experts are calling it Black October

October 2026 has delivered a troubling wave of cybersecurity developments. Hackers have gained access to more powerful tools, while researchers have uncovered serious weaknesses in widely used software. Security professionals are reportedly struggling to keep pace with increasingly automated attacks. Some have started calling the current wave "Black October."

The term describes a series of cybersecurity emergencies rather than a single coordinated hacking campaign. The biggest concern is speed. Traditionally, hackers needed significant time and technical expertise to investigate potential targets. They also had to develop attack methods and analyze the information they obtained. Now, AI tools can automate portions of that work. Some can operate continuously and pursue multiple potential targets at once. As a result, companies may have less time to respond when criminals discover a way into their systems.
Microsoft exposes AI cyberattacks moving at machine speed

One of the clearest examples comes from Microsoft. On Oct. 21, Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that a China-state-aligned hacking group called Storm-0940 had used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX. The open-source tool can automate security testing tasks, including investigating networks and identifying potential weaknesses. In the hands of criminals, those capabilities can accelerate attempts to gain unauthorized access.

According to Microsoft, the group used ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries. Several attacks resulted in unauthorized privileged access to cloud systems. In multiple cases, attackers reached that level of access in less than three hours. Although many attempts failed, the successful intrusions demonstrate how quickly AI-assisted attacks can unfold.
Hackers launch thousands of login attempts per minute

Between Oct. 10 and 14, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed login attempts in one campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations. At its peak on Oct. 11, attackers generated approximately 2,900 failed login attempts per minute. The technique, known as password spraying, involves trying passwords against multiple accounts to identify a working login.

Importantly, Microsoft did not observe successful logins during that specific campaign. However, it documented unauthorized access and suspicious activity in other environments associated with the same threat group. Microsoft also connected Storm-0940 to a compromise involving ConnectWise, a company that provides software used by IT service providers. Attackers exploited access associated with ConnectWise cloud applications to attempt entry into customer environments. Some then carried out further activity through Microsoft cloud services, including changes that could help them maintain access.

Microsoft cautioned that suspicious access does not automatically mean customer information was stolen. Nevertheless, the activity reveals how AI can help attackers move quickly once they obtain usable credentials.
A $449 AI account scare shows the financial danger

The risks become more personal when you look at what happened to Colin Parsons. Parsons reportedly woke up to roughly 50 notifications about charges involving OpenAI and Anthropic. He reported $281 in unexpected OpenAI usage and another $168 involving Anthropic. Both credentials were associated with OpenCode, an AI coding platform he used.

On Oct. 17, OpenCode disclosed a security incident involving its Console service. The company said unauthorized access to a legacy system may have exposed third-party AI provider keys stored by some users. The company reportedly notified affected customers and advised them to revoke their credentials.

OpenCode said the incident affected approximately 1.4% of its Console users who had connected external AI providers. The disclosure concerned credentials stored in Console, rather than keys stored locally in OpenCode's desktop or command-line applications. Other users also reported unexpected charges, although the amounts have not been independently verified. OpenCode associated its incident with a large-scale AI model distillation attack, but it has not publicly established exactly how the reported unauthorized usage occurred.

The concern is straightforward. If someone obtains a working API key, they may be able to use a paid AI service and generate charges against the account owner's billing arrangement. For people who depend on AI tools for work, that can become expensive before they realize anything has happened.
WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY

A wave of AI-powered cyberattacks dubbed "Black October" has exposed growing cybersecurity threats, including stolen credentials, unauthorized charges and vulnerabilities in widely used website software. (iStock)
A massive website security scare adds to Black October fears

While hackers are becoming more capable, AI-assisted security research is also uncovering dangerous weaknesses in software that supports the internet. On Oct. 21, developers released emergency fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to operate websites.

The vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are collectively known as PHP2Shell. Under certain conditions, the flaws could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers without first signing in. Successful exploitation could expose sensitive information or give criminals control over affected systems.

The potential impact is enormous because PHP powers roughly 70% of websites whose server-side programming language is known. However, that does not mean 70% of websites were hacked. It also doesn't establish that attackers could successfully compromise every website using PHP. The vulnerabilities affect PHP installations handling web requests, but successfully exploiting them can require complex technical conditions.
Federal agencies issue urgent security warnings

The situation prompted warnings from U.S. cybersecurity authorities. On Oct. 23, the FBI issued a public alert urging organizations to patch affected systems immediately. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also called for urgent updates. The PHP project released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Website administrators running older unsupported versions need to obtain appropriate vendor-supported fixes or migrate to a supported release.

Meanwhile, several government organizations in Europe temporarily took websites offline as a precaution. However, the situation became clearer as researchers investigated. On Oct. 23, the Netherlands' National Cyber Security Centre said exploiting the vulnerabilities appeared more complicated than initially feared. The agency lowered its assessment of the likelihood of widespread exploitation.

Also on Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unusual combination of server settings and application code. The project recommended a temporary configuration change while it prepares a fix through its regular release process. Website owners should continue following official PHP security guidance rather than assuming the emergency has completely passed.

Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike also reported seeing attempted attacks, but said it had not observed successful exploitation of PHP2Shell in its investigations at that point. Other security researchers, including Amazon Threat Intelligence, observed suspicious exploitation attempts beginning before the patches became publicly available. Those attempts remain important even without proof that they successfully compromised real systems.

However, new evidence emerged over the following days. On Oct. 24, security researcher Adel Karimi documented successful PHP2Shell exploitation against specially configured test servers, known as honeypots. The attacks launched 35 command shells across three honeypots. Although those findings did not establish how many real-world websites had been compromised, they demonstrated that attackers could successfully exploit the vulnerability under certain conditions.

Then, on Oct. 26, CISA added both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The designation confirms that federal authorities recognize evidence of active exploitation. It also reinforces the urgency of installing security updates, even though the full extent of attacks against real-world systems remains unclear.
AI is helping hackers, but security researchers are using it too

There's another side to this story that deserves attention. Artificial intelligence helped researchers investigate the PHP vulnerabilities before the October emergency. According to the PHP Foundation, developers had identified early signs of one underlying problem during a security investigation in 2024. However, the team struggled to develop a reliable solution. Additional research in 2026 exposed the seriousness of the issue.

The foundation worked with researchers and used AI-assisted security tools, including technology from Anthropic and OpenAI, to examine PHP's code. Researchers from security companies Calif and Wiz also contributed important findings. The PHP Foundation says these reports helped clarify the vulnerabilities' potential impact and accelerated the work needed to release fixes.

AI can therefore help defenders identify dangerous weaknesses before criminals exploit them. The challenge is ensuring security teams can investigate the findings and distribute fixes quickly enough. That challenge is becoming more urgent.
What AI-powered cyberattacks mean for your personal information

You may be wondering how any of this affects you if you're simply checking email or shopping online. The concern starts with the companies holding your information. When hackers compromise a business, they may gain access to stored customer information. Depending on the systems involved, that could include email addresses or passwords. Financial details may also be exposed. Criminals can use stolen information to launch convincing scams or attempt to take over existing accounts.

Meanwhile, AI makes it easier to produce personalized phishing messages. Attackers can incorporate leaked information into emails that appear to come from a company you recognize. Some criminals also use AI-generated voices to impersonate people and pressure their targets into making payments.

However, a security vulnerability affecting a website doesn't automatically mean your personal information has been exposed. The actual risk depends on whether attackers successfully gained access and what information they obtained. That's why it helps to focus on the steps you can control.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Internet infrastructure is at risk from critical software vulnerabilities, including the recently discovered PHP security flaws. (Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP via Getty Images)
8 ways to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks

You can't personally fix security problems affecting large companies. However, you can strengthen your accounts and reduce the potential damage if criminals obtain your information. Here are seven precautions I recommend taking now.

Start with your primary email account. Criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services you use. Create a strong, unique password for every account. A reputable password manager can help you generate and store those passwords. Next, enable multifactor authentication wherever it's available. Passkeys and hardware security keys offer especially strong protection against phishing. Authenticator apps are another useful option. Avoid relying on passwords alone.

Your phone may already have tools that can identify passwords exposed in known data breaches. On an iPhone, open the Passwords app and review its Security section. Android users who save passwords through Google can review warnings in Google Password Manager. If a password has been exposed, change it directly through the company's official website or app. Also update any other accounts using that same password. Our article explains how to find compromised passwords on iPhone and Android. Remember, a compromised-password warning does not necessarily mean someone has accessed your account. However, it gives you a chance to replace a vulnerable login.

Enable transaction notifications through your bank and credit card providers. Also review recent sign-ins on your email accounts and other important services. Watch for unfamiliar devices or changes to your recovery information. If you spot unauthorized activity, contact the provider through its official website or app. Change affected credentials and revoke unfamiliar sessions where possible. Don't wait for several suspicious charges before investigating.

Many people connect third-party apps to their Google or Microsoft accounts without thinking about the permissions they're granting. Over time, those connections can accumulate. Some applications may retain access even after you've stopped using them. Open your account's security settings and review connected applications. Remove access you no longer need or recognize. However, if a service you use has announced a security incident, follow its specific recovery instructions. Simply disconnecting an app may not revoke credentials that attackers already obtained.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads and block dangerous websites. However, antivirus protection cannot prevent every account takeover or stop a company from experiencing a data breach. That's why monitoring your financial information is also important. Consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. Keep in mind that a freeze won't protect accounts you already have. If you use AI services that require API keys, review your usage regularly. Revoke credentials that may have been exposed and set billing alerts or limits where the provider supports them. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Data brokers collect and sell personal information, including phone numbers and home addresses. Criminals can use those details to make AI-generated scams more convincing. A personal data removal service can help remove your information from people-search sites and data broker databases, making it harder for scammers to find. However, it can't erase information from past breaches or prevent cyberattacks. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.
Enable automatic security updates on your phone and computer. Keep your browser current, too. Updates frequently fix vulnerabilities that criminals may try to exploit.

AI-generated phishing messages can look remarkably convincing. They may contain personal information that makes them appear legitimate. Be cautious if someone unexpectedly claims your account has been compromised or demands immediate payment. Instead of clicking a link, open the company's official app or visit its website directly. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Criminals often create pressure because they want you to act before checking the details.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about this wave of AI-powered cyberattacks is the speed. Microsoft documented attackers gaining privileged access in less than three hours. That's a frighteningly short window for companies to react. At the same time, AI is helping security researchers uncover weaknesses before criminals exploit them. But here's what worries me. We trust companies with enormous amounts of personal information, yet we're often left dealing with the fallout when their security fails. I believe those companies need to be held more accountable. Until then, protecting our accounts and staying alert to suspicious activity remains our best defense.

If AI allows hackers to attack thousands of accounts in minutes, should companies face tougher penalties when they fail to protect our personal information? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Millions of students caught in California data breach
summary: Educational Testing Service hackers stole millions of California student records, but families who moved out of state years ago may also be affected.
story: Millions of current and former California public school students may have had sensitive personal information stolen in a massive data breach involving a state testing contractor. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

You send your child to school expecting teachers to protect their education. You probably don't think much about what happens to their personal information after they take a standardized test. But a massive data breach in California is raising some uncomfortable questions about who has access to student records and how safely that information is stored.

Hackers accessed and copied sensitive records belonging to millions of current and former California public school students. The stolen information includes home addresses, birth dates and even details about disabilities. And here's something families need to know. You could live thousands of miles from California today and still be caught up in this breach if you or your child previously attended a public school there.

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. ORACLE HEALTH DATA BREACH EXPOSES NEARLY 20 MILLION PATIENTS
How millions of California student records were stolen

The breach involves Educational Testing Service (ETS), a nonprofit organization that works with the California Department of Education. ETS helps administer statewide student assessments and maintains information connected to those tests. According to state officials, someone gained unauthorized access to an ETS-operated secure file transfer site. Investigators determined that the attacker used a compromised login credential to enter the system. The intruder then copied files containing student information at various times between May 22 and Sept. 18, 2026.

ETS discovered the suspicious activity on Sept. 25. The company disabled the affected account and took the file transfer site offline. It also brought in outside cybersecurity specialists to investigate. The company says it has since built a replacement system with stronger security controls. So far, ETS reports finding no evidence that the stolen information has been made publicly available. However, investigators have confirmed that someone accessed and copied the records.
What personal information was stolen in the student data breach?

The California student data breach involved far more than test scores. Depending on the student, the compromised files may contain information that could help someone identify a child or learn personal details about their family circumstances.
The exposed records may include:

Student names and dates of birthHome addresses, school names and grade levelsStatewide and local student identification numbersRace, ethnicity and primary languageCountry of origin and English learner statusDisability information and testing accommodationsParticipation in certain educational assistance programsStatewide assessment participation and test results
Student names and dates of birth
Home addresses, school names and grade levels
Statewide and local student identification numbers
Race, ethnicity and primary language
Country of origin and English learner status
Disability information and testing accommodations
Participation in certain educational assistance programs
Statewide assessment participation and test results

Some records also identified whether a student qualified for programs serving children experiencing homelessness or other educational needs. Fortunately, officials say the stolen files did not contain Social Security numbers, financial account details, driver's license numbers, passwords or parent and guardian personal information.

However, there is still plenty to be concerned about. Someone who knows a child's name, school and address could potentially use that information to create a convincing message that appears to come from a teacher or school administrator. Disability information also raises additional privacy concerns because those details are particularly personal.
Why this California breach could affect families nationwide

This is where the story gets especially troubling. Although the breach involves California's public school system, the people whose records were stolen may now live anywhere in the United States. According to the California Department of Education, the compromised information includes records covering all students enrolled during the previous three school years. However, the affected population extends beyond those students.

The state also identifies a group of former students who left California public schools as far back as 2006 and whose transfers to another school were never confirmed with the department. That creates a situation many families may never have considered. Say your child attended elementary school in Los Angeles before your family relocated to Texas. Perhaps you graduated from a California public school years ago and now live in Florida. Your old student information could still be among the compromised records if it falls within the affected groups.

Former students who are now adults may also be eligible for the free identity-protection services being offered. Importantly, this does not mean every student attending school outside California has been affected. In a statement to CyberGuy, ETS confirmed that no other ETS customers were affected by the incident. The concern for families elsewhere comes from their past connection to California's public schools. California has roughly 5.7 million public school students, according to reporting on the breach. Since the compromised files span multiple school years, millions of people are potentially involved. Officials have not yet released a final count of unique affected individuals.
Where the student data breach investigation stands

The California Department of Education and the State Board of Education are coordinating with cybersecurity specialists and other state agencies. The California Cybersecurity Integration Center is assisting with the technical investigation. Meanwhile, state officials are reviewing ETS's compliance with applicable data security requirements and its contractual obligations.

In its statement to CyberGuy, ETS said, "We have implemented additional safeguards, including enhanced monitoring, strengthened access controls, and further third-party review of our security practices." ETS says it continues monitoring for signs that the stolen information has surfaced publicly. For families, the unresolved question is what happens to the copied information next. Even without evidence of a public leak, sensitive student records in unauthorized hands create a privacy risk that deserves continued attention.
A SCAMMER HAS YOUR NAME, PHONE NUMBER AND ADDRESS. WHAT CAN THEY ACTUALLY DO?
Stolen student records may include names, birth dates, home addresses, disability information and statewide test results. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to find out if your information was exposed

ETS began notifying affected students and families on October 16, 2026. The state expects notifications to continue through early November. Letters and emails will explain the incident and identify the types of information involved. They will also include instructions for accessing complimentary identity-protection services. However, here's an important warning. Not receiving a notification does not necessarily mean your information is safe. Some former students may have outdated contact information on file.

Families who are concerned should visit the official California ETS incident webpage. It contains frequently asked questions and links to breach notifications available in 27 languages. You can also call the incident assistance line at 833-931-8488, Monday through Friday, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. Pacific Time.
Affected students can get two years of free identity protection

ETS is offering affected current and former students 24 months of free identity theft protection. Parents or legal guardians can enroll eligible children under 18, while adults, including former students, can enroll themselves. The services are designed to help monitor for potential identity theft and provide assistance if someone misuses their personal information.

The enrollment deadline is March 19, 2027. Eligible minors who turn 18 before March 19, 2029 may also qualify for adult coverage using the activation code provided in their notification. Enrollment is free, and no credit card is required. Identity restoration assistance is also available to eligible individuals for 24 months from their notification date, even without enrolling in monitoring services. For complete eligibility details and enrollment instructions, visit the California Department of Education's official incident webpage at at cde.ca.gov/nr/in/ets-incident.asp.
Investigators say an attacker used a compromised login credential to access and copy California student records over several months. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect your child after the California student data breach
Even without stolen passwords or financial account numbers, student records deserve serious attention. Here are practical steps I recommend taking if your family may be affected.

Scammers frequently use real data breaches as an excuse to send fraudulent emails. A message claiming to come from ETS or Experian could direct you to a fake enrollment website. Instead of clicking an unexpected link, open your browser and visit the official California Department of Education incident page. Follow the verified instructions from there.

Eligible families should take advantage of the 24 months of free identity-protection services being offered following this breach. Follow the enrollment instructions in your official notification and keep a copy for your records. No credit card is required.

For additional protection, consider an identity theft protection service which offers identity monitoring, alerts about suspicious activity and access to restoration specialists if identity theft occurs. Some services also offer paid family plans that can cover children, making it an option for parents concerned about protecting their family's personal information over the long term. Coverage and benefits vary by plan. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

One of the strongest steps you can take against certain forms of identity theft is placing a security freeze on a child's credit file. The Federal Trade Commission says parents and legal guardians can request a free credit freeze for children under 16. Teenagers ages 16 and 17 can request their own freezes. Contact Equifax, Experian and TransUnion separately. Each bureau has its own process for handling minors. A freeze can make it harder for criminals to open new credit accounts using a child's identity. However, it cannot prevent every form of fraud.

Pay closer attention to unexpected emails or text messages claiming to involve school records. A scammer with access to personal details could make a fraudulent communication seem unusually credible. For example, someone might claim that your child's testing account requires immediate verification. Before responding, contact the school using a phone number you already trust. Avoid sharing personal information through unexpected links or attachments. Consider using strong antivirus software on your family's devices. It can help detect malicious links, suspicious downloads and malware hidden in fake school notifications. While it cannot recover stolen student information, it adds another layer of protection against scammers who may try to exploit the breach. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Scammers can use information found online to build a more detailed profile of you or your family. That's why I recommend considering a personal data removal service. These services can help remove personal information from data broker websites that collect and sell details such as names, addresses and phone numbers. While these services cannot retrieve information stolen in this breach, they can help reduce how much additional information is publicly available. If you're concerned about your child's information, check whether the service offers protection for minors before signing up. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Adults who may have been affected can review their credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or suspicious activity. Visit AnnualCreditReport.com to obtain free reports from the three major credit bureaus. Parents should also watch for unexpected bills or collection notices addressed to their children. Those can be warning signs that someone has misused a minor's identity. If you discover evidence of identity theft, report it through IdentityTheft.gov . The FTC provides a recovery plan to help you address fraudulent accounts and document the problem.

You can also contact your child's school district to better understand how it handles student records. Ask what information outside contractors receive and how long they retain it. Schools may have legal obligations to maintain certain records. Still, parents can ask about retention policies and security safeguards. This conversation is worthwhile regardless of where your family lives.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've covered plenty of data breaches over the years, but this one bothers me because we're talking about children who had no choice about handing over their information. They went to school, took required tests and trusted the adults and organizations handling their records. Now, some of those details have ended up in the wrong hands. What I find especially troubling is how far back some of these records could go. Think about someone who left California years ago and has no reason to believe their old student information is still sitting on a testing company's system. That person could be living on the opposite side of the country and suddenly have to worry about a breach involving records from childhood. I appreciate that ETS is offering free identity protection, but I'd like to see schools and testing companies explain more clearly how long they keep sensitive student information and why. Parents deserve answers before a breach happens.

Should schools and outside testing companies be allowed to keep sensitive student records for years after a child leaves, or should families have more control over when that information gets deleted? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Apple confirms some iPhone Duo screen problems after launch
summary: Apple's iPhone Duo screens are cracking near the hinge just days after its $1,999 launch, and iFixit's CT scans may reveal what's going wrong.
story: D.A. Davidson head of technology research Gil Luria discusses Apple's unveiling of its first foldable iPhone, the 'Duo,' what the long-awaited device could mean for Apple's product strategy, the competitive landscape in the foldable smartphone market, consumer demand, and the company's broader innovation outlook on 'The Claman Countdown.'

Apple's first foldable iPhone has barely reached customers, and some owners are already dealing with cracked screens. The iPhone Duo launched on Oct. 23 with a starting price of $1,999. Within hours, complaints began appearing online from people who said their new phones developed cracks along the folding display.

Even more concerning, several reports describe damage appearing in nearly the same location. Some owners say their phones made unusual noises before the screens failed. Others noticed bright white lines spreading across the display. Now Apple has acknowledged the issue and says affected customers can request replacements. However, the company has yet to explain exactly what's causing the failures.

SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 LINEUP ADDS THREE CHOICES
One iPhone Duo owner says the inner display cracked before setup was complete, leaving bright lines running across the screen. (u/leftyhyzer16/Reddit)
iPhone Duo screen problems appear days after launch

Apple spent years developing its first folding iPhone. The device opens to reveal a 7.6-inch display, giving people a much larger screen without carrying a separate tablet. When closed, it looks like a compact smartphone with a 5.4-inch outer display. The design generated enormous excitement when Apple introduced it in September. However, that excitement took an unexpected turn shortly after the first phones reached customers.

Multiple iPhone Duo owners have reported cracks developing along the center of the inner display. In several cases, a bright line of damaged pixels extended from the fold toward the right side of the screen. Some owners have shared photos of the damage on Reddit, along with accounts of how quickly their new phones failed.

One owner, u/leftyhyzer16, said the screen cracked before setup was complete, after opening and closing the phone only a few times. Another owner, u/Midnight_Slump, reported a failure within six hours and received a replacement from Apple. Reddit moderators also checked additional photos and Apple paperwork provided by the owner. They confirmed the damaged phone and its replacement were genuine. Meanwhile, u/chimchambam said the display failed after just three hours. That owner reported being turned away by an Apple Store before ultimately returning the phone through Verizon. All three owners described problems appearing after very little use. Their experiences don't tell us how widespread the issue is, but they help explain why these early screen failures are getting so much attention.
Apple acknowledges the cracked iPhone Duo screens

On Oct. 26, Apple acknowledged reports about the damaged displays. In a statement provided to news outlets, the company said: "We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units." Apple has instructed affected owners to contact AppleCare for a replacement. That's encouraging news for anyone whose new phone has already failed, especially considering its $1,999 starting price.

However, Apple hasn't disclosed exactly how many devices are affected or identified what's causing the screens to crack. We also don't know whether the problem involves a manufacturing defect affecting certain phones or something in the overall design. We reached out to Apple for additional comment but did not receive a response before our deadline.
Why are the iPhone Duo screens cracking in the same place?

Here's what caught my attention. Several of the damaged screens appear to crack near the hinge, right where the phone folds. That's a pretty troubling place for something to go wrong on a $2,000 folding phone. So what's happening inside? The repair experts at iFixit took the iPhone Duo apart and used CT scans to get a closer look at its hinge. They spotted something that could help explain the damage. A small support bar may not move far enough out of the way when the phone folds. If the display presses against that bar, it could put enough pressure on the screen to cause a crack.

Now, I want to be clear. This is still a theory. iFixit hasn't confirmed that the support bar caused the reported damage, and Apple hasn't explained what's going wrong. But it does raise questions about how well the hinge and flexible screen work together, especially when people are already reporting similar cracks just days after buying the phone.
IOS 27 IS HERE: 10 IPHONE FEATURES YOU’LL WANT TO TRY NOW
An iPhone Duo owner photographed the damaged display at an Apple Store after the screen reportedly cracked within six hours of use. (u/Midnight_Slump / Reddit)
Repairing an iPhone Duo could be extremely expensive

Here's another detail that caught my attention. Although iFixit found that the iPhone Duo was more repairable than other foldable phones it had tested, replacing its inner display remains complicated. The company gave the device a provisional repairability score of 5 out of 10. More importantly, it reported that an out-of-warranty inner-screen repair costs $999. That's roughly half the starting price of the phone.

Fortunately, Apple says customers affected by this particular display issue should contact AppleCare for a replacement. An AppleCare+ subscription is not required to request help for the acknowledged defect. However, accidental damage and unrelated screen repairs may fall under different coverage terms. You can learn more in our guide to checking your Apple warranty and what it covers.
What to do if your iPhone Duo screen cracks

If you recently purchased an iPhone Duo, pay attention to how the hinge feels when you open and close the device. A sudden increase in resistance or an unfamiliar popping sound deserves attention. If you notice something unusual, avoid forcing the phone open or closed. Don't repeatedly fold it to see whether the problem happens again. If your screen develops cracks or bright lines, here are some steps worth taking.

Document the damage. Take photographs of the affected display if you can do so safely. Save your purchase receipt and note when the problem first appeared. These details may help when discussing the issue with Apple.Contact AppleCare directly. Visit Apple Support at support.apple.com/contact or arrange an appointment at an Apple Store. Explain what happened and mention Apple's acknowledgment of the inner-display issue. Even if you purchased the phone through a wireless carrier, Apple recommends contacting AppleCare for this problem.Back up your information before exchanging the phone. If your display still works, open Settings, tap your name, select iCloud, then tap iCloud Backup and choose Back Up Now. Make sure the backup finishes before handing over your device. If the screen no longer works, ask Apple about available recovery options.

Explain what happened and mention Apple's acknowledgment of the inner-display issue. Even if you purchased the phone through a wireless carrier, Apple recommends contacting AppleCare for this problem.

Back up your information before exchanging the phone. If your display still works, open Settings, tap your name, select iCloud, then tap iCloud Backup and choose Back Up Now. Ask about replacement availability. Some affected customers have received immediate exchanges at Apple Stores. However, replacement inventory may vary. Contact Apple before making a special trip and confirm the next steps for your particular device.
Why one Samsung foldable fan is returning his iPhone Duo

The concerns go beyond cracked screens. My colleague Chris was excited to switch from his Samsung Galaxy Fold to Apple’s new iPhone Duo. But after trying it, he was so disappointed that he decided to return it to Best Buy and get an iPhone 18 Pro instead.

He found the interface buggy and cumbersome, missed having Face ID and felt the cameras fell short of his expectations. He also preferred the display quality of other phones. At nearly $2,000, he simply couldn’t justify keeping it, saying, "I think the craftsmanship is phenomenal. I love the heft and the solid nature of the device, but because I’m coming from a foldable, there were so many glaring missteps that Apple made along the way, and at first they were little, but little things add up to the point where you genuinely question whether this truly was ready for prime time."

Now, Chris’s phone didn’t crack. His complaints are about the overall experience. But when someone who already enjoys using a foldable phone decides Apple’s version isn’t worth keeping, that gets my attention. I still think the Duo has some impressive features, but between these early screen problems and Chris’s experience, I’d want to try one in person before spending that kind of money.
Kurt's key takeaways

I've been looking forward to seeing what Apple could do with a foldable iPhone, and I still think the Duo is an impressive piece of technology. But I have to admit, these early screen failures would make me nervous about spending nearly $2,000 on one. I give Apple credit for acknowledging the problem quickly and offering replacements. That's the right response. What I want to know now is why these screens are failing and whether Apple can prevent the same thing from happening to replacement devices. Then there's my colleague Chris, who already knows his way around a Samsung foldable and still found Apple's version disappointing enough to return it. That tells me Apple has some convincing to do beyond fixing the screen issue. At this price, I want a phone that feels like an upgrade, not one that makes me question what I'm giving up. For now, I'd be inclined to wait rather than rush out and buy one.

title: 50,000 airline miles stolen from a travel expert
summary: Travel expert Katy Nastro says 50,000 American Airlines AAdvantage miles vanished from her account after someone redeemed them without permission.
story: Travel expert Katy Nastro tells Kurt ‘CyberGuy’ Knutsson that someone used her American Airlines miles and explained why saving your travel rewards may not pay off.

If you're anything like me, you've probably spent years collecting airline miles, dreaming about the trip you'll eventually take. Maybe it's a business class seat to Europe or that vacation you've been putting off. You keep earning points and watching the balance grow. But what happens when you finally check your account and discover someone else has already spent them?

That's exactly what happened to Katy Nastro, a travel expert with Flighty, a flight-tracking app that provides real-time updates on delays, cancellations and gate changes. During our conversation on "The CyberGuy Report" podcast, Katy shared how more than 50,000 American Airlines miles vanished from her account. Someone had redeemed them for a flight without her permission.

What surprised me was that Katy knows the travel industry inside and out. Yet she still found herself dealing with a problem that could happen to anyone with a frequent flyer account. Her experience offers a warning, especially as holiday travel approaches.
9 WARNING SIGNS OF IDENTITY THEFT YOU SHOULD NEVER IGNORE

Travel expert Katy Nastro discovered that someone had redeemed 50,000 American Airlines miles from her account without permission. (Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How a travel expert discovered 50,000 stolen airline miles

Katy had just landed in New York and was riding home in an Uber. Like many frequent travelers, she opened her American Airlines app to check how many miles she'd earned from her latest trip. Instead, she noticed a substantial drop in her balance. At first, she figured the app had made a mistake. She remembered redeeming about 10,000 miles recently, but the balance was off by roughly 50,000. So she refreshed the app. The missing miles were still missing. That's when she called American Airlines.

The airline told her that someone had redeemed the miles for a ticket in another person's name. Katy had been saving for a trip to Asia. Unfortunately, those miles were now associated with a flight she knew nothing about.
"I really had this just stomach drop moment," Katy told me.
She had spent years earning those rewards, including through long flights to Australia. Suddenly, someone else had benefited from all that travel.
"I naively never thought this could happen to me because I work in the industry," she admitted.
I found that particularly revealing. Katy had previously warned people about loyalty account theft. Even with that experience, she never expected to become a victim herself.
Getting stolen airline miles back was surprisingly complicated

You might assume the airline could simply reverse an unauthorized redemption. After all, the ticket was booked in someone else's name. Unfortunately, Katy discovered that getting her miles back required additional work. American Airlines instructed her to submit a formal fraud complaint by email. She also had to file a police report and provide documentation before the airline would restore her miles.
"I had to have the police report filed with them before anything was credited," Katy explained.

She eventually recovered her miles, but the process didn't end there. Katy also had to create a new email address and establish a replacement American Airlines AAdvantage account. Thankfully, the airline transferred her existing status along with her restored rewards. What caught my attention was the police report requirement. Katy had to involve local law enforcement even though the theft happened entirely online. She understood why the airline might want official documentation, but she questioned whether the process needed to be so cumbersome.

There's another concern for travelers. Airline loyalty points generally don't carry the same protections as money stolen through an unauthorized credit card purchase. In fact, American Airlines' current AAdvantage terms say the airline has no general obligation to restore miles withdrawn without authorization.

The company may review requests submitted within three months of the unauthorized withdrawal, but reimbursement remains discretionary. That makes discovering suspicious activity quickly especially important. Also, keep in mind that each loyalty program has its own fraud procedures. A police report may be requested, but the requirement isn't universal.
How thieves turn stolen airline miles into real trips

I asked Katy something that had been bothering me. Who was actually flying around using her miles? She had no idea. The airline identified a redemption involving someone else's name, but Katy didn't know who was behind it or where the traveler was headed. Loyalty programs often allow members to book tickets for other people. Some also permit mileage transfers or gifts. Those legitimate features can create opportunities for criminals who gain unauthorized access to an account.

For example, someone who controls your account could redeem miles for a ticket under another person's name. Depending on the program, the points might also be transferred or exchanged for other rewards. However, Katy never learned exactly how someone accessed her account. During our conversation, she acknowledged that password reuse may have played a role.
"I think I fell into the trap of using the same password for everything," she said.

That's an easy habit to fall into. If criminals obtain a password from one compromised service, they may try using it to access other accounts. And here's something worth remembering. A loyalty balance may look like a collection of numbers on your screen, but those numbers can pay for expensive flights.
Why saving airline miles forever could cost you
Katy shared another piece of advice that might surprise anyone who's been patiently saving miles for years. She believes travelers should think twice about holding on to their rewards indefinitely.
"I would highly suggest that you should not be waiting on those miles," she told me.

Her concern comes down to depreciation. Airlines can change their award pricing, which means a flight that once required 50,000 miles might eventually require considerably more. I compared holding on to miles to buying a new car and watching its value drop after driving off the lot. Katy agreed. In her view, people often wait too long for that perfect first-class redemption. She recommends considering redemptions within a year instead of endlessly saving for a future trip.

Of course, you still want to check whether an award flight offers reasonable value. Spending 80,000 miles on an inexpensive economy ticket could be a poor deal. However, if you need to travel during a busy holiday period, using miles for an economy seat may make sense.

Award tickets can also offer more flexibility than certain restrictive cash fares. Just check the airline's cancellation and redeposit rules before booking. We've shared more strategies in our article, Are airline miles still worth it?
And if you're looking to earn more rewards for your next trip, check out my picks for the best airline credit cards of 2026 at CyberGuy.com to see which programs might work best for you.
YOUR CREDIT CAN LOOK NORMAL WHILE SOMEONE STEALS YOUR IDENTITY
Travelers spend years earning airline miles, but stolen rewards can disappear before they ever reach their dream destination. (iStock)
Watch out for fake airline alerts and customer service scams

During our conversation, I told Katy about something I've been seeing more frequently. I receive emails that look like legitimate airline notifications, claiming miles were redeemed from my account. Some are convincing enough that I've nearly clicked them myself. That's a particularly sneaky approach because many airlines send real notifications when members redeem rewards. Criminals can imitate those messages to create panic and lure people toward fake login pages.

Katy warned that scammers also create fake airline support accounts on social media. Someone looking for help with a delayed flight or missing miles might contact what appears to be an official account. The conversation can then move to a private message or even WhatsApp, where the criminal asks for personal information. Katy's warning was clear. Avoid sharing sensitive account information through social media conversations. If you receive a suspicious redemption notice, open the airline's official app yourself. Check your account activity directly rather than following links in the message.
How to protect your airline miles and hotel points

Before your next trip, take a few minutes to secure the loyalty accounts you've spent years building. These steps can help you spot unauthorized activity sooner and make your accounts harder to compromise.

Open your airline and hotel loyalty apps at least once a month. Review recent redemptions and compare your current balance with what you expected. Katy said she sometimes went several months without checking her account. That made it harder to know when the unauthorized redemption occurred. Setting a recurring calendar reminder can help you catch unusual activity sooner. Also, enable account activity and redemption alerts if your loyalty program offers them. That way, you may find out about suspicious transactions before you notice missing miles.

Never reuse your airline password on another website. A password manager can generate strong, unique passwords and store them securely. Also, protect the email account connected to your loyalty program. Someone who gains access to that inbox may be able to reset your rewards password.

Look for two-factor authentication (2FA), passkeys or other login verification options offered by your airline or hotel program. These protections vary by provider, so check your account's security settings. Also, review any unfamiliar changes to your contact information and remove devices or sessions you no longer recognize when the service allows it.

If an email or text claims someone used your points, resist clicking its links. Instead, open the official airline app or type the website address into your browser. Legitimate-looking logos and familiar formatting offer no guarantee that a message is genuine.

Also, be skeptical of anyone claiming to represent airline support through an unsolicited social media message. Use strong antivirus software to help detect malicious links, block dangerous websites and protect against malware designed to steal your passwords. While antivirus software can't stop every phishing scam, it provides an additional layer of protection if you accidentally click something suspicious.
Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.
FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS
Regularly checking your airline miles balance and securing your loyalty accounts can help protect your hard-earned travel rewards. (iStock)

Contact your loyalty program through its verified customer service channels as soon as you notice an unauthorized redemption. Ask the airline to secure your account and investigate the transaction. Save your account statements and any correspondence. If the airline requests a police report, follow its instructions and keep a copy. Don't delay because some programs impose deadlines on fraud claims.

Katy suggested using a dedicated email address for loyalty programs. That can make account notifications easier to track and reduce exposure if an unrelated service suffers a breach. Another option is to use an email alias, which helps keep your primary address private. It lets you create unlimited email aliases, helping you organize travel accounts while reducing spam and unwanted exposure. You can also follow my guide on how to create and use email aliases.
For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit CyberGuy.com.

Your personal information may already be circulating on data broker websites, making it easier for scammers to target you with convincing airline phishing emails or impersonation attempts. Consider using a personal data removal service. It helps remove your personal information from hundreds of data broker and people search sites and continues submitting removal requests when your details reappear. While no service can erase everything or directly prevent someone from stealing your airline miles, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for scammers to gather personal details and tailor their attacks.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Be careful about sharing photos of boarding passes, luggage tags or travel confirmations online. These documents can contain booking reference numbers, frequent flyer details or barcodes that expose information about your trip. Criminals may use those details to access reservations or impersonate travelers. Avoid posting travel documents on social media, and securely dispose of printed boarding passes after your trip.

You can use an AI assistant like ChatGPT with scheduled tasks to monitor airline loyalty programs for changes that could reduce the value of your miles. Set up a daily alert to check for announced changes to redemption rates, award pricing or loyalty program rules. You can even ask it to track news about American Airlines AAdvantage or other programs you use.

That way, you may hear about upcoming changes while there's still time to redeem your miles at current rates. Keep in mind that airlines don't always announce devaluations in advance, so AI can't predict every change. For step-by-step guidance, check out my article on 8 seriously annoying tasks you can hand off to an AI agent.
Kurt's key takeaways

I keep thinking about Katy sitting in the back of that Uber, casually checking her mileage balance and discovering that 50,000 hard-earned miles had disappeared. I've collected airline miles for years, and I know how much planning goes into using them. The thought of some stranger enjoying a trip on my points would make me furious. What concerns me even more is that Katy works in the travel industry and still couldn't explain exactly how someone got into her account.

That tells me we should give our loyalty accounts the same attention we give our financial accounts. Check your balances, use unique passwords and pay attention to unusual activity. And while I love saving miles for a great trip, Katy makes a convincing argument for enjoying those rewards while they still offer good value.

I encourage you to listen to The CyberGuy Report podcast at cyberguy.com/podcast/ to hear my full conversation with Katy Nastro. Her experience might change how you think about the miles you've been collecting. And if you want more ways to make those rewards go further, visit CyberGuyLive.com to sign up for my free upcoming webinar: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money on Oct. 31 at 11 AM ET/8 AM PT.

title: How to get rid of unwanted AI on your phone
summary: Google AI Overviews can't be permanently turned off, but adding -AI to your searches and using the built-in Web filter can help bypass AI summaries.
story: The camera app on a Pixel 11 Pro Fold smartphone during a content capture event in New York on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

You pull out your phone to look something up on Google. Maybe you're researching a purchase or trying to find a restaurant. You expect a list of websites. Instead, Google serves up a lengthy artificial intelligence-generated answer before you even get to the search results. Sound familiar? I like AI when it helps me get something done. But sometimes I just want to search the internet without an AI summary appearing every time.

Fortunately, there are ways around it. One involves adding a few characters to your search. Another uses a built-in Google filter. And if you've had enough of Siri suggestions on your iPhone or AI features popping up on your Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel, there are settings worth changing there, too.
Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money

In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com.
HOW TO SEARCH ANYTHING ON IPHONE, GALAXY AND PIXEL
You can take back control of your smartphone by turning off unwanted AI features on your iPhone, Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to get rid of Google AI search results on your phone

Google calls those automatically generated summaries AI Overviews. They appear above traditional search results when Google's systems decide an AI-generated answer might be helpful. Sometimes they save time. However, they can also get in the way when you'd rather read information directly from a website. Unfortunately, Google confirms that AI Overviews cannot be permanently turned off through a standard Search setting. However, you have a few ways to avoid them.
This trick takes only seconds and is worth trying on an iPhone, iPad, Samsung Galaxy or Google Pixel.
Here's how.

Open Safari, Chrome or your preferred browser.Visit Google.com.Enter your search terms as usual.Tap Search.If an AI Overview appears, return to the search field.Add -AI at the end of your search.Tap Search again.
Open Safari, Chrome or your preferred browser.
Visit Google.com.
Enter your search terms as usual.
Tap Search.
If an AI Overview appears, return to the search field.
Add -AI at the end of your search.
Tap Search again.
For example, instead of searching for: best walking shoes
Try: best walking shoes -AI

Adding -AI can keep an AI Overview from appearing. However, this is an unofficial workaround, and Google doesn't guarantee that it will work every time. There's another catch. Google uses the minus sign to exclude terms from search results. Adding -AI could also remove some relevant pages containing that term. If the trick doesn't work, Google's next option is more dependable.
Google has a built-in filter that shows traditional web links without AI Overviews.
Here's how to find it.

Open Safari, Chrome or your preferred browser.Go to Google.com.Type your search.Tap Search.Look for the filters near the top of the results.Swipe across the options or tap More, if necessary.Select Web.
Open Safari, Chrome or your preferred browser.
Go to Google.com.
Type your search.
Tap Search.
Look for the filters near the top of the results.
Swipe across the options or tap More, if necessary.
Select Web.

Google will display text-based links without its AI Overview. The downside is that you generally need to select the Web filter again when starting another search. Still, it's a useful way to get straight to websites without an AI-generated answer taking up the top of the screen.
One important note: Turning off an AI Overviews experiment in Google Search Labs won't necessarily remove AI Overviews from regular Google searches.
Want an AI-free search engine? Try DuckDuckGo

If you're really tired of AI showing up in searches, there's another option worth knowing about. DuckDuckGo offers a dedicated search experience called DuckDuckGo No-AI. You can access it at noai.duckduckgo.com. According to DuckDuckGo, this version removes its AI-assisted answers and AI feature suggestions. It also filters AI-generated images from image searches. The company acknowledges that AI-image filtering may not catch everything. You can use the website directly without changing your phone's default search engine.
Change your default search engine on iPhone or iPad
If you want to use a different search engine more regularly, Apple makes switching easy.
These instructions apply to iOS 27 and iPadOS 27.
Open Settings on your iPhone or iPad.Tap Search.Select Search Engine.Choose your preferred search engine.Tap Back to save your selection.
Open Settings on your iPhone or iPad.
Tap Search.
Select Search Engine.
Choose your preferred search engine.
Tap Back to save your selection.
Keep in mind that choosing regular DuckDuckGo as your default doesn't automatically activate its separate No-AI experience. You can visit the No-AI website whenever you want to use it.
MALICIOUS BROWSER EXTENSIONS CAN HIJACK AI ASSISTANTS
Adding -AI to the end of a search may help hide AI Overviews, although the trick isn't guaranteed to work every time. (Gabby Jones/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How to remove Siri suggestions from the top of iPhone Search

Now let's talk about another feature that can get annoying. Ever swipe down on your iPhone's Home Screen to search for something and immediately see a collection of suggested apps? Those suggestions come from Siri, which can recommend apps based on your activity. Maybe you appreciate the shortcuts. Or maybe you would rather see a clean search screen until you start typing. Apple lets you turn those suggestions off.
Open Settings on your iPhone.Tap Siri.Select Suggestions.Turn off Suggest Apps Before Searching.
Open Settings on your iPhone.
Tap Siri.
Select Suggestions.
Turn off Suggest Apps Before Searching.

Your iPhone should stop showing those suggested apps before you begin searching. While you're there, you can also disable Show in App Library if you don't want suggestions appearing there. You can turn off Show When Sharing if you'd rather not see suggested contacts or other Siri recommendations when sharing content. These controls change where Siri suggestions appear. They don't disable Siri itself.
Apple's more conversational Siri AI is available in beta on supported iPhones running iOS 27.
If you enabled it and would rather return to the previous Siri experience, Apple provides that option.
Open Settings.Tap Siri.Scroll down and select Turn Off Siri.Tap Turn Off Siri again to confirm.To restore the previous assistant, tap Turn On Siri.Select Siri Classic.
Open Settings.
Tap Siri.
Scroll down and select Turn Off Siri.
Tap Turn Off Siri again to confirm.
To restore the previous assistant, tap Turn On Siri.
Select Siri Classic.
If you don't want to use Siri at all, leave it turned off.

Important: Siri AI requires an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPhone, including the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and iPhone 16 models or later. Availability also depends on language and region. Older iPhones won't have the same Siri AI options.

There's another AI feature that may bother some iPhone owners. Apple Intelligence can summarize notifications, messages and emails. While that may sound convenient, AI summaries can leave out details or misunderstand what someone wrote. If you'd rather read the original text, you can disable those features.
Turn off AI notification summaries
Open Settings.Tap Notifications.Select Summarize Notifications.Turn off Summarize Notifications.
Open Settings.
Tap Notifications.
Select Summarize Notifications.
Turn off Summarize Notifications.
Disable AI summaries in Messages
Open Settings.Tap Apps.Select Messages.Turn off Summarize Messages.
Open Settings.
Tap Apps.
Select Messages.
Turn off Summarize Messages.
You can also open Settings, tap Apps, select Mail and turn off Summarize Message Previews.
These options are available on compatible devices running iOS 27. Disabling them won't affect your ability to receive regular messages or notifications.
How to turn off unwanted Galaxy AI features on Samsung phones

Samsung has been adding AI tools to its Galaxy phones, including features that help with calls or photos. Some can be useful. However, you may have no interest in having AI analyze information or suggest actions throughout your day. Fortunately, Samsung provides individual controls for many Galaxy AI features.

Open Settings on your Samsung Galaxy.Tap Galaxy AI.On some devices, just scroll down, while on others tap Advanced features, then Galaxy AI or Awesome Intelligence.Select a feature you don't want, such as Note assist.Turn off the available switches for that feature.Repeat for any other features you want to disable.
Open Settings on your Samsung Galaxy.
Tap Galaxy AI.
On some devices, just scroll down, while on others tap Advanced features, then Galaxy AI or Awesome Intelligence.
Select a feature you don't want, such as Note assist.
Turn off the available switches for that feature.
Repeat for any other features you want to disable.

Samsung notes that some AI features are built into the operating system and cannot be disabled. Also, available controls vary depending on your Galaxy model and software version. Samsung recommends restarting your device after disabling Galaxy AI features to ensure the changes take effect.
Samsung's Now brief can show personalized information about your day, including upcoming events and other recommendations. If you don't want those briefings appearing on your Lock screen, try this.
Open Settings.Tap Lock screen and AOD or Lock screen.Select Now bar.Find Now brief among the available options.Turn Now brief off.
Open Settings.
Tap Lock screen and AOD or Lock screen.
Select Now bar.
Find Now brief among the available options.
Turn Now brief off.

You can also open Settings, tap Galaxy AI and select Now brief to adjust the information included in your briefings. On supported devices, you can disable Show Now brief while phone is locked. Keep in mind that removing Now brief from the Lock screen doesn't necessarily remove the feature from your Galaxy phone.
If you're concerned about information being sent to the cloud for AI processing, Samsung offers another option.
Open Settings.Tap Galaxy AI.Find Process data only on device.Turn the switch On.
Open Settings.
Tap Galaxy AI.
Find Process data only on device.
Turn the switch On.

This tells supported Samsung Galaxy AI features to process data locally instead of using cloud processing. However, some AI features require an internet connection and may become unavailable. Also, this control applies to Samsung's supported Galaxy AI features. It doesn't prevent every app on your phone from connecting to its own cloud services.
Circle to Search lets you search for something displayed on your screen. However, you might accidentally activate it while navigating your phone.
You can switch it off.
Open Settings.Tap Display.Select Navigation bar.Turn off Circle to Search.
Open Settings.
Tap Display.
Select Navigation bar.
Turn off Circle to Search.
How to turn off unwanted AI features on Google Pixel

Google Pixel phones have their own AI features designed to anticipate what you might need. Depending on your device, these can include Magic Cue or Google's newer Proactive Assistance. Both can provide suggestions using information from supported apps, depending on your settings and permissions. However, you may prefer to keep those suggestions out of your conversations.
On supported Pixel 10 models, Magic Cue can display helpful information while you're using your phone. For example, it might surface flight details during a conversation.
Here's how to adjust it.

Open Settings.Tap Magic Cue.Review the available suggestion types.Turn off any suggestions you don't want.Tap Base suggestions on apps.Turn off Use data from recent screen activity if you don't want Magic Cue using that information.Turn off Use foundational data if you don't want it using supported Google Account information.
Open Settings.
Tap Magic Cue.
Review the available suggestion types.
Turn off any suggestions you don't want.
Tap Base suggestions on apps.
Turn off Use data from recent screen activity if you don't want Magic Cue using that information.
Turn off Use foundational data if you don't want it using supported Google Account information.
Magic Cue is available only on supported Pixel models and in supported regions.

Google introduced a newer feature called Proactive Assistance on Pixel 11 devices in supported markets, including the United States. When enabled, it can use screen information and notifications to provide suggestions. It may also use information from connected apps and location data.
If you'd rather skip those suggestions, Google gives you a direct switch.
Open Settings.Tap Proactive Assistance.Turn off Use Proactive Assistance.
Open Settings.
Tap Proactive Assistance.
Turn off Use Proactive Assistance.
You can also tap Connected apps to decide which apps the feature can access. Proactive Assistance is opt-in, so you won't necessarily see suggestions unless you've enabled it.
Circle to Search is also available on supported Pixel phones. If you find yourself activating it accidentally, you can turn it off.
Open Settings.Search for Circle to Search.Tap Circle to Search.Turn it Off.
Open Settings.
Search for Circle to Search.
Tap Circle to Search.
Turn it Off.
Google also lists the feature under System on supported Pixel devices.

On supported Pixel phones, the Pixel Screenshots app can generate summaries and help you search through saved screenshots. If you don't want those AI features processing screenshot content, Google provides an option to disable them.
Open the Pixel Screenshots app.Tap Settings in the upper-right corner.Turn off Search your screenshots with AI.
Open the Pixel Screenshots app.
Tap Settings in the upper-right corner.
Turn off Search your screenshots with AI.

If you also want to delete previously generated AI information, select Delete all AI summaries and metadata. That last option removes the generated summaries and metadata associated with the feature. Only select it if you're comfortable deleting that information.
ANTI-SCAM SETTINGS ON IPHONE, PIXEL AND GALAXY YOU SHOULD CHECK
Smartphone users can adjust settings on their phones to turn off AI-assisted search features. (Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
How to stop Gemini from popping up on Android phones

Finally, there's Gemini, Google's AI assistant. On many Android phones, Gemini can launch when you say "Hey Google" or press and hold the power button. If you're tired of activating it accidentally, there are several ways to stop that behavior.
Turn off Hey Google in Gemini
Open the Gemini app.Tap Menu, then your profile picture or initial.Select Settings.Tap Talk to Gemini hands-free.Turn off Hey Google.
Open the Gemini app.
Tap Menu, then your profile picture or initial.
Select Settings.
Tap Talk to Gemini hands-free.
Turn off Hey Google.
This prevents Gemini from responding to the wake phrase. You can still open the app manually if you want to use it.
On Google Pixel and other supported Android phones:
Open Settings.Tap System.Select Gestures.Tap Press & hold power button.Choose a different action instead of launching the digital assistant.
Open Settings.
Tap System.
Select Gestures.
Tap Press & hold power button.
Choose a different action instead of launching the digital assistant.
On Samsung Galaxy phones, search Settings for Side button to find the equivalent shortcut control.
If you'd rather stop using Gemini as your phone's main assistant, Google provides another option.
Open Settings.Tap Apps.Select Default apps.Tap Digital assistant app.Select Default digital assistant app.Choose None if you don't want a default assistant.
Open Settings.
Tap Apps.
Select Default apps.
Tap Digital assistant app.
Select Default digital assistant app.
Choose None if you don't want a default assistant.

You can also switch back to Google Assistant through the Gemini app on supported devices. Removing Gemini as the default assistant won't necessarily uninstall the Gemini app or erase any previous Gemini activity.
Can you completely remove AI from your phone?

There isn't one universal switch that removes every AI feature from an iPhone or Android device. Some functions are built directly into the software. Others come from individual apps or online services.

However, you can make a noticeable difference by disabling the features you never use. And remember, turning off an AI assistant won't automatically remove AI Overviews from Google Search. Those require separate controls. If you're concerned about how AI services collect information, we've also covered how to opt out of AI data collection in popular apps.
Kurt's key takeaways

I use AI regularly, and I appreciate what it can do. But I also understand why people get annoyed when it starts showing up everywhere. Sometimes I want to Google something and read what an actual person wrote. I don't need an AI summary making that decision for me. That's why I like having Google's Web filter available. And discovering DuckDuckGo's No-AI search option gives people another choice. I also think it's worth taking a few minutes to look at the AI settings on your phone. You may discover features running that you never use. Turning them off can make your phone feel more like your own again. I want AI available when I need it, but I don't want companies deciding that I need it all the time.

Are Apple, Google and Samsung giving us useful AI features, or are they pushing the technology so aggressively that we're losing control of our own phones? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Is that campaign merch store official? Here's how to tell
summary: Attaxion researchers found 30 fake Texas campaign merchandise stores traced to just two sellers hawking gear for competing Republicans and Democrats.
story: George Weiner, CEO of Whole Whale and creator of PACspam.org, tells Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson why blocking political texts rarely works and how a free tool can help you fight back.

You're scrolling online when you spot a campaign T-shirt supporting your favorite candidate. The website looks professional, the merchandise looks legitimate and the address includes the candidate's name. You might even see the word "official" at the top of the page. So, you assume your purchase supports the campaign. But what if the candidate has nothing to do with that store?

With the Nov. 3 midterm elections approaching, new research shared with CyberGuy reveals a troubling discovery in Texas. Researchers at cybersecurity company Attaxion identified 626 unofficial election-related domains, including 30 online merchandise stores presenting themselves as official campaign shops.

Attaxion says it could not verify an official campaign connection for any of the 30 stores. Even more surprising, researchers found that nearly all appeared to come from just two sellers offering merchandise for competing Republicans and Democrats. The findings arrive as the FBI warns about election-related scams involving fake merchandise, fraudulent donations and websites designed to steal personal information. And while this investigation focuses on Texas, the warning signs apply to elections and online shopping across the country.

You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
