title: Tinder killer who believed he was a warlock said he 'picked the wrong person' after murdering woman
summary: Sydney Loofe's friend catfished her killer's girlfriend on Tinder, providing the first major break in the Nebraska murder investigation.
story: A voicemail from Brian Walshe's mother offers new insight into the troubled marriage at the center of the high-profile Ana Walshe murder case.

Sydney Loofe thought she was heading out for a second date with a woman she met on Tinder. Instead, the 24-year-old vanished — and the man convicted of her murder would later make a disturbing admission about why she proved to be the "wrong person" to kill.
"I don't regret killing Sydney," Aubrey Trail said, according to filmmaker Christopher St. John. "I don't regret killing somebody, but I regret killing ... I picked the wrong person."

Trail, then a 52-year-old con man, was convicted of strangling the Nebraska store clerk with an electrical cord in 2017, cutting her body into 14 pieces, placing the remains in garbage bags and dumping them in roadside ditches. At the trial, witnesses testified that Trail and his girlfriend, Bailey Boswell, then 25, had solicited them for group sex and talked about the occult and gaining "powers" through killing.
ARIZONA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING WOMAN AFTER SOCIAL MEDIA FIRST DATE ENDS IN DESERT GRAVE

Aubrey Trail, 60, remains on death row at the Tecumseh State Correctional Institution in Nebraska. He was sentenced to death in 2021 for the 2017 murder of 24-year-old Sydney Loofe. According to "Swipe Right on the Devil," Trail and his girlfriend, Bailey Boswell, used the dating app Tinder to lure victims. (Hulu)

"One of the FBI agents said that the culprits were in a frenzy," St. John told Fox News Digital. "They were looking to do this, and Sydney was the available target. She was trusting and innocent and fit the profile. You then later hear Aubrey Trail, the murderer, says, 'I picked the wrong person.'"
"I think that's incredibly chilling for me because he has no remorse, but he wishes that he hadn't chosen someone with such strong family and friends because it led to his capture."
"Swipe Right on the Devil," the three-part true crime docuseries about Sydney Loofe’s murder, is streaming now on Hulu. (Hulu)

Loofe's murder at the hands of Trail, who described himself as a "powerful warlock" and the leader of a sex cult, is explored in the new Hulu true crime docuseries "Swipe Right on the Devil." The three-part series features interviews with Loofe's loved ones and investigators, as well as recordings of Trail from death row.
Sydney Loofe went on a date before she vanished. (FBI Omaha)

Loofe, a cashier at Menards, a home improvement store, lived alone in an apartment with her cat, Mimsy. According to friends, she was yearning for a relationship. On Tinder, she came across a profile for a woman named Audrey, an alias used by Boswell. After matching and exchanging messages, the two women went on their first date. They planned a second date for the next day. Loofe was smitten.

"Sydney was like any one of us," said St. John. "She was feeling lonely and searching for belonging. She had gone on a date with this woman, and she was so excited that she immediately wrote to her friends. They were like, 'Great, nothing to worry about.' And she was never heard from again. Something awful came out of the darkness."

Sydney Loofe, a 24-year-old Nebraska store clerk, was looking for love when she connected with Bailey Boswell on Tinder in November 2017. What began as a promising match would ultimately lead to her murder. (Lincoln Police Department)

When Loofe didn't show up for her morning shift the following day, her family requested a welfare check. Police found her car in the driveway. Her work clothes and purse were laid out for work. Her cat hadn't been fed.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Sydney Loofe, 24, was reported missing in mid-November 2017. (FBI Omaha)

Loofe's friend, Brooklyn McCrystal, knew that she had been on a date the night before she disappeared. McCrystal created a Tinder profile to find Audrey in hopes of getting her contact information. When McCrystal matched with Audrey on the dating app, they exchanged phone numbers. McCrystal gave Boswell's information to police. Loofe's friends also showed investigators her final social media post, a selfie shared on Snapchat captioned "Ready for my date."

"Brooklyn provided the first big break in the case," said St. John. "She catfished the bad guys. There's digital tracking. It's got all the hallmarks of an amazing investigation. But ultimately, what led to Aubrey and Bailey's capture was the people who were devoted to Sydney searching for answers."

Corey O'Brien of the Nebraska Attorney General's Office speaks to the media following the first appearance by Aubrey Trail and Bailey Boswell after the pair were charged with first-degree murder of Sydney Loofe and improper disposal of human skeletal remains at the Saline County Courthouse in Wilber, Nebraska, June 12, 2018. (Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images)

Boswell refused to cooperate with investigators. When police tracked her phone, they learned it was a burner phone registered under a fake name. They traced the phone to hotels in the area, where surveillance video and a state-issued ID presented at check-in helped investigators identify Boswell as "Audrey." The video also showed that she was traveling with an older man, Trail. The Lincoln Journal Star reported that Loofe's phone last pinged at Boswell and Trail's apartment that night.

Bailey Boswell and Aubrey Trail were a couple living together in Wilber, Nebraska, when they were accused of luring women through dating apps and drawing them into a controlling relationship involving sex, crime and claims of witchcraft. Both were later convicted in the 2017 murder of Sydney Loofe. (Hulu)
Investigators obtained a search warrant for the apartment, which smelled strongly of bleach. Boswell and Trail had paid their rent early and left.

Police named Boswell and Trail as persons of interest. On Nov. 29, 2017, the couple released a video on social media denying any involvement in Loofe's disappearance. Boswell said she had gone on two dates with Loofe, but after their second date, she had dropped Loofe off at a friend’s house. Despite maintaining their innocence, they went on the run.

Sydney Loofe was last seen alive on Nov. 15, 2017, when she left for a second date with Bailey Boswell, whom she had met on Tinder. Prosecutors said Boswell took the 24-year-old to the Nebraska apartment she shared with Aubrey Trail, where Loofe was murdered. (FBI Omaha)
Boswell and Trail were arrested on Nov. 30, 2017, near Branson, Missouri, on unrelated federal fraud charges.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

Aubrey Trail and Bailey Boswell were arrested in Missouri on Nov. 30, 2017, on unrelated warrants as authorities investigated the disappearance of Sydney Loofe. The couple was formally charged with first-degree murder in Loofe’s death in June 2018. (Saline County Sheriff's Office)
Nearly three weeks after Loofe disappeared, investigators used cellphone data to trace Boswell and Trail's movements and identify rural areas where they appeared to have slowed down or stopped.

On Dec. 4, 2017, investigators searched a roadside ditch near Edgar, Nebraska. They found car keys, a phone, a label with Loofe's name and her dismembered upper arm, which bore a tattoo that read "Everything will be wonderful someday." The Lincoln Journal Star reported that some garbage bags contained her clothing.

Sydney Loofe had a tattoo on her left forearm that read, "Everything will be wonderful someday." The deeply personal message became a poignant reminder of the 24-year-old’s hopeful outlook on life following her 2017 murder. (Hulu)

According to court documents, Trail and Boswell were captured on surveillance video at a Home Depot in Lincoln on Nov. 15, 2017, buying tools investigators believed were used to dismember Loofe, hours before her death. Investigators believed Boswell and Trail had lured Loofe through Tinder before killing her and dismembering her body.

Bailey Boswell appears via video conference during her first court appearance before Saline County Judge Linda Bauer after being charged with first-degree murder in the death of Sydney Loofe and improper disposal of human skeletal remains at the Saline County Courthouse in Wilber, Nebraska, on June 12, 2018. (Omaha World-Herald via Getty Images)

"During the trial, the prosecutor said that Aubrey and Bailey had four arms, four legs and one mind," director Brian Biegel told Fox News Digital. "That speaks to how intertwined they were, how they fed off of each other's darkness and desire for evil."

After his arrest, investigators questioned Trail about accounts that he portrayed himself as a powerful warlock and surrounded himself with women he called witches. Trail initially dismissed the occult talk as role-playing, but later told investigators, "Witches kill ... the more they kill, their power increases."

"I spoke to Aubrey Trail for over two years on the telephone and on video conferences," said Biegel. "I do believe that he believes, based on his history growing up in rural Tennessee and the people that he was groomed by, which, according to him, were witches and they believe in dark magic."
SIGN UP TO GET THE TRUE CRIME NEWSLETTER
Aubrey Trail is seen here being interrogated by investigators. (Hulu)

"I believe, that he believes, that he has special powers and he can use them mostly to manipulate vulnerable people into bending to his will," Biegel continued. "And I think that's an important distinction because yes, in his words, he was trying to form a coven of witches and groom them to do awful, terrible things. It's his belief that if they had done that, they would have superpowers."
St. John said the filmmakers were aware during production that Trail was "a liar and a serial one."
GET REAL-TIME UPDATES DIRECTLY ON THE TRUE CRIME HUB

Prosecutors said Aubrey Trail strangled Sydney Loofe with an electrical cord and cut her body into 14 pieces, which he then dumped in various ditches along the sides of rural roads in Nebraska. (Nebraska Department of Corrections)

"There's truth in and among the lies, so we were constantly trying to check ourselves and be like, 'Are we being manipulated by him just like he manipulated these young women?' And honestly, we didn't want to give him more of a platform for his, frankly, out-there views."
The docuseries also examines how Boswell used multiple identities on Tinder to meet women, including Loofe.

Ana Golyakova said Trail required her and Boswell to be intimate in front of him, while Ashley Hills said Trail beat her if she disobeyed his demands. Hills said Trail's rules included remaining naked, asking permission to do virtually anything — even to use the bathroom — and not speaking to other men.

Bailey Boswell walks out of the courtroom after being sentenced to life in prison without parole for the 2017 murder of Sydney Loofe on Nov. 8, 2021, in Wilber, Nebraska. (Justin Wan/Lincoln Journal Star via AP)
Several women described similar patterns of control. Hills also said Trail told her he practiced witchcraft and could control people's minds.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
The filmmakers said the women's accounts were crucial to understanding how Trail and Boswell operated — and how investigators ultimately brought them to justice.

Sydney Loofe’s family and friends played a key role in the investigation after the 24-year-old disappeared in November 2017. Her best friend, Brooklyn McCrystal, created a Tinder profile to track down Loofe’s date, known as "Audrey," obtained her phone number and turned it over to police. Investigators ultimately identified "Audrey" as Bailey Boswell. (Hulu)
"At the heart of this story is Sydney Loofe and the women who were pulled into the orbit of Aubrey and Bailey," said St. John.

"These were young women who, in a very universal way, were searching for belonging in a place that was hard for them to find that. It made them vulnerable and, as a result, they fell into this awful situation. But they were incredibly brave. Other than Sydney, who unfortunately was killed, these young women have told their story in court, and they're responsible for putting these people away."
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

Aubrey Trail appears via video conference during his first court appearance before Saline County Judge Linda Bauer at the Saline County Courthouse on June 12, 2018, in Wilber, Nebraska. (Rebecca S. Gratz/The World Herald via AP)

Trail was convicted of first-degree murder and conspiracy to commit first-degree murder in 2019. He also pleaded no contest to improper disposal of human skeletal remains. He was sentenced to death in 2021.
Boswell was convicted of first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit first-degree murder and improper disposal of human skeletal remains in 2020. She was sentenced to life in prison the following year.

"There was a thirst for doing something really awful to someone that had built up in Bailey and Aubrey's orbit," said Biegel. "And so, Sydney was at the wrong place at the wrong time. She came into their world at a time when they were ready to perform some of their supposed beliefs in witchcraft and dark magic."
SEND US A TIP
Sydney Loofe was murdered on Nov. 15, 2017, the night she went on a second date with Bailey Boswell. Her remains were discovered on Dec. 4, 2017, in rural Clay County, Nebraska. (Hulu)

"This is obviously a cautionary tale about not knowing who's on the other side of the screen," Biegel said. "But had it not been for the brilliant work of the Lincoln Police Department and the FBI, there would probably still be two killers on the streets. Who knows how many other people they would have killed?"

title: Questions still haunt Houdini’s Halloween death 100 years later
summary: Harry Houdini's death 100 years ago was officially blamed on peritonitis, but theories about punches, mediums and murder still fuel debate today.
story: ‘Houdini: Back from the Dead,’ a new three-part Fox Nation series, brings the legendary illusionist’s extraordinary rise and enduring legacy to life through artificial intelligence.
Mystery cloaked the life and performances of escape artist Harry Houdini, and it followed him until his death, perplexing experts for the past century.
Houdini, a Hungarian born Erik Weisz, became one of the most famous magicians and vaudeville performers in history after immigrating with his family to the United States at 4.
He died 100 years ago on Oct. 31, 1926, at 52.
His official cause of death was listed as peritonitis, an infection caused by a ruptured appendix. But, since the day he died, theories about alternative causes have lived on.
WATCH: HARRY HOUDINI RETURNS FROM THE GRAVE IN AI-GENERATED FOX NATION SERIES 100 YEARS AFTER HIS DEATH
Harry Houdini poses with a chain of handcuffs in 1899. (Courtesy of Roger Dreyer)
Some say a surprise punch to his stomach caused deadly appendicitis to the man who kept himself in peak physical condition.
Others insist he suffered from an intestinal blockage.
Some theorize he was killed by people working as spirit mediums. He had been exposing them as frauds just before his death.
One of the most widespread myths was created by a 1953 film in which Houdini was portrayed as unable to escape the water torture cell in time to save his own life.
"There’s plenty of room for speculation, for conspiracy theories, and so it continues," Houdini historian and biographer John Cox told Fox News Digital.
"It continues to this day."

Houdini's story returns in the new three-part Fox Nation series "Houdini: Back from the Dead," in which artificial intelligence helps him appear to sit down for a modern-day interview to recount his struggles, relationships and legendary feats.
Harry Houdini appears to wave in this image taken from a teaser trailer for the new Fox Nation series, "Houdini: Back from the Dead." (Fox Nation/Screengrab)
‘Poorly timed’ punch
A key event in the timeline of Houdini’s death is the now-famous series of punches to his stomach on Oct. 22, 1926.

Nine days before Houdini died, a university student named J. Gordon Whitehead visited the performer in his dressing room at a Montreal theater. Historians report that Houdini was reclining on a couch when Whitehead asked if he could test his ability to withstand a blow to the stomach.
Houdini obliged.
But before he could brace himself, Whitehead began punching.
It continued until another person in the room begged Whitehead to stop, said Roger Dreyer, president of Houdini Revealed, a museum in New York.
Many historians agree that, because of the punches, Houdini ignored what actually were symptoms of appendicitis, Cox said.
Though some believed the blows caused the deadly inflammation, that was never proven.
WATCH: Harry Houdini returns in new AI-powered Fox Nation series
"He didn't get it treated in time," Cox said. "His appendix ruptured. This caused peritonitis, which was a massive infection. And back then, you died from that.

"Had he not been punched, this pain would have come out of nowhere, and he might have gone and sought medical attention sooner. So, the punch was very likely just a very poorly timed accident that caused him to not pay attention to what was really happening to him medically."
Regardless, the punches brought a financial windfall to his family.
Houdini was thousands of dollars in debt at the time of his death. Because the punches were blamed for killing him, his life insurance policy paid out double.
"He had a life insurance [policy] of $25,000," Dreyer said.
The agreement was that "if he died from an accident, he received another $25,000. Twenty-five-thousand dollars back then was almost $500,000" in today’s value.
Harry Houdini holds onto a railing by his chin while tied up in a straight jacket.  (Getty)
Spooky Halloween seances

title: Private jets, yachts and powerful friends helped Alexander brothers lure women — and silence them, lawyer says
summary: Private jets, superyachts and mansions helped the Alexander brothers lure sex trafficking victims into their orbit, an attorney told Fox News Digital.
story: Attorney Michael Willemin says private jets, superyachts and powerful connections helped the convicted brothers operate for years and left women fearful of coming forward.

Jets, superyachts, mansions and access to the rich and powerful helped the Alexander brothers lure women into their orbit while creating an "aura" that left victims afraid they would not be believed, an attorney representing three women pursuing civil claims against the convicted sex traffickers told Fox News Digital.

Alon, Oren and Tal Alexander were each sentenced in New York Tuesday to 30 years in federal prison for a yearslong sex-trafficking scheme that prosecutors said relied in part on the brothers' wealth, social status and luxury lifestyle to lure women before drugging and sexually assaulting them.
But the sentences that capped their federal prosecution do not mark the end of the legal reckoning facing the brothers.
ANDREW, TRISTAN TATE ARRESTED IN MIAMI AS UK SEEKS EXTRADITION ON EXPANDED RAPE, TRAFFICKING CHARGES

Michael J. Willemin, a partner at Wigdor LLP, told Fox News Digital his firm represents three women pursuing civil claims against the brothers and said evidence revealed during the federal prosecution could bolster allegations made in those cases.

Damien Williams, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, announces the arrest and indictment of Alon Alexander, Oren Alexander and Tal Alexander, on charges of sex trafficking and drugs at 26 Federal Plaza in New York City Dec. 11, 2024. (Reuters/Kent Edwards)
Willemin said the brothers surrounded themselves with wealthy and powerful people while using their lavish lifestyle to attract women and build an image that made victims fearful of coming forward.
WOMEN ACCUSE PEARADISE FOUNDER OF PREYING ON THEM BY TURNING ‘SAFE SPACE’ INTO MANSION OF MANIPULATION
"They used things like luxury trips and parties and introductions to celebrities and powerful individuals and private jets and superyachts, mansions and estates," Willemin said.

Those trappings, he said, served as "a compliment in some ways to the drugs and the alcohol that were used to impair the memory of their victims and ultimately allowed them to get away with this sort of behavior for as long as they did."
CORNELL SEXUAL ASSAULT CASE REVIVES SCRUTINY OF A LITTLE-KNOWN NEW YORK LAW ON INTOXICATED VICTIMS
Prosecutors said the brothers used their wealth and prominence to create opportunities to sexually assault women between at least 2008 and 2021.
Tal Alexander and Oren Alexander attend Howard Lorber and Susan DeFranca Host a Sunset Reception aboard Aviva Motor Yacht Dec. 7, 2013 in New York. (Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

Women were identified through social media, dating apps, in-person encounters and party promoters before being offered luxury experiences, travel and accommodations. On multiple occasions, prosecutors said, women were then drugged and forcibly raped or sexually assaulted, sometimes by multiple men.
CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE
Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Jones described it during closing arguments as a "consistent playbook to lure, isolate and rape their victims."
Willemin said the brothers' wealth and access did more than help draw women into their social circles. He said it also heightened fears about what could happen if victims accused them publicly.
"There's an added layer of concern that the women who come forward are going to be retaliated against," Willemin said.
Oren Alexander and Tal Alexander speak at a panel at the Rockstars of Real Estate event Sept. 3, 2013, in New York. (Amy Sussman/Invision for Details Magazine/AP Images, File)
That could include fears of being pushed out of social circles, being surveilled or facing other potentially violent behavior, he said.
HARVEY WEINSTEIN SENTENCED TO 15 YEARS IN PRISON FOR 2006 SEX CRIME IN NEW YORK
"That's something that is a very real fear for women that is exacerbated when someone can use wealth and power to help secure silence," Willemin said.
Willemin represents Angelica Parker, who sued all three brothers in 2024, along with Samantha Fields and a Jane Doe who have brought separate civil claims.
MAX FACTOR HEIR'S FORMER LAWYER DETAILS JUDGE'S ERROR THAT WIPED OUT 124-YEAR RAPE SENTENCE
Parker alleges Oren invited her and a friend to the New York City apartment he shared with Tal and Alon in 2012, where Oren and Alon offered the women ecstasy, which they declined.
After Parker's friend left the apartment, Parker alleges Alon and Tal sexually assaulted her together while Oren watched.

Oren Alexander and his twin brother, Alon, attend a bond hearing after being charged with multiple state and federal crimes, including sex trafficking and rape, at the Richard E. Gerstein Justice Building Dec. 13, 2024, in Miami. (Matias J. Ocner/Miami Herald via AP, Pool)
JUDGE GRILLS AG’S OFFICE IN CORNELL SEX ASSAULT CASE AS EX-FRAT BRO’S LAWYER DEMANDS OUSTER OVER ALLEGED BIAS
The allegations in Parker's lawsuit are separate civil claims and were not adjudicated by the federal jury that convicted the brothers.
Willemin said evidence that emerged during the criminal prosecution nevertheless supports Parker's contention that what allegedly happened to her was planned rather than spontaneous.

"There was a whole host of evidence with respect to text messages and videos and other behaviors that suggested that these sexual assaults were not the random acts of spontaneity, but were, in fact, planned, which help also support the allegation made by Ms. Parker," Willemin said.
The federal prosecution may now also change the landscape for the remaining civil cases.
Willemin said Parker's case has progressed further than the other two his firm is handling and is moving through an appeals process involving whether older sexual assault claims can proceed.

In this courtroom sketch, real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother Alon, who were found guilty of repeatedly drugging, sexually assaulting and raping dozens of female victims, listen as their lawyers argue for a lesser sentence on their behalf in a New York courtroom Oct. 27, 2026. (Reuters/Jane Rosenberg)
An argument is scheduled for January before the New York Court of Appeals over legal issues Willemin said could determine the outcome of numerous civil cases against the brothers.

"The civil cases are moving forward now," Willemin said. "And one of the sort of roadblocks to that was to have the criminal case completed. That's now obviously completed to a degree and now the civil cases should be able to move forward."
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
When asked whether additional women may have been victimized but never publicly came forward, Willemin said, "I wouldn't doubt that at all."
Oren Alexander, Tal Alexander and Alon Alexander attend the Chanukah With The Stars gala on Dec. 10, 2014 at Harmonie Club in New York City. (J Grassi/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

"It would be, you know, frankly, pretty surprising if every woman who had been the victim of a sexual assault by the Alexander brothers has come forward, given the evidence that we have as far as how widespread this occurred," Willemin said.
At Tuesday's sentencing, the brothers continued to deny drugging, raping or trafficking women while acknowledging and expressing regret for past attitudes and comments about women.

Federal prosecutors had sought life sentences, while defense attorneys asked for the mandatory minimum of 15 years.

U.S. District Judge Valerie Caproni ultimately sentenced each brother to 30 years in prison, followed by 10 years of supervised release. Alon and Oren were each fined $300,000, while Tal was fined $350,000.

In this courtroom sketch, Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa addresses the court and argues for a life sentence during the sentencing of real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander and their brother, Alon, who were found guilty of repeatedly drugging, sexually assaulting and raping dozens of female victims, at a New York courtroom in New York Oct. 27, 2026. (Reuters/Jane Rosenberg)

For Willemin's clients, the federal sentences represent only one part of what they are seeking.

His firm hopes to move its three civil cases through discovery and ultimately to trial, where Willemin said his clients want juries to recognize that they were wronged and provide a remedy through the civil justice system.

"The criminal convictions were welcome for sure, and the sentence, although it could have been longer, it could have been life, was also significantly longer than the minimum sentence that could have been given," Willemin said.

Asked whether he believed 30 years was a just sentence, Willemin pointed to the brothers' continued denials and said he believes accountability remains lacking.

"At this point in time, life really seems like the only fair sentence," Willemin said.

title: California police investigate deadly shooting at Spirit Halloween store
summary: Seven people suffered gunshot wounds at a Spirit Halloween store inside Fairfield's Solano Town Center on Halloween eve, with no arrests made.
story: One person was killed and six others wounded in a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Fairfield, California, Friday night. At least three victims are in critical condition.
One person was killed and at least six others were injured in a shooting at a Spirit Halloween store in Fairfield, California, on Friday evening, the eve of Halloween.
The Fairfield Police Department said officers responded to reports of a shooting around 8:30 p.m. local time at the Spirit Halloween store inside the Solano Town Center shopping mall.
Police confirmed that seven people suffered gunshot wounds, including one who later died from their injuries.
The six surviving victims were taken to local hospitals, with at least three in critical condition, according to police.

title: Cities fearing Halloween mayhem put teens on notice, announce curfews and crackdowns after violent takeovers
summary: Oak Park, Illinois, and other cities are enforcing Halloween curfews and boosting police patrols after teen takeovers sparked fights and arrests.
story: Sgt. Betsy Brantner Smith, a spokeswoman for the National Police Association, explains why cities are taking proactive steps for Halloween as teen takeovers strain police resources and fuel safety concerns.
Cities across the country are putting teens on notice for Halloween weekend, rolling out curfews and crackdowns to head off the kind of chaos that unfolds during so-called teen takeovers.

From the Jersey Shore to suburban Atlanta, officials are setting curfews for teenagers and adding police patrols, many of them in places still reeling from takeovers that drew hundreds of teens and ended in fights and arrests.
In Oak Park, Illinois, the chief of police wrote that her agency is trying to prevent a Halloween teen takeover like last year from happening again.
INSIDE THE TEEN TAKEOVERS THREATENING TO EXPLODE THIS SUMMER AS CITIES REMAIN ON EDGE: 'VERY WORRIED'

Video captures chaotic scenes in downtown Chicago’s Loop as a large group of teens floods the area with fights breaking out and police responding before a curfew enforcement order helps disperse the crowd. (Justin/Fox 32 Chicago)
Last Halloween, an estimated 500 teens swarmed downtown Oak Park, where fights and gunshots erupted, and police called in help from six neighboring agencies, according to a department memo.
Oak Park Chief of Police Shatonya Johnson said the agency will be increasing the amount of officers on shift during Halloween and several more measures aimed at preventing another teen takeover.
CHICAGO MAYOR WARNS OF ‘TEEN TREND’ AFTER TAKEOVER CHAOS, VIOLENCE CONCERNS GROW

Adults in the Hyde Park neighborhood of Chicago are taking matters into their own hands and plan to show out en masse on the streets to prevent large gatherings by teenagers. The group, called CollaBOOration, was established after a series of large Halloween gatherings from 2016 to 2019, when teen takeovers turned violent, according to Block Club Chicago.

"What we’re really trying to do is establish a critical mass on the street, possibly before the Halloween festivities even start," the group's founder, Bennie Currie, said. "So, when these large gatherings happen, like we’ve seen every year, we will already have taken over 53rd Street. … We’ll be walking up and down in orange shirts and keeping in contact with one another."

Crowds of teenagers gathered in Chicago. (X/Chitown_Crime_Chasers)

After 7 p.m. on Halloween, those under 16 in Covington, Georgia, will be required to go home or have an adult with them if they're in the city's downtown area, which is outside Atlanta, according to CBS News.
According to News 12, the Long Branch, New Jersey, police department plans to strictly enforce a Halloween curfew for those under 17 on Oct. 31, which runs from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The curfew was set in response to hundreds of people gathering for a teen takeover in May, resulting in fights breaking out and six arrests.

title: California woman accused of killing trans son-in-law puts blame on husband in new docs: reports
summary: Shili Chen claims husband Shouyong Zhang fired the fatal shots that killed Jonathan McKinsey in a Dublin, California, park amid a bitter custody battle.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Claudia Cowan reports on the arrest of Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen in Dublin, California. Police allege the elderly in-laws took turns shooting their 40-year-old son-in-law, Jonathan McKinsey, in a parking lot amid a bitter custody dispute.

One month after she and her husband were arrested for the alleged murder of their trans New York Times executive son-in-law, Shili Chen claims in new legal documents that her husband is the one to blame, according to reports.
Shili Chen, 77, and Shouyong Zhang were arrested Sept. 26 for allegedly shooting Jonathan McKinsey, 40, in a crowded park in Dublin, California.

In a new bail filing, Chen’s lawyers claim the 77-year-old watched her husband fire the fatal shots at McKinsey at the Dublin Sports Grounds from inside her car, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.
FATHER-IN-LAW OF TRANS NYT EXEC ADMITTED KILLING HIM, WORKED 'IN CONCERT' WITH MOTHER-IN-LAW: DOCS

One month after she and her husband were arrested for the alleged murder of their trans New York Times executive son-in-law, Shili Chen claims in new legal documents that her husband is the one to blame, according to reports. (Alameda County Sheriff's Office; Jon McKinsey/Facebook)
Her lawyer, Curtis Briggs, argued that Chen only got out of the car "to protect her husband from what she feared was an assault by Mr. McKinsey," the California Post reported.
She was allegedly seen on surveillance video firing a gun at McKinsey after Zhang fired the shots that killed him.
Chen’s lawyers argued she was kept "in the dark" while Zhang planned McKinsey’s murder.
Zhang allegedly admitted to the fatal shooting just days after when video footage of the attack was shown to him, court documents obtained by Fox News Digital showed.
Zhang told police he asked his wife to drive to the park but didn’t explain why, according to the Chronicle.
Prosecutors accused the couple of "lying in wait" at the park for McKinsey before the shooting, but her lawyer claims there isn’t enough evidence to prove that.
That special circumstance has been used to hold the couple without bail.

Prosecutors accused the couple of "lying in wait" at the park for McKinsey before the shooting, but her lawyer claims there isn’t enough evidence to prove that. (Jon McKinsey/Facebook)
Both Chen and Zhang are asking for pretrial release.
In a separate filing, Zhang’s public defender argued that he didn’t pose a threat because of his age and health and because the shooting was an isolated family incident.
Chen’s lawyer argues that she wasn’t the "actual killer" since she shot McKinsey when he was already dead.

Several 911 callers reported gunfire at the Dublin Sports Grounds before a Dublin Police Services sergeant arrived and found McKinsey lying face up with multiple gunshot wounds. He was pronounced dead at the scene.
Witnesses pointed police toward a black Honda Civic leaving the parking lot, leading officers to conduct a high-risk traffic stop nearby, the filings state.
Chen was driving and allegedly had a firearm in her possession when she was detained, while Zhang was in the passenger seat.
Three witnesses identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, while surveillance video allegedly captured the couple opening fire "in concert" on McKinsey.

Jonathan McKinsey, a New York Times Games engineering executive, was shot and killed in Dublin, California, last month, and his parents-in-law were arrested on suspicion of murder within minutes, authorities said. (Jon McKinsey/Facebook)
Police said the couple started shooting in a crowded park's parking lot with "blatant disregard for public safety," even as several children were nearby.
OREGON TEACHER WHO WRESTLED SHOTGUN FROM SCHOOL GUNMAN SHARES EMOTIONAL MESSAGE AFTER ATTACK
Police later searched the Honda and recovered a second firearm that Zhang allegedly admitted using in the shooting.

The complaint alleges the killing involved "great violence" and acts showing a "high degree of cruelty, viciousness, or callousness." Prosecutors also allege both defendants were armed or used a weapon during the killing.
McKinsey's killing came amid a bitter divorce and custody battle with Chen and Zhang's daughter, Candice Jang.

McKinsey accused Chen of directing anti-LGBTQ slurs at him and one of his children and alleged Zhang struck him in the chest while he was recovering from double mastectomy surgery, The Mercury News reported. Jang made competing allegations of domestic violence and child abuse against McKinsey, which he disputed.

Fox News Digital reviewed court dockets showing McKinsey and Jang were locked in multiple legal battles when McKinsey was killed, including competing domestic violence restraining order cases, a child custody dispute and a pending divorce.

title: Sheriff's department gives update on Nancy Guthrie case 9 months after kidnapping
summary: The Pima County Sheriff’s Department gave an update in the Nancy Guthrie missing person’s case Friday, saying the department continuing to work to advance the case.
story: Lisa Miller, a retired detective and law enforcement executive with the Colorado Attorney General's Office, breaks down some of the unique attributes of the purported ransom note.

The Pima County Sheriff’s Department gave an update on the Nancy Guthrie missing person’s case Friday, saying the department continues to work with the Nancy Guthrie Task Force on DNA analysis in an effort to advance the case.

"Earlier this month, investigators traveled to Florida to meet with lab scientists to see what more could be done to advance this case," the department wrote in an X post. "A number of ideas were discussed, and we continue to work with all our partners to solve this case."
The law enforcement agency reminded the public that no tip is too small.
"Even the smallest piece of information could be critical to this investigation," the department said.
NANCY GUTHRIE CASE: UNCLAIMED $1.2M REWARD SUGGESTS 'VERY SMALL CIRCLE' OF SUSPECTS, RETIRED FBI AGENT SAYS
Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break while hosting NBC's "Today Show."  ( Don Arnold/WireImage)
Guthrie, NBC journalist Savannah Guthrie’s mother, was kidnapped from her home in Tucson, Arizona, on Feb. 1.
The 84-year-old was last seen shortly before 10 p.m. Jan. 31 after a relative dropped her off at her home in the Catalina Foothills neighborhood of Tucson.
Authorities have struggled to identify a suspect or person of interest in her disappearance despite a masked man appearing on Guthrie's Ring doorbell camera.
Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos, in the days following Guthrie's disappearance, confirmed that she was taken, telling reporters during a news briefing, "She did not leave on her own. We know that."
NANCY GUTHRIE INVESTIGATORS SEE UPTICK IN TIPS AFTER RANSOM NOTES RELEASE: SHERIFF
Authorities previously released two ransom notes related to Guthrie's kidnapping in July.

A split image shows a group of Pima County deputies investigating outside the home of Nancy Guthrie in Tucson, Arizona, and a portrait of Guthrie. She has been missing since Feb. 1, when she is believed to have been abducted from her house. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital; Courtesy of NBC)

The second, sent four days later on Feb. 6, said Guthrie had died shortly after she was kidnapped.
Authorities released the ransom notes in late July, noting they were written with a unique writing style, asking anyone who recognizes the patterns to share any information with PCSD and the FBI.
A photograph of Nancy Guthrie is seen on a sign that people can leave messages on February 26, 2026, in Tucson, Arizona. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Late last month, investigators said they had been made aware of a possible new ransom note in relation to Guthrie's disappearance.
"The PCSD/FBI Guthrie Task Force was recently made aware of a new possible ransom note related to the Nancy Guthrie investigation," PCSD wrote in an X post in late September.

title: Oregon teacher who wrestled shotgun from school gunman shares emotional message after attack
summary: Cassidy Schutz, the Silver Rail Elementary teacher who wrestled a gunman's shotgun away from him, has broken her silence on the deadly Bend Oregon shooting.
story: Fox News' Sarah Alegre reports new details of the tragic Oregon school shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, where a teacher and a father took action taking down the gunman.

An Oregon elementary school teacher who fought a teenage gunman during a deadly school shooting earlier this month has broken her silence, describing the tragedy as a loss she will carry with her forever.

Cassidy Schutz, a certified learning specialist at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, released her first public statement Friday through Bend-La Pine Schools, just over two weeks after the Oct. 15 attack left three children and a teacher dead.

"There are no words to describe the depth of sadness I am feeling following the events of October 15th. This is not a story. This is a horrific and heartbreaking tragedy, and it is our real lives," Schutz said in the statement.
HERO DAD WHO TOOK DOWN OREGON SCHOOL SHOOTER IDENTIFIED ALONG WITH TEACHER, STUDENT BOTH KILLED IN ATTACK
Cassidy Schutz, a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., fought a gunman during the Oct. 15 school shooting that killed three students and a teacher. (Bend-La Pine Schools)

"My thoughts are with those who were lost, their families, those who were hurt, and those who were there that day. My heart is with you. It all happened so fast, and I wish with everything in me that we had more time. The pain of this loss I will carry with me forever."
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz previously credited Schutz with throwing her cellphone at the shooter and wrestling him for control of his shotgun during the attack.
Schutz also asked for privacy as she continues to heal.
INJURED BEND, OREGON, TEACHER TRIED TO SHUT CLASSROOM DOOR DURING SCHOOL SHOOTING BEFORE PLAYING DEAD
Flowers are placed beside a sign at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Ore., Oct. 16, a day after a deadly shooting. (Haven Daley/AP Photo)

"There are no words for this unimaginable reality we are facing. My focus is on these families, our team, our school, and my own healing," she said. "As I continue to navigate this, I ask that you please give me the time, space, and privacy I need to heal. I will not be making any additional public statements at this time."
The shooting unfolded when a 16-year-old former student entered the school and opened fire inside a classroom serving students with special needs, according to police.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, and three students, including 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and two other children, ages 8 and 11, were killed.
DEMOCRATS' LATEST GUN-CONTROL PUSH RUNS INTO INCONVENIENT FACT ABOUT HOW SCHOOL KILLER WAS STOPPED
Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail Elementary school, where a shooting took place Oct. 15, in Bend, Ore. (Joe Kline/AP Photo)

Drury previously told Fox News Digital she tried to close her classroom door after spotting the gunman but was shot before she could stop him from entering.
She suffered severe injuries to both arms and pretended to be dead to avoid being shot again before hero dad Kaylub Giamanco, 36, shot the attacker dead.

title: Aspiring NYPD officer and college hockey captain killed in crash involving twice-removed Mexican national
summary: DHS confirmed the wrong-way driver who killed University of New Haven hockey captain Ryan O'Shea had illegally reentered the United States twice.
story: Ryan O'Shea, 21, was killed by a wrong-way driver who repeatedly entered the U.S. illegally after previously being removed, DHS says.

A 21-year-old college hockey captain who dreamed of becoming a police officer was killed in a wrong-way crash involving a Mexican national who repeatedly entered the United States illegally after previously being removed, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed to Fox News Digital.

Ryan O'Shea, a senior at the University of New Haven, was driving south on Interstate 91 in North Haven late Oct. 16 when a Chevrolet Silverado traveling the wrong way slammed head-on into his Honda Accord, Connecticut State Police said.

story: Massachusetts Judge William Sullivan denies Lindsay Clancy's motion for acquittal, pushing the high-profile murder case toward a November 2 hearing.

A true crime influencer has been charged with wiretapping after police say she posted a secret recording of a call with Patrick Clancy's father, who told investigators he accidentally answered the call.

Shawna Gramkow, who operates several true crime accounts on social media and boasts a following of more than 50,000, was charged with felony unlawful wiretapping on Oct. 20 in relation to an incident that happened on Sept. 4 involving Patrick Clancy's father, Christopher Clancy, police said in an incident report obtained by Fox News Digital.

Police said Gramkow posted a video to Instagram on Aug. 30 of an unknown individual calling a phone number she claimed belonged to Patrick Clancy after Lindsay Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, read the number aloud during the murder trial.

Now on this particular call, Patrick's dad was still on the line, he was kind of mumbling still on the phone, I guess he didn't know that the phone was still going," she said in the video, police wrote in the incident report.

In the video, the detective said, an adult male can be heard speaking, though he was unable to make out what was being said. When Christopher Clancy reported the incident to law enforcement on Sept. 4, he told police he believed the voice was his and came from a phone call he received on Aug. 6.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Monday, July 27, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Christopher Clancy said he accidentally answered the call, which came from an unfamiliar number, instead of declining it. title: Death row killer Christa Pike describes waking up after execution she never expected to survive
summary: Christa Pike describes constant pain and deep isolation one month after surviving Tennessee's failed lethal injection execution on Sept. 30.
story: Anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike. Zivot, who advised Pike's attorneys, explains the complications surrounding the lethal injection drugs used in the state's attempt. Pike remains on death row following the failed execution attempt.

Death row inmate Christa Pike is speaking out one month after surviving Tennessee's attempt to execute her, saying she remains in constant pain and had never contemplated a life beyond the night she expected to die.
Pike, 50, described her condition in a statement dictated to her legal team and released Friday.
"One month ago on September 30, I walked into the execution chamber at Riverbend men’s prison prepared to die," Pike said. "I had made my peace."
CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS

(Greg Smith/CORBIS/Corbis via Getty Images | Tennessee Department of Correction via AP)

"Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain," Pike said. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."
CHRISTA PIKE NOW CONSCIOUS AND TALKING AFTER SURVIVING 2 DOSES OF LETHAL INJECTION DRUG
Pike said she had never considered what her life would look like if she survived the execution.

"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position," she said. "I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured."
EX-CHIEF SAYS CHRISTA PIKE WAS 'ALMOST GIDDY' DESCRIBING MURDER AS GOVERNOR WEIGHS IN AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow participant in a federal Job Corps program in Knoxville.

Her statement comes two days after Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said Pike remains incarcerated under state law and signaled that her death sentence is unlikely to change.
CHRISTA PIKE IS BACK BEHIND BARS AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION, BUT HER ULTIMATE SENTENCE FACES A NEW TEST
Pike's attorneys have called on Lee to commute her death sentence to life without parole after the failed execution.
Pike said Friday that she is recovering but remains in the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she has been largely isolated from other people.
CHRISTA PIKE DISCHARGED FROM HOSPITAL, RETURNED TO PRISON AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION, ATTORNEYS SAY
"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger," Pike said. "But healing is not the same as being okay."

"Since that night, I have been largely isolated in the prison’s medical ward, away from other people and the human connections that mean so much to me," she continued. "That isolation brings its own kind of pain. I spent 28 years in solitary confinement and much of what I am experiencing today is a repeat of that condition."

Randy Spivey, an attorney for Christa Pike, a death row prisoner who survived a botched execution, speaks to the media, flanked by Luke Ihnen, after a Tennessee court was presented a status update on Pike, outside a courtroom in Nashville, Tennessee, on October 7, 2026. (Reuters/Seth Herald)

title: ‘Your kids are the target’: College drug deaths, alleged coke ring expose lethal threat, warns retired cop
summary: From FIT's fentanyl poisoning to Penn State's cocaine ring, campus drug deaths reveal how organized crime networks are targeting college students.
story: From FIT's fentanyl poisoning to Penn State's cocaine ring, campus drug scares reveal how organized crime networks are targeting college students, Paul Mauro warns.
"There is a panoply of drugs out there that will destroy your kids," says retired NYPD inspector and Fox News contributor Paul Mauro.
Following recent college deaths and allegations around a campus cocaine trafficking ring, Mauro said America's students are now the primary prey for a relentless and deadly drug trade.
"If you're sending a kid off to college these days, you better sit that child down and give that child a hard primer on what could possibly happen," he said.
FIT fentanyl poisoning death

A recently unsealed indictment shows Moises Freire, 19, and Brian Peralta, 18, both from Queens, New York, are facing charges after a young woman was killed and another seriously injured after they were allegedly poisoned by fentanyl.
A student was killed in an FIT dorm room after a suspect poisoned her with fentanyl, prosecutors say. (Getty Images: Universal Images Group)
Reports indicate Annabel Richter, 20, was killed after she ingested the drug supplied by the men, who allegedly told her it was simply "cocaine."

She had moved from Brazil to live in the U.S. to pursue her studies at Manhattan's Fashion Institute of Technology, the New York Post reported. She was found unresponsive with another female victim in a dorm room.
According to the federal indictment, Freire allegedly raped the victim and "waited approximately 45 minutes to contact campus security" about the woman being unconscious.
Pills containing fentanyl are displayed at the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Northeast Regional Laboratory for testing in New York, on May 7, 2026. (Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images)
Mauro questioned why there wasn't more media attention on the case.

"It happened on a campus and the only thing I can conjure is that it happened in New York City, and so the powers that be as we come into an election season would rather these rape stories or these campus crime stories occur someplace far from New York where they could have any impact on the elections here," he said.
The indictment also alleges Freire texted photos to his friends of one unconscious victim, who was "naked below the waist."

The second victim sustained "serious bodily injury" and regained consciousness after receiving life-saving care in the hospital.

Court records indicate both men pleaded not guilty on Wednesday to federal charges of conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance resulting in death. Freire is additionally charged with distributing a controlled substance with the intent to commit rape.

In a statement, FIT President Jason Schupbach said in part, "We are thankful to our teams from Public Safety and Residential Life for their immediate response in March, and also to the Department of Justice and the NYPD for their actions in March and their continued focus on this case. As a community, we continue to support each other through difficult times."
Ole Miss deaths

Campus drug deaths extend beyond New York City, including at the University of Mississippi, where federal prosecutors and local authorities launched intensive investigations following the deaths of two students.
Ole Miss students Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20, were found dead of suspected drug overdoses in September.

Ole Miss students Robert Strang, 20, and Aidan Hamilton, 18, were found dead on Sept. 21. (Strang family; Kathleen Hamilton/Facebook; Andy Altenburger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Investigators recovered packages of kratom-related products or "gas station heroin" at both scenes where the victims were discovered.
The discovery prompted federal charges against a vape shop clerk and his son for illicitly selling dangerous, banned compounds disguised in retail packaging.
Aidan Hamilton, an 18-year-old University of Mississippi freshman, appears in these images that his mother posted to Facebook. (Facebook/ Kathie Mac Donald Hamilton)
The deaths sent shock waves through the campus community, intensifying urgent warnings from law enforcement about unregulated substances flooding college towns.

"It really is a minefield out there these days, and it's not an accident. Our enemies know what they're doing, and your kids are the target," Mauro said.

title: Three killed in midair helicopter collision near Oregon airport, authorities confirm
summary: Three people were killed when two helicopters collided midair near an Oregon airport, including a 22-year-old flight instructor and a student pilot. Federal investigators are probing the cause.
story: Two helicopters carrying three people collided near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon Thursday afternoon, crashing in a field.
Three people were killed when two helicopters collided midair near an Oregon airport Thursday afternoon, crashing in a field and prompting authorities to close a nearby highway.

A Robinson R22 helicopter and an Airbus H125 helicopter collided near McMinnville Municipal Airport around 2:15 p.m. local time, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) confirmed in a statement to Fox News Digital.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) told Fox News Digital that the collision occurred at approximately 2:10 p.m. local time.
The agency identified the Airbus helicopter as an AS350B2 operating on a maintenance flight and the Robinson R22 Beta as conducting an instructional flight.
The Yamhill County Sheriff's Office confirmed Thursday that all three people aboard both helicopters died in the crash.
TWO NAVY JETS CRASH MIDAIR AS CREW SUCCESSFULLY EJECTS DURING IDAHO MILITARY BASE AIR SHOW
A road closure sign blocks traffic near McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon on Oct. 29, 2026, following a midair collision between two helicopters. (Fox News)

The two victims aboard the Robinson R22 helicopter were identified as 22-year-old flight instructor Maddie Aasbo, of Texas, and 31-year-old student pilot Christopher James Joughin, of the United Kingdom, according to the sheriff's office.
Joughin's identity was confirmed Friday after authorities initially withheld his name pending notification of next of kin.
The sole occupant of the Airbus helicopter was identified as Tyler Delane Sturdevant, 38, of Newberg, Oregon.
The collision occurred in a field off Oregon Route 233, about one mile west of Dayton, according to Oregon Department of Transportation spokesperson Mindy McCartt.
McCartt told Fox News Digital that the highway and some nearby county roads were closed at the request of emergency responders. She said there was no estimated reopening time.
DASHCAM VIDEO CAPTURES SMALL PLANE CRASHING ON SAN JOSE HIGHWAY, INJURING THREE ON BOARD, INCLUDING CHILD

McMinnville Airport Manager John Paskell told Fox News Digital that the collision occurred off airport property and did not disrupt airport operations. The airport remained open without closures or restrictions.
Paskell said he understood that both helicopters were based at the airport but could not confirm what activities they were conducting or how the collision occurred.
The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) responded to the scene and are leading the ongoing investigation into the collision, according to the sheriff's office.
The NTSB said Friday that two investigators were traveling to the crash site. Once the wreckage is documented, it will be recovered and moved to a secure facility for further examination.
Emergency vehicles and personnel gather near a closed roadway outside McMinnville Municipal Airport in Oregon on Thursday, following a collision involving two helicopters. (Fox News)

Investigators will examine the pilots, aircraft and operating conditions, including flight tracking data, air traffic control communications, maintenance records, weather conditions and the pilots' flight experience.
They will also review witness statements, electronic devices and any available surveillance video, including doorbell camera footage.
The agency is asking anyone with information relevant to the collision to contact investigators at witness@ntsb.gov.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The cause of the collision has not been determined.The NTSB expects to release a preliminary report within 30 days containing factual information gathered during the initial investigation.
A final report identifying the probable cause and any contributing factors is expected within 12 to 24 months.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Chili's customers suffer chemical burns after dangerous margarita mix-up
summary: Three customers and two employees suffered symptoms after an industrial degreaser was mistakenly used to prepare margaritas at a North Carolina Chili's.
story: Three customers and two employees suffered chemical burns after a mislabeled container was mistakenly used to prepare margaritas at a North Carolina Chili's.

Multiple customers at a Chili's Grill & Bar reported experiencing chemical burns Wednesday after consuming margaritas that had been prepared with an industrial cleaning chemical that was mistaken for sugar or salt.
The Foothills Health District said the incident unfolded at a restaurant in Forest City, North Carolina.
Three customers consumed the contaminated margaritas, while two restaurant employees also reportedly experienced symptoms after exposure to the chemical, according to the health district.
ROACHES CAUGHT CRAWLING ACROSS POPULAR STEAKHOUSE'S KITCHEN FLOOR IN VIRAL EMPLOYEE VIDEO
Chili's customers suffered chemical burns after a cleaning chemical mistaken for sugar or salt was used to make margaritas. (Michael P. Farrell/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
According to preliminary findings, the mix-up began Monday when an employee received an industrial degreaser from a contracted worker and placed it in an unmarked container.
The container was then brought inside the restaurant and left in the bar area.

Two days later, an employee preparing the bar for lunch service discovered the unlabeled container and, believing its contents to be sugar or salt, used the chemical to prepare the margarita station, the health district said.
Shortly after the restaurant opened, three customers consumed the contaminated beverages and "immediately experienced discomfort and chemical burns in and around their mouths."

title: House Judiciary report accuses NYC DAs of downgrading charges to protect illegal immigrants from deportation

story: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin joins Bill Hemmer to discuss a new House GOP report on New York City's sanctuary policies alleging officials downgraded charges to avoid deporting illegal immigrants.

Three of New York’s top elected officials appeared surprised Thursday when pressed about a House Judiciary Committee report alleging local prosecutors intentionally downgraded charges against noncitizens to protect them from deportation.

During a Manhattan press conference, New York Attorney General Letitia James, Queens District Attorney Melinda Katz and Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez faced questions regarding claims that city prosecutors altered or reduced charges to help noncitizens avoid convictions that would trigger removal.
"Did any of you order prosecutors to downgrade gun charges to keep illegal immigrants in the U. S., per the Judiciary Committee report?" a reporter asked.

Katz threw her hands up and shrugged in response, the New York Post reported.
"Our answer couldn’t help it," Katz said, before a speaker redirected the room, asking for "any other on-topic questions" and moving the news conference along.
"We charge any defendant with an illegal firearm with the highest possible charge under the law," a spokesperson for Katz's office told Fox News Digital.
The news conference exchange followed the release of a 22-page congressional report detailing widespread practices across New York City prosecutors' offices.
According to the document, Katz's office employs an "Immigration Specialist" to help negotiate "immigration-safe" plea deals and reduce past convictions.
DOJ OPENS INVESTIGATION INTO SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF SHIELDING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS FROM CONSEQUENCES

The report also cited a 2022 memorandum from Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg allegedly instructing prosecutors to seek dispositions that avoid deportation consequences for all misdemeanors and non-carceral felonies.

In addition, the report states that the office of Bronx DA Darcel Clark trains prosecutors in "Immigration-Conscious Plea Bargaining." That includes offering non-deportable offenses, avoiding aggravated felony charges and using hypothetical or "legally impossible" charges, such as "attempted reckless assault," which lack legal intent requirements.

Prosecutors were also allegedly instructed to omit critical details from official conviction records, such as gun involvement, domestic relationships or the age of minor victims, to prevent federal immigration authorities from using them as grounds for removal.
After the news conference, a spokesperson for Katz reached out to the Post to deny that leniency is ever shown in weapons cases.
"We charge any defendant with an illegal firearm with the highest possible charge under the law," the spokesperson said.

story: Police respond to a shooting outside the Republican Party of Virginia's offices in downtown Richmond on Thursday. Party officials say all staff members are safe and there is no indication the shooting was politically motivated.

title: France deploys 70,000 police officers to prepare for new wave of protests on Halloween
summary: Emmanuel Macron's government deploys 70,000 police officers as France braces for a third week of intense protests amid over $1 billion in losses.
story: French authorities mobilize 70,000 police officers as anti-government demonstrations enter their third week, following widespread looting and property damage (Credit: Reuters).
The French government is deploying 70,000 police officers to cities across the country as authorities expect a third week of intense anti-government protests to resume Saturday.
Demonstrators objecting to rising costs and President Emmanuel Macron's government have engaged in looting and damaging property, prompting the law enforcement surge, according to officials.
"Everyone is on deck to ensure an extremely firm response to any trouble," Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said at a news conference early in the week.

A French gendarme stands amid clouds of tear gas during a demonstration over the cost of living, public services and economic policies on Oct. 24, 2026, in Nantes, France. The protest was part of nationwide demonstrations involving labor unions, students and former Yellow Vest protesters. (Guillaume Saligot/AFP via Getty Images)
FRANCE ON EDGE WITH 70,000 POLICE DEPLOYED FOR UNREST AS AUTHORITIES PROBE SUSPECTED TERROR ATTACK NEAR PARIS
The expected protests, coinciding with Halloween, introduce an additional element to authorities' response, as some protesters are expected to don Halloween masks to hide their identities.

At least 150 planned gatherings across the country have been tracked and acknowledged by the Interior Ministry.Videos circulating on social media Saturday appeared to show fresh confrontations as anti-government protests continued across France, despite the deployment of 70,000 police officers nationwide.
People run through a smoke-filled street during Halloween protests in France on Oct. 31, 2026. (Reuters)

In Paris, video posted to X by journalist Oliya Scootercaster appeared to show an object being thrown toward a group of riot police as officers moved through a street. Scootercaster identified the object as a Molotov cocktail.

Meanwhile, a separate video shared on X by the account Bleu Blanc Rouge purported to show protesters breaking into a residential building in Marseille. The video showed a crowd gathered near a building entrance.
FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC'

One of the events, a planned march between the iconic Parisian squares of Republique and Bastille, has been banned by France's top administrative court. The demonstration was instead rerouted to boulevards on the eastern fringe of the city, far from the main shopping centers.
France's Chamber of Commerce has estimated retail losses from looting and property damage at over $1 billion, while other estimates that include lost revenue calculate losses could be double that.

Boarded up stores, including Christian Dior, Parfums de Marly and Ex Nihilo, on Rue Saint-Honore following looting in central Paris, France, on Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Luxury boutiques in Paris's shopping districts have been damaged after rioting, with some boarding up windows and doors and increasing security measures. (Benjamin Girette/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
PHOTOS SHOW AFTERMATH OF RIOTS AS MASKED GROUPS CLASH WITH POLICE ACROSS FRANCE
Some of Paris' iconic luxury shops, like Hermes and Louis Vuitton, have been targeted by rioters as France's marquee shopping avenues now show scores of buildings with protective wooden boards.
In response to the unrest, France's government is crafting a law that would punish rioters who caused property damage and make them liable to pay up to €10,000, or $11,000.
VIOLENCE ERUPTS AT FRANCE PROTESTS AS MACRON WARNS UNREST IS BEING EXPLOITED

Demonstrations originated with the country's young people protesting schooling conditions and pushing for educational reform and quickly ballooned to include other social groups and issues, including economic anxieties, rising costs in fuel and borrowing.
Though the French government has vowed to reform education and reduce fuel costs, the promises have not satisfied the protesters.

French gendarmerie officers on the day of a demonstration organised by labour unions as part of nationwide protests called by the "Yellow Vests" movement joined by French high school and university students against the cost of living and rising fuel prices, in Paris, France, October 31, 2026. (REUTERS/Pedro Nunes)
"When I was little, I was told young people were the future," 15-year-old high school student Aaron Berthier de Grandry, who plans on protesting over the weekend, told Reuters.
"Well, if we, as the future of France, lack resources, that means France will end up collapsing," de Grandry added.
The U.S. Embassy in France has advised travelers to avoid areas where large gatherings are taking place.
