title: Democrats in key battlegrounds throw Joe Biden under the bus on the border
summary: Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability.
story: WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue.
Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country.

“I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan.
He’s not alone.
In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

“I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.”

Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year.

Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024.

Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings.

Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38%, polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term.
“The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night.

Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.”
In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.”
For Subscribers
Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border.
For Subscribers

In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.”
She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.”
Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement.

“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad. “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.”
Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.”
Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz.

Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum, he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people.

“We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.”
“So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.”

title: El-Sayed’s campaign asks former primary rival not to attend campaign events after clash over Israel
summary: The tensions between the former Democratic primary candidates have drawn in other Michigan Democrats as the party hopes to secure a critical Senate seat.
story: It appears that Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., will no longer attend a campaign event she planned to join on Sunday alongside Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed following days of public feuding over their stances on Israel.
An advisory for the gathering that the El-Sayed campaign sent Saturday did not list Stevens as a participant, only El-Sayed and Rep. Jim Clyburn, D-S.C.

Stevens is being asked not to attend El-Sayed campaign events in the closing days because the campaign is concerned about distractions around her, a person familiar with the decision told NBC News. Politico was first to report that Stevens was no longer welcome at El-Sayed’s events.

Stevens did not immediately respond to a phone call and text message seeking comment. She told The New York Times on Friday that she still planned to vote for El-Sayed, who beat her in an August Senate primary, despite his criticism.

Days before they were set to headline the rally in Detroit, El-Sayed and the congresswoman traded critical messages in statements released Friday, escalating tensions between the two in the final stretch of El-Sayed’s campaign for the Senate.

Stevens said that she expected El-Sayed, the progressive candidate who defeated her in a bitter Democratic primary in August, to formally condemn an ad from an outside progressive group that she called antisemitic, adding that it’s why she agreed to join El-Sayed on the campaign trail for the first time on Sunday.

“This ad tells Michigan families they cannot afford groceries because their money has to be set aside for ‘killing Palestinians,’ and it blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford,” Stevens said in a statement.
She sought to tie the ad — which is set in a grocery store and suggests Israel and the war in Gaza are squeezing American taxpayers — to comments El-Sayed has made in his own campaign.

“I therefore expect him to apologize for those statements as well,” Stevens said. “Abdul promises to get money out of politics. He can begin by getting Israel out of his explanation for everything Michigan cannot afford.”
El-Sayed is not affiliated with the group that produced the ad, Rebellion PAC, and his campaign distanced itself from the ad in statements to The New York Times earlier this week.
Stevens also called on El-Sayed to take down one of his own ads that featured right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson “out of the same respect for Michigan’s Black community.”

El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel, shot back Friday, saying in a statement that Stevens, a strong supporter of Israel, “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago” and that his campaign’s focus was on affordability and healthcare.
For Subscribers

“That focus is why our people-powered campaign defeated a historic $70M in outside spending from big corporations and AIPAC on behalf of Congresswoman Stevens,” El-Sayed said, referencing Stevens’ support from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, a pro-Israel lobbying group, during the primary.
For Subscribers

The exchange comes after the former primary opponents had seemingly reached a reconciliation, agreeing to appear at an event in Detroit alongside Clyburn a senior Democratic leader, on Sunday. The escalation is also playing out four days before voters will choose between El-Sayed and Republican candidate Mike Rogers to be the next Michigan senator in a race the nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates as a toss-up.
On Saturday morning, Stevens’ fiance, Jason Turkish, told “Fox & Friends,” he wasn’t sure whether the congresswoman still planned to campaign alongside El-Sayed on Sunday.
“I’m not sure. I don’t know where that stands as of Saturday morning,” he said.

Turkish added, “Haley has made it clear to anyone who will listen that she remains on Team Dem. That her only ask, small ask, was to say that we not blame all of society’s high costs on one group of people.”

On Wednesday, Stevens sat for an interview on CNN in which she signaled she would vote for El-Sayed while also calling on him to denounce the ad from Rebellion PAC. That interview came shortly after Turkish, told The Detroit News that he was voting for Rogers.

“Of course I’m voting for our Democratic nominee for Senate,” Stevens said. “I’m voting for the Democratic ticket. But I want to encourage this campaign to shut out the hate and to call it out and to make people who are in my coalition, make them feel comfortable about coming to the polls.”
The tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens have drawn in other Michigan Democrats as the party hopes to secure a critical Senate seat in the race to control Congress.
“First of all, I have no idea what the hell Haley Stevens is doing,” Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow said Friday on CNN. “This is a moment where we have to recognize the stakes.”

Democratic Rep. Debbie Dingell, a senior member of Michigan’s delegation, sought to downplay the conflict on NBC News’ “Meet the Press NOW,” saying Friday that she helped broker the event Sunday with Clyburn, who is close with Stevens.

“I think that, quite frankly, a lot of people are trying to create more controversy here, when I think the real discussion should be about what’s been happening in Washington and how we’ve got to stand up to what we’ve seen in the last two years,” Dingell said.

title: DOJ requests separating Alaska ballots that rank Dan J. Sullivan in Senate race
summary: The court filing, which cites the potential for “voter confusion,” did not spell out how segregating ballots would determine if a voter was confused.
story: The Trump administration asked a federal judge Friday to issue an order before Monday directing Alaska election officials to segregate all ballots ranking Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan as it continues its investigation into his candidacy.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward wrote in a court filing that state officials should “preserve and segregate all ballots ranking Daniel J. Sullivan for the purposes of investigating whether such ranking was the product of voter confusion, should such an investigation become necessary.”
“These modest precautionary measures will be impossible after Election Day, so there is good cause for expedited consideration,” he added.

The filing did not spell out a process for ballot review or explain how reviewing a ballot would show if a voter was confused about ranking the candidates. Alaska uses ranked choice voting, and there are four Senate candidates on the ballot.

The Trump administration has ramped up its efforts to inject itself into the Alaska election, which by statute is handled by state officials, after The New York Times reported this week that Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a former school teacher, to run against Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola has denied any involvement in Sullivan’s campaign.
At a campaign rally Friday evening, Peltola told supporters that she was “so deeply offended by these accusations about having any involvement with anyone else’s candidacy.”

“I want fewer candidates in the primary. I’m not out soliciting more competition,” Peltola said. “I know we can beat Dan Sullivan because every step of the way, even before I got in this race, my poll numbers were higher than his.”
Peltola urged her supporters to get out to vote and encourage those around them, warning that some voters may have been discouraged from voting for her due to the allegations.

“Our work isn’t done yet because we know that there are people out there who have not voted, who don’t have a plan to vote, who are so turned off by the smear campaigns and the garbage, and you know the accusations, the hollow accusations,” she said. “It’s really up to us to remind people why we need to get out and vote.”

Woodward, alongside Alaska’s top federal prosecutor, U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman, made three other filings Friday regarding the civil case the administration is pursuing in hopes of blocking Alaska from certifying the Senate election results.

In one filing, the prosecutors requested expedited sharing of “internal and external conversations” from Peltola’s campaign “regarding its efforts to recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.” Another filing asks for the “Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee’s internal and external conversations regarding its efforts recruit Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office.”
The DSCC has said it was “not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
An additional filing seeks a preliminary injunction in the case.
For Subscribers
Friday’s filings came shortly after Heyman held a press conference in Alaska, where he acknowledged a parallel criminal case.
For Subscribers
Asked what potential crimes prosecutors are looking into, Heyman declined to provide details.

“Because this is an ongoing investigative matter, we can’t discuss the specifics of those investigative steps, and who or may or may not be involved,” he said. “This protects the integrity of the investigation and it protects those who may be the subject or target of those investigations.”
Heyman cited the recent reporting from The New York Times, saying the “new information has resulted in a significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.”
The Justice Department issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as of Thursday, including subpoenas sent to the campaign offices of Peltola and of Dan J. Sullivan.
President Donald Trump, who has urged legal action against Peltola and the second Sullivan, said Friday morning that he doesn’t know whether Sen. Dan S. Sullivan can win with the current ballot.

“I will tell you, he’s a great senator, and what they tried to do, and he would, you know, he would have won,” Trump said in an interview with Kansas City talk radio host Pete Mundo. “I don’t know how he can win here because you’re splitting up the vote illegally. I think it’s a total fraud.”
Trump has said repeatedly that Dan J. Sullivan should be removed from the ballot.
In an interview with Fox News’ Sean Hannity earlier this week, Sen. Sullivan told supporters in Alaska how to mark up their ballot to best help him on Election Day.

“So rank me first, Sullivan, Dan S. Registered Republican incumbent. That’s what the ballot says,” he said. “Rank the other Republican second, [Gerald] Heikes. Rank, I hate to say it, Sean, but in our screwed-up system, you rank the fake guy third, and then of course blank. Do not rank Peltola. Now that is the screwed up system we have.”

title: Virginia and D.C. sue to stop proposed Trump arch
summary: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington.
story: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington.
The Trump administration has said it plans to begin construction of the arch next week, on Nov. 5.

“The construction of the Arch will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the District and Virginia,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb wrote in the lawsuit. “The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect.”

“Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added.
The attorneys general wrote that their request to block construction is urgent.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”

Jones and Schwalb added that they believe the administration is violating the Commemorative Works Act by bypassing specific congressional authorization and violating the Height of Buildings Act by constructing an arch that’s set to exceed 130 feet in height. They also alleged violations of the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Jones, in a statement Saturday, said, “Virginia takes immense pride in being home to Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place of generations of American heroes who gave their lives defending our nation. President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents. The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place. We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.”

Schwalb said, “Construction of the Arch is flagrantly illegal and will cause serious, immediate, and irreparable harm to the District and its residents. We’re filing this lawsuit now to protect DC’s unique interests and critical role in preserving the safeguards that keep our nation’s capital beautiful and safe,” in a separate statement.

Earlier this year, the National Capital Planning Commission, led by Trump appointees, approved initial plans for construction of the arch, one of President Donald Trump’s efforts to remake Washington in his own image during this term.
The commission is set to vote on final plans for the arch on Nov. 5.

In a statement, White House spokesperson David Ingle told NBC News on Saturday, “The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world. It will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today. President Trump will continue to honor our veterans and give the greatest Nation on earth — America — the glory it deserves.”
Ingle did not address a direct question from NBC News about the lawsuit filed Saturday.
Renderings obtained by NBC News in April show that the arch is slated to feature winged eagles, Lady Liberty and a line from the Pledge of Allegiance.

In September, the president said on Truth Social that the arch would also serve a national security function because it will be outfitted to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”
But final plans and renderings submitted to the NCPC do not include the military upgrades the president wrote about.

Trump has used national security as an argument in favor of other construction projects that have faced legal battles, like the new ballroom he is building at the White House. In addition to functioning as a gathering space for large events at the White House, the president has said, the addition will also house a military complex to be built underneath the ballroom.

“When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of,” the president wrote in an August Truth Social post after the Supreme Court allowed construction of the ballroom to continue, rebuffing a legal challenge from the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
The president has also drawn the ire of locals with a proposed plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, despite legal hurdles with that project.
In a post on Truth Social Thursday, Trump said why he favored renovating the golf course.

“East Potomac Golf Course is highly dangerous, dilapidated, and absolutely disgusting. Below are new photos of the deplorable conditions of the driving range building, including excrement in the stairwell. The gaping holes in the driving range’s ‘protective’ netting are highly hazardous. Golf balls soar through the holes at high speed and hit unexpecting Golfers — including a White House staffer who was, sadly, hit violently in the chest,” the president wrote.
He has promised to turn the course into “a World Class Championship Golf Course.”

title: U.S. set to deport Afghan refugees to Pakistan, despite risk they’ll be returned to Taliban
summary: The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
story: The Trump administration is preparing to deport dozens of Afghan immigrants and asylum-seekers to Pakistan on the first flight of its kind, a senior administration official told NBC News — a move critics say could put their lives at risk.
The proposed deportation flight, which has not been publicly announced, could take place as early as Monday, according to rights advocates and families of detainees.

Among those facing deportation are relatives of Afghans who worked with the U.S. military in its 20-year war against the Taliban, which is now back in power. The deportees could face severe repercussions should Pakistan return them to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan as is widely expected.

Afghans driven from their country by war and political instability have been welcomed by the U.S. for decades, including tens of thousands who fled the country following the chaotic withdrawal of U.S.-led forces in 2021. President Donald Trump halted admissions for Afghans and other refugees when he returned to office last year as part of a broader immigration crackdown.

His administration has deported thousands of people to countries that are not their own, many of them in Africa, in what immigration lawyers say is an effort to skirt international laws against returning asylum-seekers to the countries they fled from. The legality of these so-called third-country deportation agreements is set to be debated by the Supreme Court in December.

It is not clear what kind of formal agreement the U.S. may have with Pakistan, but the senior administration official said the U.S. charter flight would not be able to land there without the Pakistan government’s knowledge and approval. The deportation plan was earlier reported by Bloomberg and The New York Times.
Bloomberg cited a federal government official familiar with the plans as a source for its report, while The New York Times cited three U.S. officials.

Shawn VanDiver, president of the San Diego-based advocacy group AfghanEvac, said it had confirmed that in recent days, at least 80 Afghans have been moved to Louisiana from 34 other ICE facilities around the country, 19 of them without legal representation.
He said it was possible that there were hundreds of Afghans at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center, which has served as a hub for ICE detainees before their deportation from the U.S.

If the U.S. sends Afghan detainees to Pakistan, they are not likely to be there long. Pakistan, which has hosted millions of Afghan refugees for decades, launched a sweeping crackdown in 2023, pressuring hundreds of thousands of Afghans to leave the country and forcibly deporting others.

They are arriving to an Afghanistan battered by multiple humanitarian crises, including widespread malnutrition, as well as an ongoing military conflict with neighboring Pakistan and a dramatic rollback of women’s rights under the Taliban’s hard-line Islamic policies.
VanDiver said the Trump administration would most likely be aware that Afghans sent to Pakistan would be at high risk of being returned to Afghanistan.
“You don’t have to be that smart to figure out that they’re sending them to Pakistan so that Pakistan will finish the job,” he said.

Regardless of whether they worked with the U.S. military, VanDiver said, any Afghans flown from the U.S. would be viewed with suspicion by the Taliban and at risk of persecution, imprisonment or worse.
That does not appear to be a major concern for the White House, said the senior administration official, who declined to be identified because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
“The administration’s position is, ‘These individuals do not have status in our country, therefore we don’t really care what happens to them,’” the official said.

VanDiver and others say the Trump administration’s treatment of Afghan allies could also have long-term consequences for U.S. national security by discouraging people in other countries from working with U.S. forces in future conflicts.
Asked whether the Trump administration was concerned about that, the official said, “I don’t think they care.”

The White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.” ICE did not respond to a request for comment.
A State Department spokesperson said the agency had “no plans to announce.”

“We reaffirm our position that all countries must be able to manage their borders and immigration processes in a manner that ensures the safety, security and prosperity of their citizens,” the spokesperson said.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and its embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment.

The senior administration official said the Afghans on the flight could include people with deportation orders, people who were turned down for asylum and people whose temporary protected status was terminated by the Trump administration. Many of the Afghans facing deportation requested asylum after crossing into the U.S. from Mexico, VanDiver said, and some of their cases are still pending.
‘We just sat there and cried’

Charlotte, a U.S. citizen whose Afghan husband has been in ICE detention since early 2025, said he had been moved to the Louisiana facility from Pennsylvania this month and told he would be deported in early November. She declined to be identified by her full name out of concern that her husband could be targeted by the Taliban.

Charlotte said she and her husband, whose asylum case has been pending for nine years, were visiting family in Maryland last year when he accidentally crossed into West Virginia and was pulled over. Though he was carrying his valid Illinois driver’s license, he did not have his work permit with him.

“When he was pulled over,” she said, “the sheriff actually said, ‘I’m an ICE agent. You’re going to immigration custody. I don’t care if the charges are dismissed, or I don’t care if you have a five-year work permit or Social Security card. I don’t care if you’re legal. Trump’s administration just took over — you’re going directly to immigration custody.’”

Charlotte sold their home in Illinois and moved to Maryland with their son, now 6, in order to be able to visit her husband at the ICE facility where he was held in Pennsylvania, about 100 miles away.
“I lost my nice house, our car, we left everything behind,” she said.
Over the next 20 months, when she took her son to see his father at the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, they were always separated by plexiglass.
“They never let him hug him one time,” Charlotte said. “We just sat there and cried every time.”
But at least they knew where he was and that he was OK, she said. Now that he’s in Louisiana, she said, “we can’t even visit or even say goodbye, he’s over 1,200 miles away.”

With her husband potentially being sent to Pakistan or Afghanistan — a country he hasn’t been to since 2016 — the uncertainty is even greater; Charlotte said he is growing his beard to comply with the Taliban’s strict rules for men’s facial hair.
“I’m just terrified that he’s not going to be safe,” she said, “or he’s going to be held in the jail and there’s nothing I can do.”
Charlotte said she believed her husband had been targeted for deportation because of a past conviction for a nonviolent crime that has since been resolved.
“I still don’t think this should end our entire life, for a child not to see his dad,” she said.
“He’s completely devastated and traumatized,” she said of their son. “He wants to fight. He wants to go protest. He wants to speak to Donald Trump. He basically knows so much more than he should.”

The preparations for the deportation flight come nearly a year after a shooting in Washington that killed one National Guard member and seriously injured another. The suspect, an Afghan national who served alongside U.S. troops in Afghanistan and was evacuated to the U.S. in 2021, had been granted asylum by the Trump administration. Immigration restrictions were tightened after the shooting.

VanDiver said the Trump administration may also be using the Pakistan flight as a test case for Camp As Sayliyah, a U.S.-run camp in Qatar where more than 1,000 Afghans who had been slated for resettlement in the U.S. have been stranded since Trump returned to office last year.

Asked about VanDiver’s claim, the White House referred a request for comment to the Department of Homeland Security, whose spokesperson again said the agency could not confirm removal operations “for operational security reasons.”

According to AfghanEvac, the camp was housing 287 men, 319 women and 433 children as of July. Most of them have been approved for U.S. resettlement after extensive vetting, and many of the adults worked alongside U.S. forces in Afghanistan.
The group at Camp As Sayliyah also includes 150 relatives of U.S. military service members, AfghanEvac said.
Afghan refugees in Qatar protest over travel suspension

The State Department said earlier this year that everyone would be removed from the camp by March 31, a deadline that was later extended to Sept. 30. In September, the Trump administration delayed its closure by another nine months, The Associated Press reported.
Earlier this year, the administration  considered sending the Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah to the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which is experiencing the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

In a statement on Friday, AfghanEvac accused the Trump administration of planning the Afghan deportation flight as the country is distracted by next week’s midterm election, “hoping no one is watching.”
“The government won’t say where these flights land, because it knows what happens to the people on them when they do,” the group said. “A government confident in what it is doing does not hide it.”

title: Outcry prompts ‘Call of Duty’ to cut Seoul tragedy footage
summary: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.
story: American video game publisher Activision said Friday that it was removing controversial footage from its newly released “Call of Duty” game after an outcry in South Korea over the inclusion of real-life footage from a deadly 2022 Halloween crowd crush in Seoul.

Last week’s global release of “Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4” came days before the Oct. 29 anniversary of the disaster in the South Korean capital’s nightlife district of Itaewon, where a crowd of tens of thousands of partygoers surged beyond control in a narrow alley, causing nearly 160 deaths.

The game, which takes place amid a fictional North Korean invasion of the South, features about 10 seconds of heavily edited footage of the tragedy to illustrate what the aftermath of a Pyongyang attack might look like, though it does not refer to the Itaewon crowd crush directly.

Groups representing families of the crowd crush victims had demanded that the footage be removed, saying it was appalling that the game had directly reproduced actual scenes of people performing CPR “while victims lay on the cold streets amid chaos and desperation.”

“If the game developer has even the slightest sense of respect and empathy for the victims of the Itaewon disaster, it should promptly take corrective action,” the Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association and Itaewon Disaster Citizens’ Countermeasures Committee said in a joint statement Friday.
The California-based game publisher, Activision, apologized in a statement and said the footage would be completely removed through a game update scheduled for release Nov. 12.

“This game is a fictional work created to provide a realistic and immersive experience,” the company said, according to the South Korean public broadcaster MBC. “In using actual news footage in the game, we never intended to evoke any tragic incident, including the Itaewon disaster, or to trivialize the suffering associated with such tragedies.”

The controversy came as grieving families are still waiting for answers about authorities’ failure to prevent the disaster four years ago. Nearly two dozen officials have been charged in the investigation, which is still underway, while three former police officers have been jailed.
On Thursday, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung vowed that his government would “uncover the truth.”

title: Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen: A friendship that surpassed the stage and screen
summary: “He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” McKellen said in a statement on Stewart’s death.
story: To many, Patrick Stewart and Ian McKellen represent a formidable mutant rivalry in the “X-Men” films or two of theater’s pre-eminent Shakespearean actors, but behind the curtain the pair shared something even more enduring: a friendship that spanned decades.

Stewart died Wednesday at age 86 following a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. McKellen, Stewart’s artistic brother-in-arms, remembered him Thursday as “the most respected and beloved actor of his generation on either side of the Atlantic.”
“He wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love,” McKellen said in a statement on social media.
The pair — about a year apart in age — met at England’s esteemed Royal Shakespeare Company, with Stewart joining in 1966 and McKellen in 1974.

title: Virginia and D.C. sue to stop proposed Trump arch
summary: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington.
story: Virginia and the District of Columbia filed a lawsuit in federal court Saturday in a last-ditch effort to stop the construction of the triumphal arch planned for Memorial Circle in Washington.
The Trump administration has said it plans to begin construction of the arch next week, on Nov. 5.

“The construction of the Arch will inflict immediate and irreparable harm on the District and Virginia,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones and D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb wrote in the lawsuit. “The Arch is slated to be built on a busy traffic circle that abuts the border between the jurisdictions, at the center of a historic viewshed, in a river whose environment the District has a statutory responsibility to protect.”

“Both the construction of the Arch and the completed monument will disrupt the operations of both jurisdictions, impair their ability to carry out their responsibilities under federal and local law, and require the expenditure of substantial resources to mitigate and address those impacts,” they added.
The attorneys general wrote that their request to block construction is urgent.

“It is entirely foreseeable that, once construction begins, Defendants will argue, as they have done in other cases, that an order halting construction would irreparably harm the federal government, pose security risks, and impermissibly alter the status quo they have unilaterally created,” they said. “The Court should not allow this cynical gambit to succeed.”

Jones and Schwalb added that they believe the administration is violating the Commemorative Works Act by bypassing specific congressional authorization and violating the Height of Buildings Act by constructing an arch that’s set to exceed 130 feet in height. They also alleged violations of the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Jones, in a statement Saturday, said, “Virginia takes immense pride in being home to Arlington National Cemetery, the final resting place of generations of American heroes who gave their lives defending our nation. President Trump’s illegal vanity project is an affront to this hallowed ground and the extraordinary sacrifices it represents. The Commonwealth has a solemn duty and a profound interest in preserving the dignity of this sacred place. We will vigorously litigate to protect its sanctity and honor the legacy of those who made the ultimate sacrifice.”

Schwalb said, “Construction of the Arch is flagrantly illegal and will cause serious, immediate, and irreparable harm to the District and its residents. We’re filing this lawsuit now to protect DC’s unique interests and critical role in preserving the safeguards that keep our nation’s capital beautiful and safe,” in a separate statement.

Earlier this year, the National Capital Planning Commission, led by Trump appointees, approved initial plans for construction of the arch, one of President Donald Trump’s efforts to remake Washington in his own image during this term.
The commission is set to vote on final plans for the arch on Nov. 5.

In a statement, White House spokesperson David Ingle told NBC News on Saturday, “The Triumphal Arch in Memorial Circle is going to be one of the most iconic landmarks not only in Washington, D.C., but throughout the world. It will serve as a gateway to Arlington National Cemetery for veterans, the families of the fallen, and all Americans alike, serving as a visual reminder of the noble sacrifices borne by so many American heroes throughout our 250 year history so we can enjoy our freedoms today. President Trump will continue to honor our veterans and give the greatest Nation on earth — America — the glory it deserves.”
Ingle did not address a direct question from NBC News about the lawsuit filed Saturday.
Renderings obtained by NBC News in April show that the arch is slated to feature winged eagles, Lady Liberty and a line from the Pledge of Allegiance.

In September, the president said on Truth Social that the arch would also serve a national security function because it will be outfitted to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.”
But final plans and renderings submitted to the NCPC do not include the military upgrades the president wrote about.

Trump has used national security as an argument in favor of other construction projects that have faced legal battles, like the new ballroom he is building at the White House. In addition to functioning as a gathering space for large events at the White House, the president has said, the addition will also house a military complex to be built underneath the ballroom.

“When completed in the Summer of 2028, the magnificent Ballroom and Military Complex will be something that the entire Country is very proud of,” the president wrote in an August Truth Social post after the Supreme Court allowed construction of the ballroom to continue, rebuffing a legal challenge from the National Trust for Historic Preservation.
The president has also drawn the ire of locals with a proposed plan to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links course in Washington, despite legal hurdles with that project.
In a post on Truth Social Thursday, Trump said why he favored renovating the golf course.

“East Potomac Golf Course is highly dangerous, dilapidated, and absolutely disgusting. Below are new photos of the deplorable conditions of the driving range building, including excrement in the stairwell. The gaping holes in the driving range’s ‘protective’ netting are highly hazardous. Golf balls soar through the holes at high speed and hit unexpecting Golfers — including a White House staffer who was, sadly, hit violently in the chest,” the president wrote.
He has promised to turn the course into “a World Class Championship Golf Course.”

title: ‘There is and was no other gun’: Mangione team argues double jeopardy bars state murder trial
summary: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione on Friday continued to push for the dismissal of his state court murder and weapons case, arguing that his guilty plea to federal stalking charges two months ago bars a separate trial.
story: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione on Friday continued to push for the dismissal of his state court murder and weapons case, arguing that his guilty plea to federal stalking charges two months ago bars a separate trial.

Mangione, the admitted killer of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court in August. The plea set off a protracted battle over the future of the separate state court prosecution for second-degree murder and weapons possession.
His state trial, slated to start Sept. 18, was postponed indefinitely so the court could take up whether double jeopardy applies. A decision on the dismissal motion is expected Dec. 10.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s office maintains the state case can legally proceed because its charges differ substantially from those in the federal court case, which centered on stalking and crossing state lines and cyberstalking through use of interstate facilities, each resulting in death. The state indictment is a classic murder case, prosecutors argued, and murder is generally not defined by federal statutes.

Mangione’s team countered Friday that the charges in the two cases are materially the same. They told New York Supreme Court Justice Gregory Carro that the federal offenses Mangione pleaded guilty to, interstate stalking resulting in death, involves overlapping legal elements.

“Here, Mangione was charged by the federal grand jury with possession of the same firearm at the same time and at the same location as the People are charging here,” Mangione’s attorneys Karen Friedman Agnifilo, Marc Agnifilo and Jacob Kaplan argued in a letter to the court. “There is and was no other gun.”
Mangione faces a potential life sentence when he returns to federal court on Dec. 18. If the state case goes forward, he faces a maximum of 25 years to life in prison.

State prosecutors must overcome New York state double jeopardy law, which requires distinct “evils” between the two cases for the state matter to proceed, legal experts told NBC News. Mangione’s lawyers say the harms addressed in the state and federal cases are one and the same.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
“There is no basis to find such a difference, much less a sufficiently great difference as to fit within the narrow statutory exception,” they wrote in their most recent submission.
Earlier this month, Bragg’s office pointed to a double jeopardy exception that could give it a path forward if Carro finds that there were unique “elements” charged in the state case.

Lead prosecutor Joel Seidemann argued in a filing that earlier litigation in the federal proceeding shows the state charges are significantly different. U.S. District Judge Margaret Garnett determined that the stalking could not be considered violent under the law, a ruling that led to the dismissal of two counts that would have made Mangione eligible for the death penalty. The Justice Department had announced its intention to seek capital punishment before Garnett’s ruling.

Mangione admitted to using a 3D-printed firearm to shoot Thompson outside of the midtown Hilton early on Dec. 4, 2024, as the executive walked from his nearby hotel to his company’s investor conference.

The gunman ambushed Thompson, a Minnesota father of two, firing several times before fleeing and setting off an interstate manhunt. He was arrested five days later in Altoona, Pennsylvania, after patrons recognized him at a McDonald’s from photos circulated by the NYPD.

The Ivy League-educated Maryland native, who comes from a prominent family, said in federal court that he was motivated by a personal grievance with the health insurance industry. Investigators have said he was never a UnitedHealthcare policyholder.
His attorneys have argued that case’s notoriety led to overprosecution, with state and federal officials seeking credit by pursuing separate cases for the same event.

title: Nancy Guthrie task force meets with Florida DNA scientists as case nears 9-month mark
summary: Authorities investigating the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie said Friday that members of a task force dedicated to solving the case have traveled to Florida to push forward on DNA analysis.
story: Authorities investigating the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie said Friday that members of a task force dedicated to solving the case have traveled to Florida to push forward on DNA analysis.
The Pima County Sheriff’s Department said in a statement on X that the task force “traveled to Florida to meet with lab scientists to see what more could be done to advance the case.”
“A number of ideas were discussed, and we continue to work with all of our partners to solve this case,” the department said as the case approaches its ninth month.
Guthrie, 84, is the mother of “TODAY” co-host Savannah Guthrie. She vanished from her home in Tucson, Arizona, in February in what federal authorities have described as a kidnapping-for-ransom case.

Updates have been few in recent months in a case that has gripped the nation for much of the year. In late July, federal law enforcement officials announced that hair found during the investigation was not linked to any potential suspects.

Savannah Guthrie has continued to appeal for the public’s help. Sharing an image of her mother on Instagram in August, she wrote: “There is a hole inside us that can never be filled. There is an ache that cannot be softened.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

“And there is a determination in us that cannot be quenched - to find out what happened to her, so that we can give her the dignity of a proper goodbye - a celebration of her remarkable life that she so deserves,” she added.
The sheriff’s office stressed that “no tip is too small.”
“Even the smallest piece of information could be critical to this investigation,” the department said. “If you know something, please call 88-CRIME or 1-800-CALL-FBI.”

title: ‘Looks like Mars’: Toxic smog from Indonesia wildfires sparks health crisis, protests
summary: Wildfires in Indonesia are blanketing the country and other southeast Asian nations in toxic smog, prompting widespread protests.
story: Almost every day for months, Indonesian schoolteacher Natanael Undas has gazed up at smoke-filled skies in apocalyptic shades of yellow and orange.

“It looks like Mars, like we’re living on another planet,” said Undas, whose home in central Kalimantan province is at the heart of devastating wildfires generating toxic smog in Indonesia and across Southeast Asia.

Although his family keeps the windows shut at all times, the noxious smoke penetrates the house anyway, sending Undas’ 2-year-old daughter into constant sneezing fits amid a spike in respiratory illnesses in haze-affected regions.

Wildfires are nothing new in Indonesia, whose forests and peatlands are set ablaze each year as family and commercial farms clear land using traditional “slash and burn” methods. But the fires this year are far worse than usual, said Undas, who has been documenting Indonesia’s air quality on Instagram since 2014, as heat and drought aggravated by a “super” El Niño weather pattern make this the country’s worst fire season in over a decade.
Wildfire smoke covers Indonesia skies in orange haze

The unrelenting haze from the fires has affected millions of people in the region since they started in July, closing schools in multiple countries and spurring arguments about who is to blame. Indonesian protesters have accused their government of insufficient action, while other countries are threatening prosecution.

On Wednesday, hundreds of Indonesian students and members of civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against the policies of President Prabowo Subianto, including his resistance to declaring the fires a national disaster.
“We want transparent and independent investigations about these wildfires,” protester Natasha Ruvantina told NBC News. “And also, we want a long-term prevention strategy.”
The Indonesian government said in a statement Wednesday that it recognized the students’ concerns, adding that it was prosecuting companies linked to the fires and sending aid to affected provinces.

The fires have also caused frustration in countries such as neighboring Singapore, where air pollution this month reached its highest level since 2015, when Indonesian wildfires were also intensified by El Niño. Singapore officials have threatened to prosecute companies seen as responsible for the devastation, and on Tuesday the foreign ministers of Singapore and Indonesia said they were considering a joint task force to combat illegal land burning.
“We will use the full force of the law to make sure those who profit from fire must answer for the fires,” Indonesian Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir said.
Indonesia’s neighbors and other countries have been accused of contributing to the problem.

In a report this month, the Indonesian environmental organization Walhi named 66 companies with links to Singapore and 27 companies with links to Malaysia that it said were associated with fire hot spots. On Thursday, the Indonesian government said police had identified 20 corporations suspected of being involved in the fires, including four from Singapore, Malaysia and South Korea.

title: U.K. PM open to slave trade apology but rules out financial reparations
summary: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to am apology for his country’s role in the slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations.
story: LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that he is open to a formal apology for his country’s role in the trans-Atlantic slave trade, but ruled out financial reparations as King Charles III continued his tour of the Caribbean.
Burnham’s comments show a marked shift in stance for the U.K.,  which has consistently rejected demands for either an apology or reparations.
They came as he is due to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda next week. Charles, as head of the “family of nations,” will preside over the event.

“We are offering a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade,” Burnham wrote in an op-ed in The Guardian newspaper published Friday. “Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process, and I am open to them.”
But Burnham ruled out financial reparations, saying the British people of today who “played no personal part” in the slave trade could not be held liable.

The trans-Atlantic trade in enslaved people was central to European colonialism and the growth of the British Empire, as millions of Africans were trafficked to the Americas to grow and harvest cash crops, while being subjected to violence, torture, sexual abuse and the denial of basic human rights.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, said on X that he welcomed the prime minister’s openness to a formal apology.
Jamaica’s prime minister, Andrew Holness, also posted on X, writing: “Open-minded dialogue is always a good place to start addressing difficult issues.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
Jamaica recently took its case for reparations to Charles, and the case has since been referred to the United Kingdom’s highest court of appeal.
Caribbean nations had urged Britain to acknowledge its role in the slave trade ahead of Charles’ visit to the Bahamas and Guyana last week.
Charles last week visited Clifford Park, where in 1973 he granted the Bahamas independence after 300 years of British rule.
Members of the Bahamas’ Rastafarian community and others lined a nearby road to protest.
“Pay us what you owe us!” one woman cried out. “I stand in memory of the horrors and the atrocities committed against Black people.”

In his first public remarks on the island nation, Charles said: “It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present.”

title: Democrats in key battlegrounds throw Joe Biden under the bus on the border
summary: Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability.
story: WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates in 2026 battleground races are directly criticizing Joe Biden’s handling of border security when he was president, seeking to neutralize a political vulnerability and signaling a new path for the party on the thorny issue.
Candidates are throwing the ex-president under the bus on border policy in key states that will decide control of the Senate and some battleground House races across the country.

“I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border,” Texas’ Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico says in a recent ad airing in the closing stretch of his neck-and-neck race against Republican Ken Paxton. He also criticized Biden in July for having “failed us on our southern border” as he rolled out his own border security plan.
He’s not alone.
In Kansas, a longtime Republican stronghold, Democrat Adam Hamilton criticized Biden in a recent debate with Republican Sen. Roger Marshall.

“I want to be crystal clear, first of all: Immigration at the border under Biden was a disaster. That is how we ended up where we are today,” he said. “Second, what we did in response to that has been a disaster for people across the state of Kansas.”

Hamilton, like other Democrats in areas that voted for Trump in 2024, paired their critique of Biden with criticism that the current president has gone too far on enforcement. Polls show many Americans have soured on Trump’s handling of the issue in the wake of immigration officers fatally shooting two Americans in Minnesota and one in Maine this year.

Still, the comments reflect a recognition that the issue of border security remains a vulnerability for Democrats as Republicans continue to accuse them of promoting “open borders” in a bid to mobilize their base and win swing voters. Biden’s ratings on the issue tanked amid a surge in migrant crossings during his presidency, which Trump successfully weaponized in 2024.

Entering office in 2021, Biden inherited a Covid-era migration surge that intensified in the United States after he made good on his pledge to roll back Trump-era policies and restrictions, allowing more asylum-seekers to stay in the country as their cases were being considered. The collective result was a huge spike in border crossings that became associated with the Biden presidency and brought down his approval ratings.

Even as Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 38%, polls show border security continues to be one of his highest-polling issues, although that number has fallen from the highs of his early second term.
“The Biden administration failed at the border,” Democratic House candidate Paige Cognetti said at a debate Thursday night.

Cognetti, who is vying to unseat Rep. Rob Bresnahan, R-Pa., in a highly competitive Scranton-area working-class district, later added: “The Biden administration did fail. We need to make sure that the border is secure. It’s a good thing that it is. We do need to make sure that the pathways to citizenship are there.”
In South Carolina, Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews said in a debate, “Democrats have failed on the border.”
For Subscribers
Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said it’s “very smart” for candidates to distance themselves from Biden and that “there’s nobody contesting that interpretation” that he blundered on the border.
For Subscribers

In the 2024 election, “immigration was playing a major, major role, and it was energizing Republicans. And it was the best issue among swing voters for Republicans,” she said. “ICE has gone too far, and that has backfired now.”
She added that the “best messaging” on immigration is “some control for the border plus a humanitarian process for immigration.”
Iowa’s Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek traveled more than 800 miles to Laredo, Texas, to film an ad at the border touting his support for tougher enforcement.

“I came to the border to meet firsthand with the people who work to keep it secure. What happens down here affects us up in Iowa, so we’ve got to address it,” Turek says in the ad. “I voted with Republicans to allow law enforcement to arrest and deport criminals.”
Weeks earlier, he released another ad speaking to Iowans and vowing that he would “work with anyone” to fix immigration — “including President Trump, to secure the border.”
Closer to the border, Democrat Johnny Garcia is trying to win Texas’ redrawn and Republican-friendly 35th Congressional District against GOP nominee Carlos De La Cruz.

Garcia criticized Trump’s ICE raids as detrimental to the economy. But at a recent forum, he also blamed Biden’s policies for failures at the border and referred to a fatal smuggling conspiracy in 2022 that led to the deaths of dozens of people.

“We’ve also gotten to see, unfortunately, how Biden got it wrong on the border,” Garcia said. “I’ll admit that every single day. We got to see one of the largest migrant fatalities in this district in south San Antonio, with 53 migrants that were locked in a trailer.”
“So we can’t afford to just turn a blind eye to our border,” he added. “But at the same time, we can’t turn a blind eye to what we’re seeing happening on our streets.”

title: 19+ products we tried and gave our stamp of approval in October
summary: October is when the real holiday shopping starts, and this month we tried new barrel jeans, Jellycat plushies, hairstyling appliances, kitchen accessories and more.
story: While fall technically starts at the end of September it often doesn’t actually feel like it until we’re well into October. Here at NBC Selected, the true signs of fall are easy to spot, not just by a breeze in the air or the crunch of leaves, but by how many seasonal sales take place.

Earlier this month, we wrote about hundreds of deals during fall Prime Day, and even shopped a bunch of them ourselves. Over the course of several sale events — including Target Circle Deal Days and Walmart’s major fall sale — we wrote about, bought and tested products from categories like footwear, beauty, apparel, skin care, appliances and more.
Below, my colleagues and I recommend the products we tested and truly believe are worth sharing. Some of the brands we loved this month include Adidas, Jellycat, Anyday and Bombas.
The best products we tried in October 2026
All of the products below were either sent courtesy of the brand for testing or items that we bought ourselves.
Cory Fernandez, commerce editor
Adidas Handball Spezial Shoes

These shoes have been the ultimate casual sneaker for a few years now and every once in a while I’m inspired to shop for a new color. I recently bought a pair in a brown and white shade that would be perfect to pair with fall fits, including dark-wash jeans and jewel-toned sweaters. They’re comfortable and provide a small amount of arch support, though they’re definitely better suited for weekday commutes rather than long-distance walks. I love that they come with an extra pair of shoe laces and that the laces are long, which makes them easy to double knot. Plus, I enjoy the suede appearance over the leather — something about it feels more cozy and appropriate for this season.
Wine Country Grand Gourmet Gift Basket

Ahead of the holidays and fall hosting season, this brand sent me its marvelous gift basket, which I think is the ultimate gift for a host or anyone you want to say thank you to. title: Your dandruff shampoo might help with breakouts, but there’s a catch
summary: Anti-dandruff shampoos only treat one type of blemish: fungal acne. Shop the best dandruff shampoos from Head & Shoulders, Nizoral and Vanicream to treat fungal acne.
story: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends (and questions) on our timelines, like whether you need pet laundry detergent to clean your dog’s things.

Sometimes, the most surprisingly effective products for your skin aren’t found in the skin care aisle. Dandruff shampoos have become a viral hack for treating acne-like breakouts, with people using them as both face and body washes. But can swapping your face wash for a bottle of Head and Shoulders actually help your skin?

While certain ingredients in dandruff shampoos may help with fungal acne, they won’t necessarily work for every type of blemish. I asked dermatologists to explain why dandruff shampoos may work for acne and when you’re better off sticking with traditional acne treatments.

Why are people using dandruff shampoo for acne?

The idea took off on social media because there are actual results: “Many people have been fighting stubborn, itchy bumps for months with acne products that never worked, then try an inexpensive drugstore shampoo and see clearer skin within a couple of weeks,” says Dr. Mona Foad, board-certified dermatologist and founder of MONA Dermatology. “That kind of before-and-after is made for TikTok. The bottom line is that dandruff shampoo is a fantastic tool for fungal acne, but it is not an acne treatment.”
Can dandruff shampoo actually treat acne?

Yes, anti-dandruff shampoo can treat acne, but only one specific type of breakout: fungal acne. “Fungal acne, which we call Malassezia folliculitis, isn’t true acne at all,” says Foad. It’s caused by an overgrowth of the same yeast (Malassezia yeast) responsible for dandruff, which is exactly why dandruff shampoo works on it. The overgrowth of yeast causes inflammation and infection around the hair follicle on your scalp, forehead, chest and back, causing small red bumps that are usually mistaken for regular acne, says Katharine Perry, board-certified nurse practitioner at MONA Dermatology.

But it doesn’t treat traditional acne (called acne vulgaris), which is driven by oil, clogged pores, bacteria and inflammation. That means someone with hormonal acne, blackheads or deep, painful pimples probably won’t see the same results, says Dr. Ariel Ostad, New York City-based dermatologist and reconstructive surgeon. “Many people actually have both types of acne at the same time, which is why some see partial improvement and assume the shampoo is working,” says Foad. “The bottom line is that if you have blackheads, whiteheads or deep, painful cysts, you need a true acne treatment.”

Even for fungal acne, it controls the problem rather than cures it. “Malassezia yeast lives on everyone’s skin naturally, so the goal is to keep it in balance, not eliminate it,” says Foad. If you stop treating fungal acne entirely, it usually comes back, especially in hot, humid weather. So, think of dandruff shampoo as a management tool with ongoing maintenance, rather than a one-time cure, says Foad.
Best dandruff shampoos for fungal acne
Nizoral Anti-Dandruff Shampoo

This shampoo, which has 1% ketoconazole, is one Foad regularly recommends to her patients dealing with fungal acne on their face or body. “The key is using it as a short-contact mask, not a regular cleanser,” she says. “Lather it onto the affected areas, leave it on for three to five minutes, then rinse thoroughly. That contact time is what allows the active ingredient to work.” For the face, Foad recommends keeping it targeted and limiting it to a few times a week to avoid dryness.

This is a classic for a reason: Head and Shoulders’ anti-dandruff shampoo lathers well, smells good and has zinc pyrithione, which has both antifungal and antibacterial properties, says Foad. It’s also under $10, making it one of the most affordable options on this list. The shampoo combats dryness, relieves irritation and itchiness, reduces flakes and redness, and controls oil.
What ingredients in anti-dandruff shampoo can help treat fungal acne?
Not every dandruff shampoo has the same active ingredients, so the results can vary from product to product. The ingredients commonly in anti-dandruff shampoos that help treat fungal acne are:

Ketoconazole: This is one of the most well-known ingredients in anti-dandruff shampoo. It’s an antifungal medication that helps control the yeast associated with dandruff and certain conditions that look like acne. “Ketoconazole has some of the strongest evidence for treating fungal acne,” says Ostad. Selenium sulfide: This reduces yeast growth and is sometimes used for fungal skin conditions, like seborrheic dermatitis and scalp ringworm. However, it has a strong odor and can discolor metal jewelry, so remove rings and necklaces first, says Foad.Zinc pyrithione: Like the others, this ingredient helps reduce yeast, inflammation and excess oils. While zinc pyrithione has mild antibacterial properties, it isn’t a substitute for benzoyl peroxide or a retinoid to treat traditional acne.

What about salicylic acid in dandruff shampoos?

Some anti-dandruff shampoos have salicylic acid, which can help treat scalp conditions like dandruff, dermatitis, scalp acne and psoriasis, experts say. It’s also a common acne-fighting ingredient that exfoliates dead skin and helps clear clogged pores. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean a dandruff shampoo with salicylic acid should double as an acne cleanser: Shampoos are formulated for the scalp and may have fragrance, strong surfactants and conditioning agents that can irritate acne-prone skin or even clog pores, says Foad. “Some also contain 3% salicylic acid, which is higher than the 0.5% to 2% range used in over-the-counter acne products and can be too harsh for the face,” she says. Using a medicated shampoo is also not a good idea if you’re using other acne products: “That’s when we start to see dryness, stinging and a really unhappy skin barrier,” says Perry.

For body acne, a salicylic acid shampoo can work in a pinch on tougher areas like the back and chest, but a product designed for your skin will always be the better option, says Foad. In other words, a salicylic acid shampoo isn’t usually interchangeable with a salicylic acid acne cleanser or body wash just because they share the same active ingredient.
How can you tell fungal acne from regular acne?

Fungal acne and regular breakouts look very similar, but their causes are very different. In fact, fungal acne isn’t even acne at all. “Fungal acne happens when yeast that naturally lives on the skin grows excessively and causes inflammation around hair follicles,” says Ostad. That can create small, itchy bumps that look similar to pimples, especially on the forehead, chest and back.

Traditional acne, on the other hand, is driven by oil, clogged pores, bacteria and inflammation. It’s not usually itchy like fungal acne is, and they’ll sometimes appear as whiteheads and blackheads (while fungal acne does not).
Can you use dandruff shampoo as a face wash?

Yes, and the dermatologists I spoke to actually recommend it often. “When someone has a confirmed diagnosis of fungal acne on the face, chest or back, a medicated shampoo is one of the most effective and affordable treatments available,” says Foad. It’s not limited to fungal acne either; for example, someone with seborrheic dermatitis may experience redness, flaking and irritation around the nose, eyebrows or hairline. Because yeast can contribute to this condition, an antifungal shampoo may help reduce those symptoms, says Ostad.
Frequently asked questions

The biggest difference is that anti-dandruff shampoos target yeast, while traditional acne treatments address the causes of regular acne, says Ostad. Benzoyl peroxide, for example, helps reduce acne-causing bacteria, while salicylic acid exfoliates inside the pore to clear blackheads and whiteheads. Adapalene and prescription retinoids help prevent pores from becoming blocked and can improve breakouts over time. “If someone has traditional acne, these treatments have much stronger evidence than anti-dandruff shampoo, but someone with fungal acne may benefit more from an antifungal treatment,” says Ostad.

Fungal acne usually responds quickly, which is part of what makes this approach so satisfying. You’ll likely notice less itching and fewer new bumps within one to two weeks of consistent use, with significant clearing by around four weeks, says Foad. “If you’re not seeing any improvement after two to four weeks, that’s a strong sign the bumps aren’t fungal, or that you need a prescription-strength treatment,” she says.

Since the scalp tends to be tougher than facial skin, the most common side effects are dryness, redness and irritation, especially if you use a dandruff shampoo daily or with other actives like retinoids or exfoliating acids, says Foad. Fragrances and harsh surfactants in some formulas can also trigger allergic reactions or contact dermatitis.
The biggest risk, though, is misdiagnosis. “Using dandruff shampoo on something that isn’t fungal acne can delay the treatment you actually need,” says Foad.

If you’re noticing excessive dryness or your skin starts stinging when washing it, it may be time to back off from the dandruff shampoo, says Perry. You can also reduce how often you use it, so you can switch to once a day or once every other day.
